events.title: Traditional foundation of Rome
events.summary: Varro's foundation date for Rome, 21 April (the Parilia) 753 BC, fixed by Atticus and Varro in the late Republic; Fabius Pictor gave 748/747, Cincius Alimentus 729/728, Timaeus 814/813 (the same year as Carthage).
events.detail: The date is a learned construct: Varro's friend L. Tarutius of Firmum even cast Rome's horoscope. Archaeology shows Iron Age huts on the Palatine from the 9th-8th centuries, a fortification wall on the north slope of the Palatine (Carandini's excavations, dated c. 730-720 by him, contested), and the first beaten-earth Forum floors around 700-650. The synoecism of village communities into a single city is a process of the 8th-7th centuries, not an act. Romulus, the twins, the asylum and the Sabine women are etiological legend.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 70-80
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 78-93
Carandini, Rome: Day One (2011)
events.debate: Carandini reads the Palatine wall as evidence of a real founding act c. 750; most (Cornell, Forsythe, Smith) prefer gradual state formation.

events.title: Numa Pompilius and the religious calendar
events.summary: Tradition credits the Sabine king Numa (r. 715-673) with the pontiffs, flamines, Vestals, Salii, the twelve-month calendar adding January and February, and the temple of Janus whose closed doors signified peace.
events.detail: The story that Numa was a pupil of Pythagoras was already rejected on chronological grounds by Cicero and Livy (Pythagoras flourished c. 530). In 181 BC 'books of Numa' were allegedly found in a chest on the Janiculum and burned by the praetor Q. Petillius as subversive. The Regia in the Forum, traditionally Numa's house, has building phases from the late 7th century.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 118-119

events.title: Destruction of Alba Longa under Tullus Hostilius
events.summary: Traditionally under Tullus Hostilius (r. 673-642) Rome fought Alba Longa, the duel of the Horatii and Curiatii decided the war, and the Alban dictator Mettius Fufetius was torn apart by chariots for treachery; Alba was razed and its people moved to the Caelian.
events.detail: The story explains Rome's later presidency of the Latin festival on the Alban Mount (feriae Latinae) and the presence of Alban gentes (Julii, Servilii, Quinctii, Cloelii) among the patricians. No urban site of Alba Longa has been securely identified; scattered Iron Age cemeteries around Lake Albano suggest villages rather than a city.

events.title: Draining and paving of the Forum; the Cloaca Maxima
events.summary: Tradition assigns the drainage of the Forum valley by the Cloaca Maxima to the Tarquins; archaeology shows the Forum was landfilled and given its first pebble pavement c. 625-600 BC, the moment Rome becomes recognisably urban.
events.detail: The Cloaca was originally an open channel; the surviving vaulted conduit in peperino and travertine is of the late Republic. The Comitium, Regia and the Volcanal/Lapis Niger area also show 6th-century monumental phases; the Lapis Niger cippus carries one of the oldest Latin inscriptions (mid-6th century) naming a 'recei' (rex).
scholarship: Holloway, The Archaeology of Early Rome and Latium (1994)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 102

events.title: Reforms attributed to Servius Tullius
events.summary: Servius Tullius (trad. r. 578-535) is credited with the first census, the five property classes and 193 centuries of the comitia centuriata, the four urban tribes, and a city wall; the census allegedly counted 80,000 men (Fabius Pictor in Livy).
events.detail: The full 193-century system with its bronze-asses ratings is anachronistic for the 6th century (coinage begins c. 300); Cornell and Forsythe accept a simpler early classis/infra classem division tied to hoplite equipment. Claudius' Lyons speech (ILS 212) preserves an Etruscan tradition identifying Servius with Mastarna, companion of Caelius Vibenna, whom the François Tomb paintings at Vulci show freeing Caile Vipinas and killing a 'Cneve Tarchunies Rumach' (Gnaeus Tarquinius of Rome). The so-called Servian wall of cappellaccio tufa may be 6th century in parts, but the surviving circuit is of 378 BC.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 173-197
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 108-115

events.title: Battle of Alalia (Sardinian Sea)
events.summary: Sixty Phocaean penteconters from Alalia in Corsica met a combined fleet of 60 Carthaginian and 60 Etruscan (Caeretan) ships; the Phocaeans won a 'Cadmean victory', lost 40 ships, and abandoned Corsica for Rhegium and then Elea.
events.detail: Herodotus records that the Caeretans stoned their Phocaean prisoners to death, were afflicted with a plague, and consulted Delphi, which ordered annual funeral games; this links Caere to Delphi a generation before Rome. The battle shows the Etrusco-Punic alignment that underlies the Pyrgi tablets and the first Rome-Carthage treaty. Date c. 540-535.

battle.significance: Phocaean victory in name but they abandoned Corsica; Etruscans secured Corsica, Carthage Sardinia. The Greek third side (Phocaeans of Alalia) is not a polity in this dataset.

events.debate: Exact date (c. 540-535) and location unknown.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus
events.summary: The great triad temple of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva on the Capitol, begun by the Tarquins, was dedicated on the Ides of September in the first year of the Republic by the consul M. Horatius Pulvillus.
events.detail: Its podium measured c. 53 x 62 m (cappellaccio tufa foundations survive in the Palazzo Caffarelli), making it among the largest temples of the Mediterranean in its day. The terracotta cult statue and the quadriga on the roof were commissioned from Vulca of Veii (Pliny). Pulvillus' rival Valerius' family supposedly tried to disrupt the dedication with false news of his son's death. The dedication date anchored the 'era of the Capitol' and the nail-count of years; Polybius dates the first Carthage treaty to the consuls of the year 28 years before Xerxes' crossing.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 128
Hopkins, The Genesis of Roman Architecture (2016)
events.debate: Some (e.g. Hopkins vs. Mura Sommella's critics) question whether the vast podium supported a single 6th-century temple of that size.

events.title: Expulsion of the Tarquins and end of the monarchy
events.summary: After Sextus Tarquinius raped Lucretia, L. Junius Brutus and L. Tarquinius Collatinus led an aristocratic coup that expelled Tarquinius Superbus, then besieging Ardea, and replaced the king with two annual magistrates.
events.detail: The Lucretia story is a moral drama modelled partly on Greek tyrant-expulsions (Brutus' feigned stupidity, the Delphic oracle, the Peisistratid parallel of 510 BC at Athens, which may have influenced the date). The underlying fact, the fall of a monarchy at the end of the 6th century, is broadly accepted: the Regia ceases to be a residence, the rex sacrorum survives as a priestly relic, and the Capitoline temple dedication and first Carthage treaty (Polybius) cluster at the start of the Republic. What replaced the king is debated: two consuls from the start (the Fasti), a single praetor maximus (Livy 7.3.5 on the nail law), or a period of Etruscan condottieri such as Porsenna. Collatinus was soon exiled merely for bearing the name Tarquinius.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 215-239
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 147-155
Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 218-232
events.debate: Alföldi (Early Rome and the Latins, 1965) argued for a later date c. 470 and Etruscan rule continuing; Gjerstad down-dated the kings too. Cornell defends a date c. 509-505 because the Fasti and the Polybian treaty fit it.

events.title: First annual magistrates of the Republic
events.summary: The Fasti list five consuls in 509 (Brutus, Collatinus, Sp. Lucretius Tricipitinus, P. Valerius Publicola, M. Horatius Pulvillus), an overcrowding that betrays later reconstruction of the year.
events.detail: The chief magistrates were probably originally called praetores (Livy 3.55.12; Festus on 'praetor maximus'), with 'consul' a later title. The Fasti for the early 5th century contain names of families later plebeian (Iunii, Cassii, Minucii, Genucii, Sempronii), which Cornell uses to argue the patriciate was not yet closed and that the list is substantially authentic rather than invented. A 'lex vetusta' required the praetor maximus to drive a nail into the wall of the Capitoline temple each Ides of September, so the nails could count years.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 1-3
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 218-223, 226-230
events.debate: Whether the dual collegial consulship goes back to 509 or developed later (De Martino, Heurgon) is unresolved.

events.title: First treaty between Rome and Carthage
events.summary: Polybius transcribed from bronze tablets in the treasury of the aediles a treaty of the first consuls: Romans and allies were not to sail beyond the Fair Promontory except under duress, trade in Libya and Sardinia only before a herald or scribe, and Carthage was not to harm Ardea, Antium, Laurentum, Circeii, Tarracina or any Latin city subject to Rome.
events.detail: The treaty claims Roman suzerainty over coastal Latium, matching the regal Rome of Livy book 1, and treats Rome as a junior trading partner of a Punic maritime power. Polybius says even the most learned Romans could barely read its archaic Latin. The Fair (Kalon) Promontory is probably Cape Farina (Ras Sidi Ali el Mekki) north of Carthage, or Cape Bon. The Pyrgi tablets (c. 500) show comparable Etrusco-Punic ties at Caere.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 337-345
Scardigli, I trattati romano-cartaginesi (1991)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 210-214
events.debate: Mommsen and others redated it to 348 because Livy and Diodorus know no treaty before 348; most now accept Polybius' date (Walbank, Cornell), not least because the archaic language and context make better sense c. 509.

events.title: Battle of the Silva Arsia
events.summary: Veii and Tarquinii, supporting the exiled Tarquins, fought the new Republic in the Arsian wood; Brutus and Arruns Tarquinius killed each other in a cavalry duel, and a divine voice (Silvanus) proclaimed that the Etruscans had lost one man more.
events.detail: The Roman matrons mourned Brutus for a year. Publicola celebrated the first triumph of the Republic (the Fasti Triumphales record a triumph over the Veientes and Tarquinienses on 1 March 509). The story belongs to the patriotic legend of the founding year.
events.locName: Silva Arsia, between Rome and Veii (unlocated)

sides.losses: 11,301 (one more than the Romans, per the divine voice)

battle.significance: Legendary first victory of the Republic and death of Brutus.

events.title: Lex Valeria de provocatione (509)
events.summary: Publicola is said to have carried a law granting citizens the right of appeal (provocatio) to the people against a magistrate's capital sentence, and to have lowered the fasces before the assembly.
events.detail: Livy reports three Valerian laws of appeal (509, 449, 300) and himself notes that the 300 law was 'the third, always by the same family'. Most scholars regard the 509 and 449 laws as retrojections of the 300 law (or of the Twelve Tables' rule that only the comitia maximus could pass capital sentence).
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) on 10.9
events.debate: Doublet of the lex Valeria of 300.

events.title: Lars Porsenna's attack on Rome
events.summary: Lars Porsenna of Clusium seized the Janiculum and blockaded Rome; Roman legend tells of Horatius Cocles holding the Sublician bridge, Mucius Scaevola burning his hand in Porsenna's brazier, and the escape of the hostage Cloelia, after which Porsenna made peace in admiration.
events.detail: A different tradition survives: Tacitus says Rome was surrendered to Porsenna (dedita urbe), and Pliny cites a treaty in which Porsenna forbade the Romans to use iron except for agriculture. The likeliest reconstruction (Cornell, Forsythe) is that Porsenna captured Rome, perhaps not to restore Tarquin but in his own interest, and lost his grip after his son's defeat at Aricia. The Roman custom of 'selling the goods of King Porsenna' at auctions (Livy 2.14.1) hints at a real occupation. Porsenna's name may be an Etruscan title (purth, a magistracy).

battle.significance: Roman tradition claims a moral victory; Tacitus and Pliny imply Rome capitulated. Porsenna's peace returned the Septem Pagi to Veii and took hostages.

scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 215-218
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 147-149
events.debate: Whether Porsenna took Rome. Livy's dating to 508/507 depends on the inflated Varronian fasti.

events.title: Battle of Aricia
events.summary: A Latin army reinforced by Aristodemus of Cumae defeated and killed Arruns, son of Porsenna, beneath the walls of Aricia, breaking Clusine power in Latium; Etruscan survivors fled to Rome and settled in the Vicus Tuscus.
events.detail: The battle is attested independently in a Cumaean chronicle used by Dionysius (book 7), which makes it one of the best-founded events of the period and the start of Aristodemus' tyranny at Cumae, where he later sheltered Tarquin. Dionysius places it some 20 years before 492, Livy right after Porsenna's peace; c. 505-504 is usual.

battle.significance: Ends Clusine control of Latium and launches Aristodemus' tyranny at Cumae.

scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 217
Alföldi, Early Rome and the Latins (1965) 56-72
events.debate: The 'Cumaean chronicle' (Alföldi) is hypothetical but widely accepted.

events.title: Migration of Attus Clausus and the Claudii
events.summary: The Sabine noble Attus Clausus of Regillum migrated to Rome with a large following (5,000 clients in Dionysius), was enrolled as a patrician as Appius Claudius, and received land beyond the Anio that became the tribus Claudia.
events.detail: A key piece of evidence for archaic horizontal mobility of elites with private armies of clients, comparable to the Lapis Satricanus 'suodales' of Publius Valerius and the Fabii at the Cremera. Tacitus (Ann. 11.24) has Claudius cite it in his speech on admitting Gauls to the Senate. Suetonius (Tib. 1) dates it to the time of Romulus with Titus Tatius instead.
scholarship: Smith, The Roman Clan (2006)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 144-145

events.title: First dictator: Titus Larcius
events.summary: Facing a threat from the Latins and Sabines, Rome appointed its first dictator, T. Larcius (Livy 2.18 gives 501 or 498 depending on his sources), with Sp. Cassius as master of the horse.
events.detail: Livy admits his sources disagree on who was first dictator and when; some named M'. Valerius. The dictatorship (originally magister populi, with a magister equitum) was a six-month emergency office named by a consul; it may reflect an archaic Latin office (the dictator of Lanuvium, the dictator Latinus who dedicated the Diana grove at Aricia per Cato).
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 9-10

events.title: Lapis Satricanus inscription
events.summary: A dedication to Mars (Mamars) by 'the companions (suodales) of Poplios Valesios' reused in the foundations of the temple of Mater Matuta at Satricum, found in 1977 and dated c. 500.
events.detail: Poplios Valesios is the archaic form of Publius Valerius, and some identify him with Publicola himself. Whether or not, the stone documents a warlord's sodales operating outside any state structure, the kind of band seen in the Fabian clan war at the Cremera and Attus Clausus' migration, and it shows that names in the early Fasti correspond to real archaic gentes.
scholarship: Stibbe et al., Lapis Satricanus (1980)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 144-145
events.debate: Identification of Poplios Valesios with Publicola is possible but unprovable.

events.title: Pyrgi tablets: Thefarie Velianas' dedication
events.summary: Three gold tablets (two Etruscan, one Phoenician) found in 1964 at the sanctuary of Pyrgi, Caere's port, record the dedication of a shrine to Uni-Astarte by Thefarie Velianas, ruler (Phoenician 'king over Kysry') of Caere, c. 500.
events.detail: The bilingual is the longest Etruscan-Phoenician text known and shows a Caeretan ruler courting Carthage, the same Tyrrhenian world in which the first Rome-Carthage treaty was concluded. Pyrgi's temples were plundered by Dionysius I of Syracuse in 384.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 212, 232
Serra Ridgway, 'Etruscans, Greeks, Carthaginians: the sanctuary at Pyrgi', in Descœudres (ed.), Greek Colonists and Native Populations (1990)

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Saturn
events.summary: The temple of Saturn at the foot of the Capitol was dedicated on 17 December (the Saturnalia) in 497 according to Livy (others gave 498 or 501); it later housed the aerarium, the state treasury.
events.detail: Its podium is under the eight Ionic columns of the 4th-century AD rebuilding. The temple's early date is one of several dedications clustered in the first decades of the Republic (Saturn 497, Mercury 495, Ceres 493, Castor 484) that suggest a still-prosperous city before the 5th-century recession visible in imports.
scholarship: Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

events.title: Battle of Lake Regillus
events.summary: The dictator A. Postumius Albus defeated the Latin League, led by Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum with the aged Tarquinius Superbus, near Lake Regillus; Castor and Pollux reportedly fought for Rome and watered their horses at the Juturna spring in the Forum.
events.detail: Postumius vowed a temple to Castor, dedicated in 484; the Ides of Quinctilis became the day of the transvectio equitum, the cavalry parade. Livy places the battle in 499 or 496 (he cites both). Mamilius was killed by T. Herminius. The epic detail (single combats, the divine twins) suggests a heroic poem or family tradition behind the narrative. A dedication to the Dioscuri ('Castorei Podlouqueique qurois') from Lavinium, c. 500, shows the cult was Latin-Greek and already present in the region.
events.locName: Lake Regillus (probably Pantano Secco near Frascati)

battle.significance: Ends Tarquin's hopes of restoration; leads to the Foedus Cassianum of 493 on terms of equality.

scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 285-289
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 293-294
events.debate: Date 499 or 496; location of the lake. The outcome was probably less decisive than claimed since the 493 treaty is between equals.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Mercury
events.summary: The temple of Mercury by the Circus Maximus was dedicated on the Ides of May 495; when the consuls quarrelled over who should dedicate it, the people gave the honour to the senior centurion M. Laetorius, who also founded a guild of merchants (collegium mercatorum).
events.detail: The placement outside the pomerium by the Aventine and the river harbour links it to trade with Greek and Etruscan merchants; the episode is also an early instance of popular assertion against the consuls before the secession of 494.

events.title: Death of Tarquinius Superbus at Cumae
events.summary: The last king died in exile at Cumae at the court of the tyrant Aristodemus; Livy notes that news of his death prompted the patricians to begin oppressing the plebs.
events.detail: Aristodemus inherited Tarquin's property and later seized Roman grain ships sent to buy corn during the famine of 492, using it as a claim against Rome.

events.title: Colonists sent to Signia
events.summary: Livy reports that Signia, founded by Tarquinius Superbus, received a fresh draft of colonists in 495 to hold the Monti Lepini against the Volsci.
events.detail: Signia's polygonal walls (late 6th-4th century) and the temple on its acropolis survive. Early 'Latin colonies' like Signia, Norba, Velitrae and Circeii were joint foundations of Rome and the Latin League placed on the Volscian front.

events.title: First Secession of the Plebs and creation of the tribunate
events.summary: Plebeian soldiers crushed by debt bondage (nexum) refused to fight and withdrew to the Mons Sacer (or the Aventine, per Piso); they returned after Menenius Agrippa's fable of the belly and the limbs, having won sacrosanct tribunes of the plebs to protect them.
events.detail: The plebs swore a lex sacrata making anyone who harmed a tribune sacer (killable with impunity). Sources disagree on the first number of tribunes (two, four or five) and their names (L. Sicinius Bellutus and L. Iunius Brutus are suspiciously named). The plebeian aediles, guardians of the temple of Ceres, appear at the same time. The secession created a state within the state with its own assembly (concilium plebis), officers and treasury, and set the template of the Struggle of the Orders. Modern debate concerns whether 'plebs' were the whole non-patrician population or a poorer, organised movement (Raaflaub, Mitchell), and whether the patriciate was already closed.
events.locName: Mons Sacer (by the Anio, 3 Roman miles from Rome)
scholarship: Raaflaub (ed.), Social Struggles in Archaic Rome (1986; 2nd ed. 2005)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 256-271
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 170-177
events.debate: Mons Sacer vs Aventine. Dionysius turns the episode into long Thucydidean speeches. Mitchell (Patricians and Plebeians, 1990) denies the patrician-plebeian division is archaic at all.

events.title: Foedus Cassianum
events.summary: Sp. Cassius concluded a treaty of perpetual peace and mutual defence between Rome and the Latin League: equal shares of booty, alternating command, and no aid to each other's enemies.
events.detail: The bronze text stood behind the Rostra and Cicero says it was still remembered in his day. Dionysius preserves its terms: 'Let there be peace between the Romans and all the cities of the Latins as long as heaven and earth remain in the same place'. Legal rights of conubium, commercium and the ius migrationis shared by Latins probably date from this framework. The joint foundation of 'Latin colonies' on the Volscian front (Signia, Velitrae, Norba, Antium, Ardea, Circeii, Satricum, Setia, Sutrium, Nepet) followed the treaty's logic.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 299-301
Alföldi, Early Rome and the Latins (1965) 111-122
events.debate: Whether booty was split equally between Rome and the League collectively (thus Rome as half) or among all members; whether command alternated (Festus' 'praetor' at the Ferentine spring).

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera
events.summary: Sp. Cassius dedicated the temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera on the Aventine, vowed by A. Postumius during a famine in 496; it became the religious centre of the plebs, seat of the plebeian aediles and archive of plebiscites and senatus consulta.
events.detail: Pliny says the Greek artists Damophilus and Gorgasus decorated it with painting and terracotta and signed their work in Greek verse, the earliest attested Greek artists at Rome. The triad mirrors the Eleusinian Demeter, Iacchus and Kore, probably via Cumae, and the temple's Greek priestesses were recruited from Naples and Velia (Cicero).
events.locName: Aventine slope above the Circus Maximus
scholarship: Spaeth, The Roman Goddess Ceres (1996)
Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

events.title: Capture of Corioli
events.summary: During the consul Postumus Cominius' attack on the Volscian town of Corioli, the young patrician Gnaeus Marcius forced his way through the gate and took the town, earning the cognomen Coriolanus.
events.detail: Livy remarks that the consul's name had been eclipsed so thoroughly that only the treaty with the Latins preserved it. Corioli was already forgotten by Pliny's day (he lists it among vanished peoples of Latium). The cognomen derived from a place is anachronistic for 493.

sides.strength: town garrison and relief army from Antium

battle.significance: Source of the Coriolanus legend.

events.title: Famine and grain embassies of 492
events.summary: After the secession left fields unsown, Rome sent grain buyers to Etruria, Cumae (where Aristodemus seized their ships) and Sicily, where 'the tyrant' supplied corn; in 491 Coriolanus allegedly proposed withholding it unless the tribunate was abolished.
events.detail: Dionysius names Gelon of Syracuse as the Sicilian donor, an anachronism (Gelon took Syracuse in 485) already noticed by Dionysius himself, who criticised Licinius Macer and Gellius for it; Livy merely says 'the tyrant'. The annalistic record of famines (492, 456, 440-439, 411) and grain purchases from Etruria, Campania and Sicily probably derives from the pontifical tables and is among the more credible 5th-century data.
scholarship: Garnsey, Famine and Food Supply in the Graeco-Roman World (1988) 167-181
Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 320-322

events.title: Colony at Norba
events.summary: A colony was sent to Norba, on the edge of the Monti Lepini overlooking the Pontine plain, as a citadel against the Volsci.
events.detail: Norba's superb polygonal walls and gates (2.5 km circuit) survive; the town was destroyed by Sulla's forces in 82 BC and never reoccupied, so the street grid is visible from the air.

events.title: Coriolanus leads the Volsci against Rome
events.summary: Exiled after a tribunician prosecution, Coriolanus joined the Volscian leader Attius Tullius of Antium and led a Volscian army that took a string of Latin towns and camped at the Fossae Cluiliae, five miles from Rome, until his mother Veturia and wife Volumnia persuaded him to withdraw.
events.detail: The temple of Fortuna Muliebris at the fourth milestone of the Via Latina was said to commemorate the women. The story has a real background: the Volscian advance into Latium in the early 5th century, which took Satricum, Antium, Velitrae, Circeii and the Pontine plain from Latin control. But the hero is probably fictitious, or a much reworked folk figure; the list of towns he captured mirrors later Volscian conquests.
events.locName: Fossae Cluiliae, 5 miles from Rome on the Via Latina
scholarship: Cornell, 'Coriolanus: myth, history and performance', in Braund & Gill (eds.), Myth, History and Culture in Republican Rome (2003)
events.debate: Historicity of Coriolanus; Fabius Pictor had him live to old age in exile.

events.title: Treaty with the Hernici
events.summary: Sp. Cassius in his third consulship brought the Hernici of the Sacco valley into the Roman-Latin alliance on the same terms as the Latins, taking two-thirds of their land according to Livy.
events.detail: The Hernici held the strategic wedge between Volsci and Aequi; the triple alliance enabled the slow 5th-century counter-offensive. Livy's land confiscation is probably a confusion; Dionysius describes an equal treaty.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 299

events.title: Agrarian proposal and execution of Spurius Cassius
events.summary: Sp. Cassius, three times consul, proposed distributing public land to plebs and Latins in 486; next year he was condemned for aiming at kingship (adfectatio regni) and executed, by the quaestors or by his own father, and his house razed.
events.detail: The tale of the first agrarian law looks heavily coloured by the Gracchan crisis; but the motif of the aristocrat who courts the plebs and is killed for 'regnum' (Cassius 485, Maelius 439, Manlius 384) seems to be a real archaic pattern of elite self-policing. A bronze statue of Ceres made from his confiscated property bore the inscription 'ex Cassia familia datum'.
scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 192-193
events.debate: Gracchan retrojection of the agrarian law is likely.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Castor
events.summary: The son of the dictator Postumius dedicated the temple of Castor (and Pollux) in the Forum beside the spring of Juturna, fulfilling his father's vow at Lake Regillus.
events.detail: Excavations (Danish-Italian, 1980s) found the 5th-century podium under the Augustan-Tiberian rebuilding whose three standing columns are a Forum landmark. The temple was a meeting place of the Senate and later a weights-and-measures office.
scholarship: Nielsen & Poulsen (eds.), The Temple of Castor and Pollux I (1992)

events.title: Battle of Himera
events.summary: Gelon of Syracuse and Theron of Acragas annihilated a large Carthaginian expedition under Hamilcar the Magonid at Himera; Greek tradition placed it on the same day as Salamis (Herodotus) or Thermopylae (Diodorus).
events.detail: Carthage paid 2,000 talents indemnity, and Gelon's Demareteion coinage and the Himera victory temple (the 'Temple of Victory', Doric) commemorate it. Carthage withdrew from Sicilian expansion for seventy years, turning to its African hinterland. The battle frames the western Greek world into which Rome's first contacts (grain from Sicily, Cumae) fall.

sides.losses: army destroyed; Hamilcar killed or self-immolated

battle.significance: Halts Carthaginian expansion in Sicily for 70 years; Syracusan hegemony under the Deinomenids.

scholarship: CAH IV2 (1988) ch. 17 (Asheri)

events.title: Disaster of the Fabii at the Cremera
events.summary: The gens Fabia undertook the war against Veii as a private enterprise, garrisoning a fort on the Cremera with 306 Fabii and their clients; they were ambushed and all killed, leaving a single boy to continue the line.
events.detail: Ovid dates the disaster to the Ides of February; Livy (6.1.11) and Tacitus treat 18 July as the day of both the Cremera and the Allia. The '306' and the surviving child are legend (and modelled on the 300 Spartans), but the clan war of a gens with its clients against a neighbour fits the archaic world of the Lapis Satricanus. The Fabii vanish from the Fasti for a decade after 479, which may reflect a real catastrophe. The Porta Carmentalis through which they marched was thereafter ill-omened (the 'Porta Scelerata').
events.locName: River Cremera (Fosso della Valchetta) near Veii

battle.significance: Veii seizes the Janiculum briefly; war ends with a 40-year truce in 474.

scholarship: Richardson, 'The Fabii and the Cremera', in Richardson & Santangelo (eds.), Andreas Alföldi in the Twenty-First Century (2015)
Smith, The Roman Clan (2006) 290-295
events.debate: Date (13 Feb vs 18 July) and the role of the gens as a private army.

events.title: Naval battle of Cumae
events.summary: Hiero I of Syracuse, answering an appeal from Cumae, destroyed an Etruscan fleet off Cumae, ending Etruscan naval dominance in the Tyrrhenian and isolating the Etruscan cities of Campania.
events.detail: Hiero dedicated captured Etruscan helmets at Olympia; two survive, one in the British Museum inscribed 'Hiaron son of Deinomenes and the Syracusans to Zeus, Tyrrhenian spoils from Cumae'. Pindar's first Pythian celebrates the victory. Syracuse then planted a short-lived base on Pithecusae (Ischia). Weakened by the defeat, Etruscan Capua fell to the Samnites in 423.

battle.significance: End of Etruscan sea power in the southern Tyrrhenian.

scholarship: Meiggs & Lewis, Greek Historical Inscriptions no. 29 (helmet)

events.title: Forty-year truce with Veii
events.summary: The first Veientine war ended with a 40-year truce (indutiae), a typical early Roman instrument; Veii paid grain and money.
events.detail: Truces of fixed length (Veii 474, 40 years; Tarquinii 351, 40 years; Caere 353, 100 years; Volsinii 308, 30 years) were archaic Italian practice that pre-dated the formal foedus.

events.title: Lex Publilia Voleronis
events.summary: The tribune Volero Publilius, a former centurion who had resisted being enrolled as a common soldier, carried a law that tribunes be elected by an assembly organised by tribes rather than curiae.
events.detail: The consul Appius Claudius' resistance led to a battle in the Forum; his army then deserted against the Volsci and he decimated it, the first recorded decimation. The tribal assembly of the plebs (concilium plebis tributum) based on residence weakened patrician clientage in the curiate system. Number of tribunes may have been raised to four or five at this time.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 259-260

events.title: Census of 465: 104,714 citizens
events.summary: Livy records a lustrum in 465 counting 104,714 citizens (some manuscripts 124,214), 'besides orphans and widows'.
events.detail: Early census figures (Servius 80,000; 508 c. 130,000 per Dionysius; 465 104,714; 459 117,319) are far too high for a city-state whose territory in c. 500 was about 822 km2 (Beloch's estimate): even counting all free males they imply a population greater than the land could carry. They are probably later inventions or back-projections, though the mid-Republican figures (from 293 onward) are generally taken seriously.
scholarship: Beloch, Römische Geschichte (1926)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 204-208
events.debate: Figures generally considered unreliable for the 5th century.

events.title: Plague of 463
events.summary: A pestilence struck Rome and its allies, killing both consuls (L. Aebutius and P. Servilius) or one of them, many senators and a large part of the population; the Aequi and Volsci exploited the paralysis.
events.detail: Livy's sequence of 5th-century epidemics (463, 453, 436-433, 412, 399-398) is plausibly drawn from the pontifical annals; the 433 epidemic produced the vow of a temple to Apollo Medicus.

events.title: Appius Herdonius seizes the Capitol
events.summary: The Sabine Appius Herdonius with c. 2,500 exiles and slaves occupied the Capitol by night, calling on slaves to rise; the Romans, with help from a Tusculan army under L. Mamilius, retook it after several days, but the consul P. Valerius was killed in the assault.
events.detail: Like Attus Clausus, Herdonius illustrates the archaic warlord with a private following; a Turnus Herdonius of Aricia appears in the Tarquin saga. The tribunes had initially obstructed the levy, arguing the threat was a patrician trick.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 144

events.title: Census of 459: 117,319 citizens
events.summary: Livy gives 117,319 citizens counted at the lustrum of 459.
events.detail: See census_465 on the reliability of 5th-century census figures. Dionysius gives slightly different numbers.

events.title: Cincinnatus' dictatorship and the battle of Mount Algidus
events.summary: When the Aequi under Gracchus Cloelius trapped the consul L. Minucius in the Algidus pass, envoys found L. Quinctius Cincinnatus ploughing his four-iugera farm across the Tiber; named dictator, he relieved Minucius, sent the Aequi under the yoke, and resigned after sixteen days.
events.detail: The tale became the paradigm of Republican virtue, but Livy's account of an army enclosing the besiegers with a ditch and stockade overnight, each man carrying twelve stakes, is a stock motif. The Algidus pass, carrying the route from the Aequian hills to the Alban plain, was the recurrent front of the 5th-century Aequian wars. Dionysius gives a different chronology.

sides.strength: relief army from the city plus Minucius' trapped consular army

sides.losses: surrendered and sent under the yoke

battle.significance: Legendary model of the citizen-dictator; one of many Algidus engagements.

scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 437-444

events.title: Tribunes of the plebs increased to ten
events.summary: The number of plebeian tribunes was raised to ten, two from each of the five classes according to one tradition; the number remained ten thereafter.
events.detail: A larger college made intercession (veto by a single colleague) a tool that the patricians could exploit by winning over one tribune, a tactic used against the Licinio-Sextian rogations and the Gracchi.

events.title: Lex Icilia de Aventino publicando
events.summary: The tribune L. Icilius carried a law distributing the Aventine, then public land outside the pomerium, to plebeians for houses; several families could share one building plot by floors.
events.detail: Dionysius says the bronze text was set up in the temple of Diana on the Aventine. The Aventine became the plebeian quarter par excellence and the site of the second secession.

events.title: Lex Aternia Tarpeia on fines
events.summary: A consular law set the maximum fine a magistrate could impose at two sheep and thirty oxen, values later converted to bronze (10 asses per sheep, 100 per ox) by the lex Iulia Papiria of 430.
events.detail: The law is a precious glimpse of a pre-monetary economy in which value was reckoned in livestock (pecus, whence pecunia) and uncoined bronze by weight.

events.title: Embassy to Greece to study the laws of Solon
events.summary: Three envoys (Sp. Postumius Albus, A. Manlius, P. Sulpicius Camerinus) were reportedly sent to Athens and other Greek cities to copy the laws of Solon before codification; they returned in 452.
events.detail: Most scholars doubt an Athenian mission: the Twelve Tables show few specifically Solonian features (a funerary restriction and the rule on boundary strips, which Gaius compared to Solon, are the strongest). Influence via the Greek cities of southern Italy, and the tradition that Hermodorus of Ephesus, an exile, helped the decemvirs (a statue of him stood in the Comitium per Pliny), are more plausible.
scholarship: Crawford (ed.), Roman Statutes II (1996) 555-721
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 275
events.debate: Historicity of the embassy widely doubted.

events.title: First Decemvirate
events.summary: Consulship and tribunate were suspended and ten patrician decemviri legibus scribundis, headed by Appius Claudius, governed with full powers and drafted ten tables of law.
events.detail: The first board was remembered as moderate; each decemvir held the fasces in turn for a day. Its laws were ratified by the comitia centuriata. The suspension of the tribunate shows the decemvirate was a compromise in which the plebs traded protection for written law.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 45-46

events.title: The Law of the Twelve Tables
events.summary: Rome's first written code, ten tables drafted in 451 and two more in 450, was set up in bronze (or wood) in the Forum: Livy called it 'the fount of all public and private law', and Cicero learned it by heart as a schoolboy.
events.detail: It survives only in c. 100 quoted fragments (reconstructed by Crawford et al. in Roman Statutes). Content: procedure (summons, 'si in ius vocat, ito'), debt bondage (the creditor may cut the defaulting debtor's body after three market days: 'partes secanto', Table III), patria potestas (a son sold three times is free from his father), usus marriage and the trinoctium escape from manus, intestate succession to sui heredes then agnates then gentiles, tort with talio ('si membrum rupsit, ni cum eo pacit, talio esto'), night-time thieves may be killed, magical crop-charming (fruges excantare) and libellous songs (malum carmen) as capital offences, restrictions on funeral display (no gold except dental gold, no more than ten flute-players), and in the last two tables the notorious ban on patrician-plebeian intermarriage, repealed in 445. It reflects a small agrarian community of farmers, debtors and clans, not a codification of constitutional law.
scholarship: Crawford (ed.), Roman Statutes II (1996) 555-721
Watson, Rome of the XII Tables (1975)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 272-292
events.debate: Authenticity is now generally accepted (archaic language, agrarian content) against Pais and Lambert, who dated the code much later.

events.title: Verginia, the fall of the decemvirs and the Second Secession
events.summary: The second decemvirate became a tyranny; when Appius Claudius tried to claim the plebeian girl Verginia as a slave, her father killed her in the Forum, the armies mutinied and the plebs seceded to the Aventine and the Mons Sacer until the decemvirs abdicated.
events.detail: Appius died in prison awaiting trial (suicide, by one version) and his colleague Sp. Oppius likewise; the others went into exile. The Verginia story is a deliberate doublet of Lucretia: a sexual outrage by a tyrant triggers liberation. Tribunes were restored (the first being Verginius and Icilius, Verginia's betrothed), and the consuls L. Valerius Potitus and M. Horatius Barbatus carried the Valerio-Horatian laws.
scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 476-497
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 222-225

events.title: Leges Valeriae Horatiae
events.summary: The consuls of 449 carried laws making plebiscites binding on the whole people, renewing provocatio and forbidding magistracies without appeal, and confirming the sacrosanctity of tribunes and plebeian aediles.
events.detail: The plebiscite clause also appears in the lex Publilia of 339 and the lex Hortensia of 287, so the 449 and 339 versions are probably either conditional (requiring senatorial approval) or retrojections. Livy adds that senatus consulta were now deposited with the plebeian aediles in the temple of Ceres to prevent tampering.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 277-278
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 230-233
events.debate: Triple tradition (449, 339, 287) on binding plebiscites.

events.title: Quaestors first elected by the people
events.summary: Tacitus records that quaestors, previously appointed by the kings and then the consuls, were first elected by the people 63 years after the expulsion of the Tarquins (c. 447), when Valerius Potitus and Aemilius Mamercus held the office.
events.detail: The quaestores parricidii (criminal investigators) and the treasury quaestors may originally have been separate; numbers rose to four in 421, with plebeians eligible, and eight in 267.

events.title: The Roman people award themselves disputed land
events.summary: Asked to arbitrate a boundary dispute between Ardea and Aricia, the Roman assembly, prompted by the old soldier P. Scaptius, voted the land to Rome; Livy calls it a disgraceful verdict that the senate tried in vain to stop.
events.detail: Rome made amends to Ardea in 442 by sending a colony there, ostensibly to protect it from Volscian pressure and internal strife. The territory may be the origin of the tribus Scaptia (created 332).

events.title: Lex Canuleia: intermarriage between patricians and plebeians
events.summary: The tribune C. Canuleius carried a plebiscite repealing the ban on conubium between patricians and plebeians that the second decemvirate had added to the Twelve Tables.
events.detail: Livy composes a long speech for Canuleius on the absurdity of a citizen body that could not intermarry. A second Canuleian proposal to open the consulship to plebeians was deflected by the creation of military tribunes with consular power. That the ban was introduced by the decemvirate suggests the patriciate was trying to close itself as a hereditary caste precisely in the mid-5th century (Cornell's 'serrata').
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 252-256, 292

events.title: First military tribunes with consular power
events.summary: In 444 three tribuni militum consulari potestate replaced the consuls; in about 50 of the years from 444 to 367 the state was headed by colleges of three, four or six consular tribunes rather than two consuls.
events.detail: Livy explains the office as a device to admit plebeians to supreme command without opening the consulship, yet the first plebeian consular tribune is recorded only in 400 (P. Licinius Calvus) and few plebeians held it. Modern explanations prefer military need: more commanders for simultaneous wars on several fronts, which fits the rise to six tribunes during the Veientine war. The first college of 444 abdicated after 73 days for a fault in the auspices.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 334-339
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 234-239
Broughton, MRR I 52-53
events.debate: Political vs military explanation of the consular tribunate.

events.title: Creation of the censorship
events.summary: Two censors, L. Papirius Mugillanus and L. Sempronius Atratinus, were elected to take the census, a task the consuls (or consular tribunes) no longer had time for; the office grew to control the roll of the Senate and public contracts.
events.detail: The first censors held the census in the Villa Publica on the Campus Martius from 435. The lex Aemilia of 434 limited the censorship to 18 months within a five-year cycle, the lustrum.
scholarship: Suolahti, The Roman Censors (1963)
Broughton, MRR I 53-54

events.title: Colony at Ardea
events.summary: A Latin colony was planted at the Rutulian city of Ardea to protect it after a civil conflict between its nobles and plebs had drawn in the Volsci.
events.detail: Ardea, on a tufa spur near the coast, was one of the Latin cities named in the 509 Carthage treaty. Camillus later went into exile there (391).

events.title: Spurius Maelius and the famine of 440-439
events.summary: During a famine the rich plebeian knight Sp. Maelius distributed grain he had bought in Etruria; accused of seeking kingship, he was summoned by the dictator Cincinnatus and killed by the master of horse C. Servilius Ahala; his house was razed (the Aequimaelium).
events.detail: L. Minucius, praefectus annonae, was honoured with a column outside the Porta Trigemina; the columna Minucia appears on a denarius of 135 BC. Cicero celebrated Ahala as a tyrannicide (Brutus the assassin claimed descent from him). An older version (Cincius, Piso) had Ahala act as a private citizen without a dictatorship; the dictatorship may be later justification.
scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 240-241
Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) no. 243

events.title: Fidenae revolts; Cossus wins the spolia opima
events.summary: Fidenae, a Roman colony on the Tiber, defected to Lars Tolumnius of Veii and murdered four Roman envoys; in the ensuing battle the military tribune A. Cornelius Cossus killed Tolumnius and dedicated his armour to Jupiter Feretrius, the second spolia opima after Romulus.
events.detail: Livy reports that Augustus told him he had read on the linen corslet in the temple of Jupiter Feretrius that Cossus was consul when he won the spoils (so 428). The emperor's interest was political: in 29-27 BC Augustus denied M. Licinius Crassus (proconsul, not commander under his own auspices) the right to dedicate spolia opima. Statues of the four murdered envoys stood on the Rostra.
events.locName: Fidenae, on the Tiber north of Rome

battle.significance: Second of three spolia opima in Roman history.

scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 563-567
Rich, 'Augustus and the spolia opima', Chiron 26 (1996)
events.debate: Date of Cossus' feat (437 as military tribune, 428 as consul or 426 as magister equitum); Augustus' evidence is suspect.

events.title: Construction of the Villa Publica
events.summary: The censors C. Furius Pacilus and M. Geganius Macerinus approved the Villa Publica on the Campus Martius and held the first census there.
events.detail: The Villa Publica remained the census office and the place where returning generals awaiting a triumph and foreign envoys were lodged outside the pomerium; Sulla massacred Samnite prisoners there in 82.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Apollo Medicus
events.summary: Vowed during the plague of 433, the temple of Apollo the Healer in the Prata Flaminia was dedicated by the consul Cn. Iulius in 431, the first Roman temple of a purely Greek god.
events.detail: Apollo came to Rome via the Sibylline Books, purchased from the Cumaean Sibyl according to legend. The temple stood near the later Theatre of Marcellus; its Augustan rebuilding by C. Sosius (the Apollo Sosianus) survives in three restored columns. The Senate met there to hear generals and envoys outside the pomerium.
scholarship: Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

events.title: Battle of Mount Algidus (431)
events.summary: The dictator A. Postumius Tubertus decisively defeated a combined Aequian and Volscian army on the Algidus; the victory, unlike earlier Algidus stories, marks a real turning point after which the Aequi ceased to threaten Latium.
events.detail: Livy tells that Postumius had his own son executed for leaving his post to fight, a story he doubts (and which recurs with Manlius Torquatus in 340, 'imperia Manliana'). Rome now began to take the offensive: Labici (418), Bolae, Ferentinum (413).

sides.strength: dictator's army with Latin and Hernican contingents

battle.significance: End of the Aequian threat to the Alban Hills; beginning of Roman counter-offensive in the Volscian and Aequian hills.

scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 307-309

events.title: Capture and destruction of Fidenae
events.summary: After Fidenae revolted again with Veii, the dictator Mam. Aemilius defeated the Veientines and Fidenates (who attacked with burning torches) and took Fidenae through a tunnel; it was sacked and the population sold.
events.detail: Fidenae controlled the Tiber crossing and the salt route upstream; its loss severed Veii from the Sabine and Faliscan hinterland and gave Rome both banks of the lower Tiber. A 20-year truce with Veii followed.

sides.strength: dictator Mam. Aemilius Mamercinus with master of horse A. Cornelius Cossus

battle.significance: Rome secures the lower Tiber and the Via Salaria.

events.title: Samnite highlanders seize Etruscan Capua
events.summary: Oscan-speaking Samnite settlers, admitted as partners, massacred the Etruscan inhabitants of Capua in a night attack (Livy, 423), creating the Oscan Campanian people; Diodorus dates the formation of the Campanian nation to 438.
events.detail: Part of a wider movement of Sabellian peoples (the ver sacrum, 'sacred spring', migrations) from the Apennines into the lowlands and Greek south in the later 5th century: Lucanians took Poseidonia (Paestum) c. 410-400, the Bruttii emerged c. 356. The Campanians soon diverged from their Samnite kin and appealed to Rome against them in 343.
scholarship: Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 37-39
Frederiksen, Campania (1984) 134-157

events.title: Campanians capture Greek Cumae
events.summary: The new Oscan masters of Capua stormed Cumae, the oldest Greek colony in the west and Rome's former refuge for Tarquin; Cumae became an Oscan town and Greek civic life in Campania contracted to Neapolis.
events.detail: Survivors fled to Neapolis. Cumae retained its oracle of the Sibyl, but Oscan inscriptions dominate from now on. Livy and Diodorus give 421/420.
scholarship: Frederiksen, Campania (1984)

events.title: Quaestorship doubled and opened to plebeians
events.summary: The number of quaestors rose from two to four, two to accompany the consuls in war, and plebeians became eligible; the first plebeian quaestors were elected in 409.
events.detail: Patricians won all quaestorships until 409, when three of four went to plebeians, an index of the gradual erosion of the patrician monopoly.

events.title: Colony at Labici
events.summary: After Labici joined the Aequi and was captured, 1,500 Roman colonists were sent there, each receiving two iugera.
events.detail: The first colony recorded after the Algidus victory, it consolidated Rome's hold on the north side of the Alban Hills. The small allotment size (about half a hectare) is a striking datum for archaic Roman smallholding.

events.title: Soldiers stone the consular tribune M. Postumius
events.summary: After capturing the Aequian town of Bolae, the consular tribune M. Postumius Regillensis denied his soldiers the promised booty and threatened them; they stoned him to death, the first Roman commander killed by his own army.
events.detail: The episode was entangled with tribunician demands for an agrarian law dividing the territory of Bolae.

events.title: Capture of Anxur (Tarracina)
events.summary: The consular tribune N. Fabius Ambustus took the Volscian coastal stronghold of Anxur by a feint, opening the coast road south toward Campania.
events.detail: Anxur changed hands repeatedly (lost 402, retaken 400); Rome planted a citizen colony at Tarracina in 329. The Temple of Jupiter Anxur on Monte S. Angelo overlooks the site.

sides.strength: army of the consular tribune N. Fabius Ambustus

battle.significance: Rome reaches the southern edge of the Pontine plain.

events.title: Introduction of military pay (stipendium)
events.summary: The Senate decreed that soldiers should be paid from public funds, financed by a property tax (tributum), so that a long winter siege of Veii became possible.
events.detail: Diodorus confirms the introduction of pay in connection with the war against Veii. Payment preceded coinage, so it must have been in weighed bronze. The new burden of tributum on landholders and the obligation of year-round service became a lever in the debt crisis that followed. In 403 the censors, Camillus among them, imposed a tax on unmarried men (aes uxorium).
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 187, 313

events.title: Siege and fall of Veii
events.summary: Rome besieged Veii, its great Etruscan neighbour 15 km up the Cremera, traditionally for ten years; in 396 the dictator M. Furius Camillus took the city through a tunnel, called out its goddess Juno Regina by evocatio, sold the inhabitants and annexed its territory, nearly doubling the ager Romanus.
events.detail: The Homeric ten years and the cuniculus emerging inside Juno's temple are legend; the 'Alban lake prodigy' (an oracle that Veii would fall only when the lake was drained) has a real counterpart in the 1.4 km emissarium tunnel of Lake Albano. The other Etruscan cities, meeting at the Fanum Voltumnae, refused to help Veii, which had chosen a king. Camillus' triumph with a chariot drawn by four white horses was attacked as hubris, and the gold bowl promised to Apollo at Delphi from a tenth of the booty was melted down from matrons' jewellery. Archaeology confirms continuity of some sanctuaries (Portonaccio) but a sharp break in urban life. Veii's territory (perhaps 560 km2) became four new tribes in 387 and was distributed in seven-iugera lots.

sides.strength: Roman army with Latin and Hernican allies; volunteers flocked for booty

sides.losses: city sacked; survivors sold into slavery

battle.significance: Doubles Roman territory and manpower; the first great conquest and the model for later expansion.

scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 626-680
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 309-313
Ward-Perkins, 'Veii: the historical topography of the ancient city', PBSR 29 (1961)
events.debate: Duration and details; the evocatio story; the real scale of the war.

events.title: Solar eclipse 'around the 350th year from the foundation'
events.summary: Cicero quotes Ennius: 'on the Nones of June the moon and night covered the sun', about the 350th year from the foundation, and says the pontifical annals calculated earlier eclipses back from it; the eclipse of 21 June 400 BC fits.
events.detail: The passage is precious evidence that the Annales Maximi recorded eclipses from at least c. 400 and that the pontifical calendar was then still roughly in step with the seasons (Nones of June = late June). Precise identification is debated; some prefer an earlier eclipse (e.g. 404) depending on calendar slippage.
scholarship: Skutsch, The Annals of Q. Ennius (1985) 311-313
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 69-70
events.debate: Which eclipse is meant; calendar slippage.

events.title: First plebeian consular tribune
events.summary: P. Licinius Calvus became the first plebeian elected military tribune with consular power; in 399 plebeians held five of six places.
events.detail: The sudden plebeian success during the Veientine war and its equally sudden reversal show how fragile plebeian access remained before 367. Some names in Livy's lists may be later interpolations by plebeian families.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 84-85

events.title: First lectisternium
events.summary: During a plague after a harsh winter the duoviri sacris faciundis, on the authority of the Sibylline Books, held Rome's first lectisternium: for eight days images of Apollo and Latona, Hercules and Diana, Mercury and Neptune reclined on couches before banquets.
events.detail: A Greek rite (theoxenia) channelled through the Sibylline Books; householders kept open house and prisoners were unchained. Lectisternia recur in crises (364, 349, 217).

events.title: The Alban Lake prodigy and emissarium
events.summary: When Lake Albano rose to an unprecedented level without rain, a captured Veientine haruspex and the Delphic oracle declared Veii would not fall until its water was drawn off; Rome cut a drainage tunnel.
events.detail: The tunnel (emissarium) is real: about 1,450 m long through the crater rim, still functioning, and probably of the 5th-4th century. It probably served agriculture and flood control; the prodigy legend rationalised the work.

events.title: Dionysius I destroys Motya
events.summary: Dionysius I of Syracuse besieged and stormed the Punic island-city of Motya in western Sicily using a mole, six-storey siege towers and the newly invented arrow-firing catapult (gastraphetes/oxybeles).
events.detail: The siege is a landmark in Greek siege technology. Carthage replied under Himilco by recapturing the west and besieging Syracuse in 396, until plague destroyed his army. Survivors founded Lilybaeum nearby, later Carthage's chief Sicilian base against Pyrrhus and Rome.

sides.losses: city destroyed; inhabitants massacred or enslaved

battle.significance: First use of torsion-free catapults in a siege; leads to the founding of Lilybaeum.

scholarship: Marsden, Greek and Roman Artillery: Historical Development (1969) 48-56
Caven, Dionysius I (1990)

events.title: Golden bowl to Delphi intercepted by Liparaean pirates
events.summary: Roman envoys carrying a gold bowl to Apollo at Delphi from the Veientine spoils were captured by ships of Lipara; the chief magistrate Timasitheus released them and escorted them to Delphi, and Rome granted him public hospitality.
events.detail: The bowl was placed in the treasury of the Massaliots at Delphi; Appian says it stood on a bronze base until melted down by Onomarchus in the Third Sacred War. When Rome took Lipara in 252 it exempted Timasitheus' descendants from tribute. The story places Rome in the network of Delphi, Massalia and the Tyrrhenian Greeks well before the 3rd century.

events.title: Surrender of Falerii and the schoolmaster
events.summary: Besieging the Faliscan capital Falerii, Camillus refused the offer of a schoolmaster who brought him the children of its leading men, and had the boys whip the traitor back to the city; moved by this fides, the Faliscans surrendered.
events.detail: A moralising tale; in fact Falerii remained hostile into the 350s, and the town (Civita Castellana) was destroyed by Rome in 241 and its people moved to Falerii Novi on the plain. Capena had surrendered in 395.

sides.losses: surrendered; paid soldiers' pay for the year

battle.significance: Ends the Veientine war's Faliscan front.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Juno Regina on the Aventine
events.summary: Camillus dedicated on the Aventine the temple of Juno Regina, whose cult statue had been 'invited' from Veii by evocatio in 396; a young soldier allegedly asked the statue if it wished to go to Rome and it nodded.
events.detail: Evocatio, summoning the protecting deity of an enemy city with promise of a better cult in Rome, was used again at Carthage in 146 (Macrobius preserves a formula) and possibly at Volsinii (Vertumnus) in 264 and Isaura Vetus in 75.

events.title: Gauls besiege Clusium
events.summary: The Senones under Brennus crossed the Apennines and besieged Clusium; Roman envoys, three sons of M. Fabius Ambustus, violated the law of nations by fighting in the Clusine ranks, one killing a Gallic chief, and Rome refused to surrender them.
events.detail: Livy reports the story that a Clusine, Arruns, had lured the Gauls with wine to avenge his wife's seduction. The Fabii were then elected consular tribunes for 390, which gave the Gauls their casus belli. Diodorus says the Gauls had been in Iapygia (in Dionysius' service?) and were returning. The Gallic settlement of the Po valley (Insubres, Cenomani, Boii, Lingones, Senones) had begun at least a century earlier; Livy himself dates the first crossings to the time of Tarquinius Priscus.
scholarship: Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001) 140-150

events.title: Battle of the Allia
events.summary: A Gallic war band of Senones under Brennus routed the Roman army at the Allia stream, 11 Roman miles north of Rome, on 18 July; most survivors fled to Veii rather than Rome, leaving the city undefended.
events.detail: The Roman left, on the plain, collapsed at the first Gallic charge; the right on high ground retreated to Rome. The dies Alliensis remained a black day (dies ater) in the calendar for the rest of antiquity. Roman numbers are unknown (Plutarch's 40,000 is a guess). Polybius dates the capture of Rome to the year of the King's Peace and Dionysius I's siege of Rhegium, 387/386 BC, while Varronian reckoning gives 390; the difference arises from the Varronian fasti's inflation, including the four 'dictator years' and the five-year anarchy of the 370s. The site lay where the Allia (probably the Fosso della Bettina or Fosso Maestro) joins the Tiber on the left bank near Crustumerium; Diodorus puts the battle on the right bank, a minority view.
events.locName: Allia stream at its confluence with the Tiber, near Crustumerium

sides.losses: heavy; most survivors fled to Veii

battle.significance: Leaves Rome open to capture; the greatest humiliation of early Roman history and a lasting Roman fear of Gauls (metus Gallicus).

scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 715-722
Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001) 140-184
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 313-318
events.debate: Varronian 390 vs Polybian 387/386; which bank of the Tiber.

events.title: Gallic sack of Rome and siege of the Capitol
events.summary: The Gauls entered undefended Rome three days after the Allia, massacred the old senators sitting in their curule chairs, and besieged the Capitol for seven months; after Juno's geese warned M. Manlius of a night assault, the defenders bought them off with 1,000 pounds of gold.
events.detail: Livy's version has Camillus, recalled from exile at Ardea and named dictator, arrive as the gold was weighed, as Brennus threw his sword on the scales with 'vae victis', and drive the Gauls out ('non auro, sed ferro'). Polybius knows nothing of this: the Gauls left with the gold because the Veneti invaded their lands. Diodorus and Strabo say the Caeretans later defeated the Gauls returning laden and recovered the gold; Suetonius (Tib. 3) has a Livius Drusus recover it in Gaul. The Vestals and the flamen Quirinalis escaped to Caere with the sacra in the cart of the plebeian L. Albinius. Aristotle (via Plutarch) knew that 'a Lucius' saved Rome, and Heraclides Ponticus reported that an army of Hyperboreans had taken a Greek city called Rome: the earliest Greek notices of Rome. Archaeologically, the burnt layer once ascribed to the sack in the Comitium is now dated earlier; damage may have been limited, though the trauma was lasting and Rome built the 'Servian' wall in 378.

sides.strength: garrison of the Capitol (men of military age)

sides.losses: disease in the summer heat (Livy); Gauls left with ransom

battle.significance: Only capture of Rome by a foreign enemy until 410 AD. Roman recovery was rapid: within a generation Rome dominated southern Etruria and Latium.

scholarship: Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001) 142-184
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 313-318
Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 719-748
events.debate: Camillus' rescue is fiction; whether Caere defeated the Gauls; the scale of destruction; date 390 vs 387/386.

events.title: Battle of the Elleporus
events.summary: Dionysius I of Syracuse, allied with the Lucanians, crushed the army of the Italiote League under Heloris on the river Elleporus near Caulonia, then released 10,000 prisoners without ransom and broke up the league.
events.detail: Dionysius then destroyed Caulonia (389) and Hipponium, and after an eleven-month siege took Rhegium in 387, the year Polybius synchronises with the Gallic sack of Rome and the King's Peace. His empire spanned Sicily and the toe of Italy, and his fleet raided Pyrgi in 384 and founded posts on the Adriatic (Ancona, Issa, Lissos).

battle.significance: Syracusan hegemony over southern Italy; the Italiote League's centre shifts to Tarentum.

scholarship: Caven, Dionysius I (1990) 154-165

events.title: Rejection of the move to Veii and rebuilding of Rome
events.summary: Tribunes proposed moving the population to empty Veii; Camillus' speech and an omen (a centurion's 'Standard-bearer, plant the standard; here we shall best remain') kept Rome on its site, and the city was rebuilt in haste with state-supplied tiles and free quarrying.
events.detail: Livy blames the haste for Rome's irregular street plan, with sewers running under private houses; this is probably an etiological explanation of the city's archaic layout. The pontifical records were believed lost in the fire, Livy's explanation for the obscurity of earlier history (6.1.2), though much survived.

events.title: Battle of Maecium
events.summary: Camillus as dictator relieved a Roman army surrounded by Volsci at Maecium near Lanuvium, burned the Volscian camp and subdued the Volsci after 70 years of war; he then defeated the Aequi at Bolae and the Etruscans at Sutrium, triumphing three times in one year.
events.detail: Livy's triple victory is patriotic inflation. Yet the period 389-358 does see Volscian, Aequian, Etruscan and Latin enemies probing a weakened Rome and Rome reasserting control.

sides.strength: Volscian army with Latin and Hernican volunteers

battle.significance: Rome reasserts itself after the sack.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 395-420

events.title: Four new tribes on Veientine land
events.summary: The territory of Veii, Capena and Falerii was organised into four new rural tribes, Stellatina, Tromentina, Sabatina and Arnensis, bringing the total to 25.
events.detail: Livy reports that Veientine, Capenate and Faliscan deserters were given citizenship and land, a precedent for absorption of defeated peoples. Tribes were the units of the census, levy and the tribal assemblies; their creation registers Rome's territorial growth, ending with 35 in 241.
scholarship: Taylor, The Voting Districts of the Roman Republic (1960; rev. 2013)

events.title: Colony at Satricum
events.summary: Two thousand Roman citizens were sent to Satricum, each with two and a half iugera, but the site was repeatedly lost to the Volsci and Latins and burned in 377 and 346.
events.detail: Satricum, with its temple of Mater Matuta (findspot of the Lapis Satricanus), was the hinge between the Alban hills and the Pontine plain.

events.title: Trial and execution of M. Manlius Capitolinus
events.summary: M. Manlius, the saviour of the Capitol, championed indebted plebeians, paying off a centurion's debt with his own money; accused of aiming at kingship, he was condemned and thrown from the Tarpeian Rock, and the gens Manlia banned the praenomen Marcus.
events.detail: Livy notes the first trial was abandoned because the jury could see the Capitol he had saved, so it was moved to the Peteline grove outside the Porta Flumentana. His house on the Capitol was razed and the site later given to the temple of Juno Moneta (344). The episode belongs to the debt crisis that produced the Licinio-Sextian laws; the template of the ambitious patrician 'popularis' killed for regnum (Cassius, Maelius, Manlius) is suspiciously regular.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 476-567

events.title: Dionysius I sacks the sanctuary of Pyrgi
events.summary: A Syracusan fleet of 60 triremes under Dionysius I raided Pyrgi, port of Caere, looting at least 1,000 talents from the temple of Leucothea/Ilithyia and defeating a Caeretan relief force.
events.detail: The raid funded Dionysius' war against Carthage. It may explain why Caere, weakened, sought Roman friendship, sheltering Rome's sacra in 390 and receiving hospitium publicum.
scholarship: Caven, Dionysius I (1990)

events.title: Latin colonies at Sutrium and Nepet
events.summary: Sutrium and Nepet, 'the gates of Etruria' on the edge of the Ciminian hills, were made Latin colonies to guard the newly won Veientine territory.
events.detail: Velleius dates Sutrium to seven years after the Gallic sack and Nepet ten years later (373); Livy places Nepet's colony in 383. Sutrium was besieged by the Etruscans in 311-310 and became the base for Fabius Rullianus' march through the Ciminian forest.
scholarship: Salmon, Roman Colonization under the Republic (1969)
events.debate: Velleius and Livy disagree on Nepet's date.

events.title: Tusculum incorporated with Roman citizenship
events.summary: When Camillus marched on Tusculum for aiding the Volsci, the town met him with open gates and business as usual; Rome granted it full citizenship, making Tusculum the first municipium.
events.detail: The incorporation of a whole community, retaining its own magistrates (the Tusculan dictator, later aediles), was a decisive innovation, the model for 338. Tusculum produced many noble families (Mamilii, Fulvii, Porcii, Juventii, Coruncanii) who reached the consulship.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 650-668
Sherwin-White, The Roman Citizenship (2nd ed. 1973) 29-31
events.debate: Some see the 381 grant as civitas sine suffragio upgraded later; most accept full citizenship.

events.title: Battle at the Allia against Praeneste
events.summary: Praeneste, leading the rebel Latins, marched to the Allia hoping the ill-omened site would unnerve Rome; the dictator T. Quinctius Cincinnatus Capitolinus routed them, took eight towns subject to Praeneste and brought back a statue of Jupiter Imperator.
events.detail: The statue was placed on the Capitol with an inscription claiming he had taken nine towns, a boast corrected by Livy and Festus. Praeneste, with its huge territory and later the great sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia, remained a rival until 338.

battle.significance: Breaks the Praenestine-led Latin revolt of the 380s.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 669-686

events.title: Construction of the 'Servian' Wall
events.summary: The censors let contracts for a stone wall of squared tufa blocks enclosing c. 426 hectares and about 11 km of circuit, the largest city wall in Italy at the time.
events.detail: The wall uses Grotta Oscura tufa from quarries in the newly conquered territory of Veii, and blocks carry Greek-style quarry marks, suggesting Greek contractors (perhaps Syracusan). Sections survive outside Termini station and on the Aventine; the Aventine stretch includes a later arch for a catapult. Tradition attributed the wall to Servius Tullius, and an earlier 6th-century cappellaccio rampart (agger) on the Esquiline may lie beneath parts of it.
scholarship: Säflund, Le mura di Roma repubblicana (1932)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 331-332
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997)

events.title: The 'anarchy' of 375-371
events.summary: Livy says the tribunes Licinius and Sextius, re-elected every year, blocked the election of curule magistrates for five years ('solitudo magistratuum'), leaving only plebeian officers.
events.detail: Diodorus records only one year of anarchy, and many scholars see the five years as an artifice of chronographers padding the list to synchronise with Greek dates (like the dictator years of 333, 324, 309 and 301). The fasti for 376-367 are among the most manipulated in the record.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 645-661
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 262-264
events.debate: One year (Diodorus) or five (Livy); relevance to Varronian chronology.

events.title: Gallic incursion to the Alban Hills
events.summary: Livy has Camillus, in his fifth dictatorship at about 80, defeat Gauls in the Alban territory; Polybius says that thirty years after the sack the Gauls came to Alba and the Romans, surprised, did not dare meet them.
events.detail: A good case of Polybius' sober Gallic chronology (2.18) against Livy's glorifying annalists. Gallic bands raided Latium repeatedly in the 360s-350s (Livy has battles in 367, 361, 360, 358, 350, 349), probably reduced to a few real incursions, perhaps some of them mercenaries in the service of Dionysius I.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 727-735
Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 184-186
events.debate: Livy vs Polybius.

events.title: Licinio-Sextian laws
events.summary: After ten years of agitation the tribunes C. Licinius Stolo and L. Sextius Lateranus carried three laws: one consulship to be open to (or reserved for) a plebeian, interest already paid to be deducted from debt principal with the rest payable in three years, and no one to hold more than 500 iugera of public land.
events.detail: The decemviri sacris faciundis (half plebeian) replaced the duoviri as keepers of the Sibylline Books. L. Sextius became the first plebeian consul in 366, and the consular tribunate disappeared. The consulship was not regularly shared until after 342 (patricians held both posts in several years of the 350s). The 500-iugera limit is widely regarded as a retrojection of Gracchan-era rules (Tiberius Gracchus' law reaffirmed it in 133), though Cato's speech for the Rhodians (167) refers to a law on land holdings 'more than 500 iugera', showing it existed by then. Livy adds that Licinius himself was fined in 357 for exceeding his own limit by holding land in his son's name. Cornell sees the laws as creating the patricio-plebeian nobility that ruled thereafter.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 645-661
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 327-340
Hölkeskamp, Die Entstehung der Nobilität (1987)
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 262-267
events.debate: Whether the 500-iugera law is authentic; whether the consulship law required or merely permitted a plebeian consul.

events.title: Camillus' vow of a Temple of Concord
events.summary: Ovid and Plutarch say Camillus vowed a temple to Concordia to mark the reconciliation of the orders in 367; Livy is silent.
events.detail: Momigliano argued the story was invented to give a respectable pedigree to the Temple of Concord rebuilt by L. Opimius in 121 after the murder of Gaius Gracchus, an act of 'concord' through bloodshed. Gnaeus Flavius dedicated a small bronze shrine of Concord in 304, the first securely attested.
scholarship: Momigliano, 'Camillus and Concord', CQ 36 (1942)
events.debate: Probably later invention.

events.title: First praetor and curule aediles; first plebeian consul
events.summary: In 366 L. Sextius took office as the first plebeian consul, while the patricians secured a new magistracy, the praetor, with imperium for jurisdiction, and two curule aediles, initially patrician only.
events.detail: Sp. Furius Camillus, son of the dictator, was the first praetor. The ludi Romani were extended by a day. The curule aedileship alternated between patricians and plebeians within a few years. The praetorship was opened to plebeians in 337 (Q. Publilius Philo).
scholarship: Brennan, The Praetorship in the Roman Republic (2000) I 58-69
Broughton, MRR I 114

events.title: Plague, death of Camillus, and the first stage performances
events.summary: A plague in 365-363 killed Camillus among many; to appease the gods Rome held a second lectisternium and, for the first time, stage performances by Etruscan ludiones dancing to the pipe, the origin of Roman drama in Livy's famous sketch.
events.detail: Livy traces a development from Etruscan dance to Fescennine-style improvised verse, saturae with music, and finally Livius Andronicus' plays with plot in 240. The word histrio came from Etruscan ister. In 363 a dictator was appointed solely to drive the annual nail into the temple of Jupiter as a plague remedy.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 40-72

events.title: Defeat by the Hernici; first plebeian consul to command killed
events.summary: L. Genucius, the first plebeian consul to conduct a war under his own auspices, was ambushed and killed by the rebel Hernici; patricians cried that the gods had punished the plebeian auspices.
events.detail: The dictator Ap. Claudius restored the situation. The Hernican revolt (362-358) shows that the alliance of 486 frayed as Rome grew stronger.

battle.significance: Ammunition for patrician arguments against plebeian auspices.

events.title: Duel of Manlius Torquatus at the Anio bridge
events.summary: With Gallic and Roman armies facing each other across the Anio, a giant Gaul challenged any Roman to single combat; the young T. Manlius killed him, took his torque and earned the cognomen Torquatus.
events.detail: The earliest version, by Claudius Quadrigarius (preserved verbatim by Gellius), is a vivid piece of Sullan-era prose and dates the duel to 361 (Livy) or 357. The torque motif appears on coins of the Manlii Torquati. The Gauls withdrew toward Tibur and Campania.

battle.significance: Founding legend of the Manlii Torquati.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 113-148
Oakley, 'Single combat in the Roman Republic', CQ 35 (1985)

events.title: Battle of Pedum against the Gauls
events.summary: The dictator C. Sulpicius Peticus defeated a Gallic army near Pedum after a long delay, using camp followers mounted on mules as a mock cavalry to frighten the Gauls; he dedicated gold from the spoils on the Capitol.
events.detail: Livy's report of the camp-follower ruse resembles stratagems told elsewhere. Rome's renewed treaty with the Latins this year is linked to the Gallic danger.

battle.significance: Restores Roman prestige in Latium.

events.title: Renewal of the treaty with the Latins and Hernici
events.summary: Under pressure from the Gauls the Latins renewed their alliance with Rome and sent troops 'in accordance with the treaty'; the Hernici were forced back into alliance after their revolt.
events.detail: Livy's language implies the Foedus Cassianum had lapsed. The renewed treaty may have been less equal, with Rome now taking the lead; resentments built toward the war of 340.

events.title: Tribus Pomptina and Publilia created
events.summary: Two new tribes were formed on conquered Volscian land in the Pontine plain (Pomptina) and Hernican land (Publilia), making 27.
events.detail: The same year the tribune C. Poetelius carried the first law on electoral malpractice (lex Poetelia de ambitu), aimed against 'new men' canvassing at markets.

events.title: Tarquinii sacrifices 307 Roman prisoners
