events.locName: Confluence of the Sorgue and Rhône

battle.significance: Broke the Allobroges and opened the Rhône corridor to Roman control.

events.title: Battle of the Isara
events.summary: Quintus Fabius Maximus, grandson of Aemilius Paullus, crushed a huge army of Arverni and Allobroges under the Arvernian king Bituitus near the Isère. Bituitus, famous for his silver chariot and hounds, was later seized at a parley by Ahenobarbus and interned at Alba Fucens.
events.detail: Ancient totals of 120,000 to 130,000 Gauls killed against 15 Roman dead are fantastical, but the victory ended Arvernian hegemony in southern Gaul. Fabius took the name Allobrogicus and, with Ahenobarbus, set up stone trophy towers on the battlefields, a novelty Florus remarks on.
events.locName: Confluence of the Isère and Rhône

battle.significance: Destroyed the Arvernian hegemony and led directly to the creation of the province of Transalpine Gaul.

events.debate: Casualty figures are rhetorical.

events.title: Trial and acquittal of Opimius
events.summary: Prosecuted before the people for killing citizens without trial, Opimius argued that the senate's decree justified him and was acquitted. His defender was Gaius Papirius Carbo, once a Gracchan ally, now consul.
events.detail: The acquittal gave the senatus consultum ultimum practical force. Opimius was convicted in 109 by the Mamilian commission for taking Jugurtha's bribes and died in exile at Dyrrachium.

events.title: Marius' tribunate and the lex Maria
events.summary: As tribune Gaius Marius passed a law narrowing the gangways (pontes) by which voters passed to cast their ballots, to prevent aristocrats from inspecting votes, and threatened to have the consul Cotta arrested when the senate opposed it. He then surprised everyone by vetoing a grain bill.

events.title: Foundation of Narbo Martius
events.summary: A citizen colony was founded at Narbo, championed by the young orator Lucius Licinius Crassus against senatorial objection. It anchored the new province of Transalpine Gaul and the road to Spain.
events.detail: Narbo was the first citizen colony outside Italy that survived (Junonia having been abolished). The Via Domitia, built by Ahenobarbus, ran through it; a milestone naming Gnaeus Domitius as imperator, found at Treilles near Narbonne, is the oldest Roman milestone known in Gaul.

events.title: Construction of the Via Domitia
events.summary: Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus built the road linking Italy to Spain along the Mediterranean coast of Gaul, from the Alps via Nemausus and Narbo to the Pyrenees. Pompey later fortified its Pyrenean pass with his trophies (71).
events.note: Date of construction c. 120-118; Cicero mentions its upkeep in the 70s.

events.title: Death of Micipsa and partition of Numidia
events.summary: King Micipsa, son of Masinissa, left Numidia jointly to his sons Adherbal and Hiempsal and to his adopted nephew Jugurtha, a veteran of Numantia with friends among the Roman nobility. Jugurtha had Hiempsal murdered at Thirmida within a year.
events.detail: In 116 a senatorial commission led by Opimius divided the kingdom: Jugurtha got the richer, more populous west; Adherbal the east with Cirta and its ports. Sallust says the commissioners were bought.

events.title: Trial of the Vestals and human sacrifice in the Forum Boarium
events.summary: After a prodigy in which a girl riding on horseback was struck dead by lightning, three Vestals, Aemilia, Licinia and Marcia, were accused of unchastity. The pontiffs condemned only Aemilia; a special tribunal under Lucius Cassius Longinus Ravilla condemned the other two in 113. Two Gauls and two Greeks were buried alive in the Forum Boarium, and a temple was vowed to Venus Verticordia.
events.detail: This was the last recorded Roman human sacrifice of this ritual type (also performed in 228 and 216). Cassius was the judge famous for asking 'cui bono?'. The affair shows religious anxiety about the Cimbri and the political use of religious courts: the tribunal was set up by a tribune's law over pontifical jurisdiction.

events.title: Battle of Noreia
events.summary: The consul Gnaeus Papirius Carbo, trying to protect the Taurisci of Noricum, Roman guest-friends, ambushed the migrating Cimbri after negotiating their withdrawal, and was routed. Only a storm saved his army from annihilation.
events.detail: This was the first Roman encounter with the Cimbri, a people whose origin the ancients placed in Jutland. Carbo was later prosecuted by Marcus Antonius and killed himself. Noreia's site is unknown; the Magdalensberg and sites near Neumarkt in Styria have been proposed.

battle.significance: Opened twelve years of Cimbrian warfare and exposed Roman treachery as counterproductive.

events.title: Siege of Cirta and the massacre of the Italians
events.summary: Jugurtha besieged Adherbal in Cirta for months while senatorial embassies came and went. The Italian traders defending the city persuaded Adherbal to surrender on terms; Jugurtha tortured him to death and massacred the adult Numidians and Italian merchants (negotiatores) alike.
events.detail: The killing of Italici, men with links to the equestrian business class, made war unavoidable: the tribune-elect Gaius Memmius whipped up the people and the senate assigned Numidia to the consul of 111, Bestia.

battle.significance: Turned a dynastic dispute into a Roman war.

events.note: Both sides are Numidian; Adherbal's faction is given as numidia.

events.title: Jugurtha in Rome and the murder of Massiva
events.summary: After Bestia granted Jugurtha lenient terms, the tribune Memmius summoned him to Rome under safe conduct to testify against the nobles he had bribed. Another tribune, Baebius, forbade him to speak. While in Rome Jugurtha had his cousin Massiva, a rival claimant, assassinated by his agent Bomilcar and was expelled.
events.detail: Leaving the city, Jugurtha is said to have looked back and called Rome a city for sale and doomed to perish if it found a buyer. Sallust built his whole monograph around this theme of aristocratic venality.
scholarship: Paul, A Historical Commentary on Sallust's Bellum Jugurthinum (1984)

events.title: Lex agraria of 111
events.summary: An agrarian law, preserved on the reverse of the bronze Tabula Bembina (CIL I2 585), converted Gracchan allotments and permitted holdings of ager publicus into private land free of rent and halted further distribution. It effectively wound up the Gracchan programme in Italy and regulated public land in Africa and at Corinth.
events.detail: It is the longest surviving Republican statute text. Appian's account (BC 1.27) of three post-Gracchan laws, first allowing sale of allotments, then stopping distribution, then abolishing rent, is usually reconciled with it.
scholarship: Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)

events.title: Capitulation of Aulus Albinus at Suthul
events.summary: Aulus Postumius Albinus, left in command by his brother the consul, marched in midwinter to seize Jugurtha's treasury at Suthul. A night attack, helped by bribed centurions and auxiliaries, broke his camp; the army passed under the yoke and agreed to leave Numidia within ten days.
events.detail: The senate repudiated the agreement. The humiliation produced the Mamilian commission and, indirectly, Marius' consulship.

sides.losses: camp taken, army sent under the yoke

battle.significance: The low point of the war; discredited the senatorial leadership at Rome.

events.note: Suthul is sometimes identified with Calama (Guelma).

events.title: The Mamilian commission
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Mamilius Limetanus established a special court, with equestrian juries, to try those who had taken Jugurtha's money. It condemned Opimius, Bestia, Spurius Albinus, Gaius Cato and the priest Gaius Sulpicius Galba. Scaurus, himself implicated, contrived to be one of the three presiding commissioners.

events.title: Battle of the Muthul
events.summary: Jugurtha ambushed Quintus Caecilius Metellus' column from a scrub-covered ridge parallel to its march. After a long day's fighting the Romans drove off the Numidian infantry while Publius Rutilius Rufus defeated Bomilcar's elephants, killing or capturing all 44.
events.detail: Sallust's set-piece is the best tactical narrative of the war. The battle showed Metellus' disciplined army could beat Jugurtha in the open but not catch him; Jugurtha simply dispersed and reassembled.

sides.strength: consular army of perhaps 2 legions plus allies

battle.significance: Tactical Roman success that did not end the war; Jugurtha turned to guerrilla warfare.

events.title: Failed siege of Zama
events.summary: Metellus besieged Zama to force Jugurtha to battle but failed to take it and withdrew to winter quarters. Over the winter the garrison at Vaga was massacred in a rising, and its commander Turpilius, a friend of Metellus, was executed.

battle.significance: Showed the limits of siege warfare against a mobile enemy.

events.title: Scaurus builds the Pons Mulvius and Via Aemilia Scauri
events.summary: As censor Marcus Aemilius Scaurus rebuilt the Milvian Bridge over the Tiber in stone and built the Via Aemilia Scauri along the Tyrrhenian coast from Pisa via Vada to Dertona. The bridge's piers still carry traffic.

events.title: Siege of Thala
events.summary: Metellus marched across waterless country, carrying water in skins on pack animals, and took Jugurtha's treasure town Thala after a 40-day siege. Jugurtha escaped with his children and much of the treasure; Roman deserters inside burned themselves in the palace.

battle.significance: Showed Rome could reach Jugurtha's strongholds; prompted Bocchus of Mauretania to join Jugurtha.

events.title: Marius elected consul for 107
events.summary: Gaius Marius, a novus homo from Arpinum and Metellus' legate, returned to Rome against his commander's wishes, campaigned on Metellus' slowness and was elected consul. A tribunician law then gave him the Numidian command, overriding the senate's decision to prorogue Metellus.
events.detail: Metellus had told him not to hurry: he could stand when Metellus' son did, a jibe at a man of nearly fifty. Sallust stresses the support of equites and Italian businessmen frustrated by the war's cost. The popular reassignment of a command against the senate's allocation was a precedent repeated in 88 with fatal results.

events.title: Marius enrols the capite censi
events.summary: Raising reinforcements for Numidia, Marius enrolled volunteers from the proletarii (capite censi, those assessed by head count) rather than conscripting from the property classes. Sallust says he did it to court popularity or because the poor had nothing to lose.
events.detail: This is the core of what modern textbooks call the Marian reforms, a bundle that also includes the modification of the pilum with a wooden rivet (Plut Mar 25), the eagle as the legion's sole standard (Pliny NH 10.16, dated to his second consulship, 104), the soldier carrying his own kit (Marius' mules) and the cohort as tactical unit. The property qualification had been falling for a century (Polybius' 400 drachmae, later 1,500 or 4,000 asses), the cohort appears already in Polybius' Spanish narratives, and conscription continued after 107. The real change was a gradual one: armies of poor long-service men dependent on their general for discharge bounties of land.
scholarship: Gabba, Republican Rome: The Army and the Allies (1976)
Cadiou, L'armée imaginaire (2018)
Matthew, On the Wings of Eagles: The Reforms of Gaius Marius (2010)
Rich, Historia 32 (1983)
events.debate: Gabba saw a decisive proletarianisation; Rich and Cadiou argue the 'Marian reforms' are largely a modern construct, the army changing gradually and recruitment of the poor being neither new nor universal after 107.

events.title: Defeat of Cassius Longinus by the Tigurini
events.summary: The consul Lucius Cassius Longinus, Marius' colleague, was killed with his legate Lucius Piso in an ambush by the Tigurini, a Helvetian canton, led by the young Divico. The legate Gaius Popillius Laenas saved the survivors by surrendering half the baggage and sending the army under the yoke.
events.detail: Caesar used the memory in 58 to justify attacking the Tigurini on the Arar, noting with satisfaction that the canton that had killed Lucius Piso, his father-in-law's grandfather, was the first to pay. Popillius was prosecuted for the surrender.
events.locName: territory of the Nitiobriges, near Agen

sides.losses: consul and legate killed; army under the yoke

battle.significance: Another consular army lost; the Volcae Tectosages of Tolosa defected.

events.note: Orosius places it near Burdigala; Livy's Periocha says in the territory of the Nitiobriges (Agen).

events.title: Marius takes Capsa
events.summary: Marius marched for days across desert, driving cattle for food and water, and stormed Capsa at dawn. Though it surrendered, the town was burned, its adult men killed and the rest sold, the booty divided among the troops.
events.detail: Sallust admits the act was contrary to the laws of war, justified as necessary against a fickle and hostile population. The exploit established Marius' reputation and his soldiers' loyalty.

battle.significance: Bold deep raid that demonstrated no Numidian town was beyond reach.

events.title: Capture of the fort on the Mulucha
events.summary: On the far western border of Numidia Marius besieged a fort on a sheer rock holding a royal treasury. A Ligurian auxiliary, climbing to gather snails, found a route up the back; a small party with trumpeters scaled it and panicked the defenders.

battle.significance: Deprived Jugurtha of treasure on the Mauretanian border, pressuring Bocchus.

events.title: Battles near Cirta
events.summary: Returning east to winter quarters, Marius' army was attacked at dusk by Jugurtha and Bocchus combined and held a pair of hills through the night; a dawn sally routed the Africans. A few days later a second battle near Cirta, with Sulla commanding the cavalry, ended in another Roman victory.
events.detail: Sallust describes Jugurtha in the second fight brandishing a bloody sword and shouting in Latin that he had killed Marius. After this Bocchus opened negotiations through Sulla.

sides.strength: large combined Numidian and Moorish cavalry and infantry

battle.significance: Broke the Numidian-Mauretanian alliance militarily and led Bocchus to betray Jugurtha.

events.title: Lex Servilia Caepionis
events.summary: The consul Quintus Servilius Caepio carried a law restoring senators to the extortion juries, alone or alongside equites. Crassus the orator's speech for it (attacking equestrian juries) was a celebrated model. It was reversed within a few years by Glaucia's law.
events.debate: Whether juries were wholly senatorial or mixed is uncertain.

events.title: The gold of Tolosa
events.summary: Caepio occupied Tolosa, whose Volcae Tectosages had joined the Cimbri, and seized temple treasures and sacred lakes of bullion that Posidonius put at 15,000 talents. The convoy sent to Massalia was ambushed and the treasure vanished; Caepio was widely suspected, and 'having Tolosan gold' became a proverb for ill-gotten wealth that brings ruin.
events.detail: Strabo, following Posidonius, rejects the legend that it was Delphic gold looted by Brennus' Gauls in 279. Caepio was condemned in 103 by a quaestio set up by the tribune Norbanus, partly over the treasure, partly over Arausio, and died in exile at Smyrna.

events.title: Bocchus hands Jugurtha to Sulla
events.summary: After months of secret negotiation, Bocchus of Mauretania lured Jugurtha to a meeting and handed him in chains to Marius' quaestor, Lucius Cornelius Sulla, ending the war. Bocchus received the western part of Numidia.
events.detail: Sulla had a signet ring cut showing the surrender and used it all his life; Marius regarded the credit as his own. In 91 Bocchus set up a gilded group of the scene on the Capitol, which provoked a near-riot between Marius' and Sulla's partisans. Sulla's son Faustus struck a denarius of it in 56 (RRC 426/1). Jugurtha walked in Marius' triumph on 1 January 104 and was then starved to death in the Tullianum.

events.title: Marius' Numidian triumph and death of Jugurtha
events.summary: Marius celebrated his triumph over Jugurtha on the day he entered his second consulship, then entered the senate still in triumphal dress, a breach of custom. Jugurtha was thrown naked into the Tullianum; Plutarch has him exclaim how cold the Romans' bath was before he starved six days later.

events.title: The Praetorians auction the empire to Didius Julianus
events.summary: After murdering Pertinax on 28 March 193, the Praetorian Guard sold the throne to the senator Marcus Didius Julianus, who outbid Pertinax's father-in-law Flavius Sulpicianus with a promise of 25,000 sesterces per guardsman.
events.detail: Dio, an eyewitness senator, describes the bidding conducted from the walls of the Castra Praetoria, Sulpicianus inside the camp and Julianus shouting offers from outside. Julianus never won the urban plebs, who pelted him in the Circus and called on Pescennius Niger, and within two weeks three provincial armies had proclaimed their own commanders. The episode became the classic illustration of the Guard's power and directly prompted Severus to abolish the old Italian Praetorian cohorts.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Herodian and Dio dramatise the 'auction'; the HA life is late and partly derivative, but the core sequence is accepted.

events.title: Pescennius Niger proclaimed emperor at Antioch
events.summary: Gaius Pescennius Niger, governor of Syria, was acclaimed by the eastern legions and enjoyed the support of the Roman populace, but delayed in Antioch while Severus took Rome.
events.detail: Niger controlled nine legions and Egypt's grain, and won the backing of Antioch and, crucially, Byzantium, which controlled the Bosporus crossing. Parthian and client rulers (Hatra, Osroene, Adiabene) offered or promised help, giving Severus his pretext for the eastern wars of 195 and 197-198.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: The HA life of Niger is among the most fictional in the collection (forged letters and documents).

events.title: Septimius Severus proclaimed emperor at Carnuntum
events.summary: Lucius Septimius Severus, legate of Pannonia Superior, was hailed Augustus by the Danube legions at Carnuntum, posing as the avenger of Pertinax and adding Pertinax to his name.
events.detail: Severus, an African senator from Lepcis Magna, could count on all sixteen legions of the Rhine and Danube. He marched on Rome so fast that Julianus' attempts to fortify the city, train elephants and send assassins collapsed. To secure his rear he offered the title of Caesar to Clodius Albinus in Britain, isolating Pescennius Niger in the East.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Severus enters Rome and disbands the Praetorian Guard
events.summary: After the Senate condemned Julianus, who was killed in the palace on 1 June 193, Severus summoned the Praetorians unarmed, cashiered them and replaced them with a doubled guard drawn from his Danubian legionaries.
events.detail: The new Guard of ten milliary cohorts, with the Urban Cohorts and Vigiles also enlarged, made Rome a garrison city of perhaps 30,000 men once II Parthica was stationed at Albanum. Italians lost their near-monopoly on Guard service, a change Dio deplores as filling the capital with savage-looking soldiers. Severus deified Pertinax and staged a lavish funeral to legitimise himself.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Clodius Albinus accepts the title of Caesar
events.summary: Decimus Clodius Albinus, governor of Britain with three legions, accepted Severus' offer of the rank of Caesar and coinage in his name, neutralising him while Severus dealt with Niger.
events.detail: Albinus, an aristocrat from Hadrumetum, struck coins as Caesar at Rome and held the consulship of 194 with Severus. The arrangement implied succession, a promise Severus cancelled in 195 when he made his elder son Caesar.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Battle of Cyzicus
events.summary: Severan forces defeated and killed Niger's general Asellius Aemilianus near Cyzicus, opening Asia Minor to Severus.
events.detail: Niger had crossed into Europe and occupied Byzantium and Perinthus, but Severus' troops, crossing the Propontis elsewhere, caught Aemilianus, proconsul of Asia, near Cyzicus. Aemilianus was killed (Dio says while fleeing; Herodian hints he was already disloyal to Niger).

battle.significance: First major defeat for Niger; he withdrew behind the Taurus and the Cilician Gates.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Exact date (late 193 or early 194) uncertain; commander on the Severan side probably Ti. Claudius Candidus.

events.title: Siege of Byzantium
events.summary: Byzantium, having sided with Niger, held out against Severan forces for some two and a half years, surviving even after Niger's death until famine forced surrender in late 195.
events.detail: Dio gives a vivid account of the city's walls of squared stone bound with bronze plates, the engines of the engineer Priscus of Nicaea, and the citizens reduced to eating hides and finally each other. Severus executed the magistrates and soldiers, razed the walls, and subordinated the city to Perinthus as a village; it was soon rebuilt, reportedly at Caracalla's request.

sides.strength: citizens and Nigerian remnants; c. 500 small boats

battle.significance: Destroyed the walls guarding the Bosporus, which Dio later blamed for opening the straits to raiders.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Marius Maximus, later biographer of emperors and a lost source of the HA, commanded Moesian forces in the siege according to his career inscription.

events.title: Battle of Issus
events.summary: On the plain of Issus, where Alexander had beaten Darius, Severus' general Publius Cornelius Anullinus decisively defeated Pescennius Niger, whose army broke after a storm blew in its face.
events.detail: Niger's army held a strong position in the pass, but a cavalry force under Valerianus outflanked it through the woods while a thunderstorm, beating into the faces of Niger's men and at the backs of the Severans, was read as divine favour. Dio claims 20,000 of Niger's men died. Niger fled toward the Euphrates hoping to reach Parthia but was caught and beheaded near Antioch; his head was displayed before Byzantium to break its resistance.

battle.significance: Ended Niger's bid; the East passed to Severus, who punished Antioch and rewarded Laodicea.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Date usually spring 194; Dio's casualty figure is a round literary number. Both authors stress the Alexandrian echo.

events.title: Battle of Nicaea
events.summary: Niger in person was defeated by the Severan general Tiberius Claudius Candidus in the defiles between Cius and Nicaea, and retreated through the Cilician Gates.
events.detail: Dio describes a battle fought partly on the plain and partly in the narrows and on the lake of Ascania, with Niger's appearance briefly rallying his men. Candidus' victory exposed Bithynia and led cities such as Nicaea and Nicomedia to declare for opposite sides, a vivid sign of civic rivalry exploited in civil wars.

battle.significance: Drove Niger out of Asia Minor.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Syria divided; Antioch humiliated
events.summary: After Niger's defeat Severus split Syria into Syria Coele and Syria Phoenice, stripped Antioch of its city status in favour of Laodicea, and punished other Nigerian cities.
events.detail: The division continued the Hadrianic and Antonine practice of reducing the number of legions under any single governor; Britain was likewise split into Superior and Inferior, probably early in the third century. Antioch was made a village of Laodicea and its Olympic games transferred, while Laodicea, Tyre and other loyal cities received colonial or metropolitan titles. Antioch's status was restored under Caracalla.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Date of the British division (197, c. 213 or later) disputed; Herodian 3.8.2 places it under Severus.

events.title: Severus' first eastern campaign: Osroene and Adiabene
events.summary: In 195 Severus crossed the Euphrates against Osroene, Adiabene and Arab allies who had supported Niger and besieged Nisibis, taking the titles Arabicus and Adiabenicus.
events.detail: Using the pretext of the clients' support for Niger, Severus based himself at Nisibis and sent columns across northern Mesopotamia. Much of Osroene was annexed, leaving the Abgarid king at Edessa with a rump. The campaign laid the groundwork for the province of Mesopotamia and was cut short by news of Albinus' defection. Severus refused the title Parthicus to avoid provoking Vologaeses.

events.title: Severus declares himself son of Marcus Aurelius
events.summary: Severus retroactively adopted himself into the Antonine house as 'divi Marci filius', renamed his son Bassianus Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (Caracalla) and made him Caesar, an open break with Albinus.
events.detail: The fiction, ridiculed by a senator who congratulated Severus on finding a father, gave the new dynasty Antonine legitimacy and allowed the rehabilitation of Commodus, deified as Severus' 'brother' in 197. Inscriptions trace Severus' lineage back to Nerva. The making of Caracalla Caesar, probably at Viminacium in 195 or 196, converted the agreement with Albinus into war.

events.title: Clodius Albinus proclaimed Augustus
events.summary: Cut out of the succession, Albinus was hailed Augustus by the British legions and crossed to Gaul, setting up his base at Lugdunum, where he minted coins; the Senate declared him a public enemy in December 196.
events.detail: Albinus had senatorial sympathy at Rome, where crowds at the Circus chanted against a new civil war. In Gaul he defeated the governor of Germania Inferior, Virius Lupus, but failed to win over the Rhine legions, which remained loyal to Severus.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Battle of Lugdunum
events.summary: Severus defeated Clodius Albinus in a vast battle north of Lyon; Dio puts some 150,000 men on each side. Albinus committed suicide or was killed and his corpse was mutilated; Lugdunum was sacked.
events.detail: Albinus' left wing was routed, but his right lured Severus' men into concealed trenches and pits; Severus himself was unhorsed and threw off his purple cloak, and only the arrival of the cavalry under Julius Laetus decided the day (Dio insinuates Laetus had waited to see who was winning, and Severus later had him executed). Albinus' head was sent to Rome. Severus confiscated vast estates of Albinus' partisans in Gaul, Spain and Britain, creating the res privata as a major branch of imperial finance. Preliminary fighting took place near Tinurtium (Tournus), named in the HA.

sides.strength: c. 150,000 (Dio); British legions and Gallic recruits

battle.significance: The largest battle between Roman armies recorded; ended the civil wars of 193-197 and left Severus sole ruler.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Dio's 300,000 total is impossible for the forces available; modern estimates are far lower. The exact field is unknown.

events.title: Severus' purge of the Senate
events.summary: Returning to Rome in June 197, Severus praised the cruelty of Marius, Sulla and Augustus before the Senate and executed 29 senators accused of supporting Albinus, while sparing 35 others.
events.detail: Severus deified Commodus as his adoptive brother, a deliberate insult to senators who had hated him. The confiscations, together with those of Niger's partisans, filled the treasury and enabled the first pay rise for soldiers since Domitian.
events.debate: The HA lists 41 names, many probably invented.

events.title: Severan army reforms: pay, marriage and new legions
events.summary: Severus raised military pay (legionary stipendium probably from 300 to 450 or 500 denarii), allowed serving soldiers to marry legally, and raised three new legions, I, II and III Parthica, the latter two under equestrian prefects.
events.detail: Herodian attributes to Severus the dying advice to his sons to 'enrich the soldiers and scorn everyone else'. Legal marriage formalised long-standing unions in the canabae; centurions gained the right to wear the gold ring of equestrian rank. II Parthica's base at Albanum, 20 km from Rome, put a legion in Italy for the first time since Augustus, creating a central strategic reserve that anticipated later field armies. I and III Parthica garrisoned the new province of Mesopotamia at Singara and Rhesaina.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: The size of the pay increase is reconstructed from papyri and Speidel's calculations; dates for the marriage concession range 197-200.

events.title: Parthian siege of Nisibis
events.summary: While Severus fought Albinus, Vologaeses V attacked the new Roman positions in Mesopotamia and besieged Nisibis, defended by Julius Laetus until Severus' arrival in summer 197 lifted the threat.

battle.significance: Gave Severus his casus belli for a full invasion of Parthia.

events.title: Severus sacks Ctesiphon
events.summary: Sailing down the Euphrates with a river fleet, Severus took Seleucia and Babylon, then stormed the Parthian capital Ctesiphon in late 197 or January 198, sacking it and, according to Dio, carrying off 100,000 captives.
events.detail: Vologaeses V fled. The sack, the third Roman capture of Ctesiphon in eighty years (Trajan 116, Avidius Cassius 165), was timed to the centenary of Trajan's accession and was celebrated with the title Parthicus Maximus on 28 January 198. Severus did not hold the city: supply failures forced a return up the Tigris. The repeated blows on Ctesiphon gravely weakened Arsacid prestige and are usually seen as a background cause of the Persian revolt of Ardashir a generation later.

sides.strength: perhaps 3 Parthian legions plus vexillations and a river fleet

battle.significance: Humiliated the Arsacids and made Mesopotamia a permanent Roman province.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Herodian makes the fleet's arrival at Ctesiphon accidental; Dio's captive total is implausibly round.

events.title: Caracalla raised to Augustus, Geta to Caesar
events.summary: On the centenary of Trajan's accession and the day of the victory proclamation over Parthia, Severus made the ten-year-old Caracalla co-Augustus and his younger son Geta Caesar.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: First Severan siege of Hatra
events.summary: Returning up the Tigris, Severus attacked Hatra, the walled Arab caravan city in the desert, but its engines and naphtha bombs burned his siege works and he withdrew.

battle.significance: Repeated Trajan's failure of 117 at the same city.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Herodian telescopes the two sieges into one; Dio distinguishes them.

events.title: Creation of the province of Mesopotamia
events.summary: Severus organised northern Mesopotamia as a province under an equestrian prefect with legions I and III Parthica, centred on Nisibis, now a Roman colonia.
events.detail: Dio judged the province a source of constant wars and expense, a drain that drew Rome into every Persian quarrel. In fact Nisibis and Singara became the hinge of Roman-Persian conflict for 165 years until Jovian surrendered them in 363. Osroene was reduced to a rump client around Edessa and annexed in 213/214 and finally in 242.

events.title: Second Severan siege of Hatra
events.summary: Severus returned to Hatra in 199 with larger engines; when a breach was made, he called off the assault, hoping the city would surrender its treasure intact, but his exasperated European troops refused to renew the attack and the siege was abandoned after 20 days.
events.detail: Dio records that the Syrian troops ordered to attack were slaughtered and that Severus could not get his men to try again. The failure marked the limit of Severan expansion; Hatra later became a Roman ally with an attested Roman garrison (cohors IX Maurorum) in the 230s.

battle.significance: Ended Severus' eastern offensives.

events.title: Severus in Egypt; Alexandria receives a council
events.summary: Severus toured Egypt and Upper Egypt, visiting Memphis, Thebes and the 'singing' colossus of Memnon, and granted Alexandria and the metropoleis of the nomes town councils (boulai), a major change in Egyptian administration.
events.detail: The grant of councils, completed in 200/201, aligned Egypt with the civic organisation of the rest of the East and made councillors liable for tax collection. Severus is said to have repaired the Memnon colossus, after which it ceased to sing at dawn. He also issued responses to petitions (apokrimata) preserved on papyrus, a rare direct view of the emperor's justice.

events.title: Severus visits Africa; building at Lepcis and the Tripolitanian frontier
events.summary: Severus returned to his native Lepcis Magna, which received the ius Italicum, a new forum, basilica, colonnaded street and harbour, while the frontier of Tripolitania was pushed south with forts at Gholaia (Bu Njem), Gheriat and Cidamus (Ghadames).
events.debate: Whether Severus visited Africa in 202/203 is inferred from coins and the HA; Gholaia's foundation is dated 201 by inscription.

events.title: Martyrdom of Perpetua and Felicity at Carthage
events.summary: The young noblewoman Vibia Perpetua and her slave Felicitas, catechumens, were killed in the amphitheatre of Carthage at games for Geta's birthday; the Passio preserves Perpetua's own prison diary, the earliest surviving text by a Christian woman.
events.detail: The Passio Perpetuae records her dreams of a ladder to heaven and of fighting an Egyptian as a man, and her refusal of her pagan father's pleas. The text, possibly edited by a Montanist (Tertullian has been suggested), is a central document for women, martyrdom and North African Christianity. The HA claims Severus banned conversion to Judaism and Christianity, a statement most scholars doubt.
events.debate: Whether there was a general Severan persecution is rejected by most; prosecutions were local.

events.title: Arch of Septimius Severus dedicated in the Forum
events.summary: The Senate dedicated a triple arch at the foot of the Capitol celebrating the Parthian victories, with panels showing the sieges of Nisibis, Edessa, Seleucia and Ctesiphon; Geta's name was later erased from the inscription.

events.title: Secular Games of Septimius Severus
events.summary: Severus celebrated the seventh Ludi Saeculares in June 204, following the Augustan schedule of 110-year cycles; the acta, partly preserved on inscriptions, list Julia Domna leading 109 matrons in prayers.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Fall of the praetorian prefect Plautianus
events.summary: Gaius Fulvius Plautianus, Severus' fellow Lepcitane and all-powerful praetorian prefect, whose daughter Plautilla had married Caracalla in 202, was accused of conspiracy and cut down in the palace in Caracalla's presence.
events.detail: Plautianus had accumulated statues, wealth and influence beyond any prefect since Sejanus; Dio says he castrated a hundred free Romans to attend his daughter. The plot charge was probably fabricated by Caracalla, who loathed his wife. Plautilla was exiled to Lipara and killed in 212. Papinian and Maecius Laetus replaced Plautianus, inaugurating the age of jurist-prefects.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Bulla Felix's bandit band in Italy
events.summary: For two years the brigand Bulla Felix and 600 followers plundered Italy, freeing imperial slaves and robbing travellers under the noses of the emperors, until he was betrayed by a mistress and thrown to the beasts.
events.detail: Dio attributes to Bulla a Robin Hood maxim to the praetorian prefect Papinian, telling him to 'feed your slaves, so they won't turn bandit'. The episode, whatever its embellishment, reflects rural insecurity and the absorption of runaway and underpaid imperial slaves.

events.title: Severus' expedition to Britain and Caledonia
events.summary: Severus, his sons and the court moved to Britain in 208, made Eboracum the imperial capital and campaigned deep into Caledonia in 209 and 210 against the Caledonii and Maeatae, building a legionary base at Carpow on the Tay.
events.detail: Dio reports 50,000 Roman casualties from ambush and disease, a figure probably inflated. The Maeatae and Caledonians submitted in 209 and revolted in 210, when Severus ordered genocide ('let no one escape sheer destruction', quoting Homer). Coins of 210-211 proclaim VICTORIAE BRITTANNICAE. Hadrian's Wall was heavily restored in this period, and Severus' death in February 211 ended the project of conquest; Caracalla made peace and withdrew to the wall.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Whether Severus intended permanent conquest of all Scotland or a punitive war is debated; the Carpow fortress (with stamps of II Augusta and VI Victrix) argues for occupation.

events.title: Death of Septimius Severus at Eboracum
events.summary: Severus died of illness, probably gout-related, at York aged 65, leaving his sons as joint emperors with the advice, per Dio, to 'agree with each other, enrich the soldiers and scorn all others'.
events.detail: His ashes were carried in a porphyry urn to the Mausoleum of Hadrian. Severus' reign, dominated by the army, the jurists and the Syrian-African court, is often taken as the hinge between the Principate and the third-century military monarchy, though Millar and others emphasise continuity in the civil administration.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Caracalla murders Geta
events.summary: After ten months of joint rule, during which the brothers divided the palace and reportedly considered splitting the empire, Caracalla had centurions kill Geta in the arms of their mother Julia Domna.
events.detail: Caracalla claimed to have foiled a plot and rushed to the Praetorian camp with a large donative. Dio says 20,000 of Geta's household and partisans were killed; Geta suffered a thorough damnatio memoriae, his face scraped from the Severan Tondo and his name chiselled from inscriptions across the empire. The jurist Papinian was executed in 212, reportedly for refusing to compose a justification of the murder.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Date sometimes given as 19 December or February 212; 26 December 211 is the most common reconstruction from the Chronograph of 354.

events.title: Constitutio Antoniniana: citizenship for all free inhabitants
events.summary: Caracalla granted Roman citizenship to virtually all free inhabitants of the empire, excepting only the dediticii; Dio says the real motive was to extend the 5% inheritance tax (raised to 10%) and the manumission tax.
events.detail: The edict survives in a damaged Greek copy on P.Giss. 40, in which Caracalla thanks the gods for his preservation (probably from Geta's 'plot') and offers citizenship to the inhabitants of the oikoumene. Hundreds of thousands of new citizens took the nomen Aurelius, which makes third-century prosopography a sea of Aurelii. Long-term consequences included the gradual displacement of local legal systems by Roman law (though local practice persisted, as Egyptian papyri show), the collapse of the citizen/peregrine distinction in the army and the hardening of the honestiores/humiliores divide as the main legal status line. The exact scope of the dediticii exclusion is one of the most debated cruxes in Roman legal history.
scholarship: Buraselis, Theia Dorea (1989/2007)
Ando, Imperial Rome AD 193 to 284 (2012)
Besson, Constitutio Antoniniana (2020)
events.debate: Date (212 or 213), identity of the dediticii, whether P.Giss. 40 is the edict itself, and motive (fiscal, religious thanksgiving, ideological unification) are all disputed.

events.title: Caracalla's campaign against the Alamanni
events.summary: Caracalla crossed the Raetian limes in August 213 and defeated a Germanic coalition near the Main, taking the title Germanicus Maximus; Dio's account contains the first apparent mention of the Alamanni.
events.detail: The Acta of the Arval Brethren record sacrifices on 11 August 213 for Caracalla's entry into barbarian territory through Raetia. The victory was followed by payments to tribes, which Dio criticises. Whether the name Alamanni in Dio's text is original or inserted by the Byzantine excerptor Xiphilinus is a well-known controversy; Drinkwater argues the Alamanni as a people coalesced only in the later third century.
events.locName: Beyond the Raetian limes, Main region
scholarship: Drinkwater, The Alamanni and Rome 213-496 (2007)
events.debate: Dio's 'Alamanni' may be anachronistic.

events.title: Introduction of the antoninianus
events.summary: Caracalla introduced a new silver coin, the radiate 'antoninianus', apparently tariffed at two denarii but weighing only about 1.5 denarii, a concealed debasement to fund army pay.
events.detail: The denarius itself had already fallen to around 50% silver under Severus after his pay rise. The antoninianus (a modern name; its ancient name is uncertain, perhaps argenteus Antoninianus) was dropped under Severus Alexander and revived in 238, after which it drove out the denarius. Repeated debasement reduced it to under 5% silver by 268-270, the core of the third-century monetary collapse.
scholarship: Walker, The Metrology of the Roman Silver Coinage III (1978)
Estiot, in Metcalf (ed.), Oxford Handbook of Greek and Roman Coinage (2012)
events.debate: The face value of the antoninianus (two denarii is the usual but unproven assumption) is disputed.

events.title: Caracalla's massacre at Alexandria
events.summary: Offended by Alexandrian lampoons mocking him as a fratricide and his pretensions to be Alexander, Caracalla had the city's youths assembled for supposed recruitment into a phalanx and massacred, then expelled non-resident Egyptians.
events.detail: Dio and Herodian both describe thousands killed. A papyrus (P.Giss. 40 col. II) preserves Caracalla's order expelling Egyptian peasants from Alexandria, except those engaged in trade or worship, with the line that true Egyptians can be recognised by their speech and manners. The Museum's scholars lost their privileges.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Baths of Caracalla dedicated
events.summary: The Thermae Antoninianae on the Via Appia, begun by Severus around 211, were dedicated in 216; the central block covered c. 2.5 hectares and could serve perhaps 1,600 bathers at once.
events.detail: The complex contained libraries, a natatio, and colossal sculptures such as the Farnese Bull and Farnese Hercules. Its frigidarium vaults and brick-faced concrete remained the model for later imperial baths, including those of Diocletian.

events.title: Caracalla's invasion of Parthia
events.summary: After Artabanus IV refused Caracalla's request to marry his daughter (a project to unite the two empires, according to Herodian), Caracalla invaded Media and Adiabene in 216, sacking towns and desecrating the royal tombs at Arbela.
events.detail: Herodian's tale of Caracalla massacring Parthian wedding guests is probably invented; Dio's version has Artabanus refusing outright. Caracalla advanced from Edessa, where he wintered, and planned a new campaign for 217 when he was murdered.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Assassination of Caracalla near Carrhae
events.summary: Travelling from Edessa to the temple of the Moon god at Carrhae, Caracalla dismounted to relieve himself and was stabbed by the guardsman Julius Martialis, acting for the praetorian prefect Macrinus, who feared exposure by an astrologer's prophecy.
events.detail: Martialis was killed by Scythian bodyguards. After three days of uncertainty the army acclaimed Macrinus on 11 April, the first equestrian emperor, who had never sat in the Senate. Julia Domna, at Antioch, starved herself to death.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Battle of Nisibis
events.summary: Artabanus IV invaded Mesopotamia to avenge Caracalla's attacks and fought Macrinus near Nisibis for three days; the outcome was bloody and inconclusive, and Macrinus bought peace with 200 million sesterces.
events.detail: Herodian says the Parthian cataphracts and camel-riders were hampered by caltrops strewn by the Romans, and that the field was so heaped with bodies the armies could not see each other. The payment, presented as gifts, was the last major Roman-Arsacid settlement: within seven years Artabanus was dead and the Sasanians ruled Iran.

battle.significance: Last great Roman-Arsacid battle; Macrinus' payment damaged his standing with the troops.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Some (on Herodian's account) count it a Parthian victory.

events.title: Revolt of Elagabalus at Raphanea
events.summary: Julia Maesa, sister of Julia Domna, had her fourteen-year-old grandson Varius Avitus Bassianus, priest of the sun god Elagabal at Emesa, presented to Legio III Gallica at Raphanea as Caracalla's bastard son; the troops proclaimed him emperor as 'Marcus Aurelius Antoninus'.
events.detail: Maesa's wealth (distributed freely), the boy's resemblance to Caracalla and dissatisfaction with Macrinus' pay cuts for new recruits all played a part. The eunuch Gannys organised the coup.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Battle of Antioch (Immae)
events.summary: Macrinus' Praetorians were winning against the army of Elagabalus at a village about 180 stades from Antioch when Macrinus fled the field; his son Diadumenianus was caught and killed and Macrinus himself was captured in Cappadocia and executed.
events.detail: Dio describes Julia Maesa and Julia Soaemias leaping from their chariots to rally the wavering Elagabalan troops and the boy emperor charging with drawn sword. Macrinus fled disguised, shaved his head and beard, and got as far as Chalcedon.

battle.significance: Restored the Severan house through its Syrian female line.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Elagabalus imposes the cult of Elagabal on Rome
events.summary: The boy emperor brought the black conical baetyl of the Emesene sun god to Rome, built the Elagabalium on the Palatine, placed Elagabal above Jupiter and married the Vestal Virgin Aquilia Severa as a sacred union.
events.detail: Elagabalus also 'married' the god to Urania of Carthage, whose cult image was brought to Rome, and moved the Palladium and Vesta's fire into the new temple. Midsummer processions saw the emperor running backwards before the god's chariot. Dio and Herodian present the reign as a catalogue of sexual and religious outrages, and the HA life adds much fiction; modern work (Icks, 2011) sees a real religious programme alienating the Roman elite and army. Coins with the legend SANCT DEO SOLI ELAGABAL confirm the cult.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Icks, The Crimes of Elagabalus (2011)
events.debate: The HA life is largely invented; Herodian moralising; the god's Syrian character is overplayed in sources.

events.title: Assassination of Elagabalus
events.summary: After Elagabalus tried to remove his popular cousin and adopted Caesar Alexianus, the Praetorians killed him and his mother Julia Soaemias, dragged the bodies through the streets and threw them into the Tiber, and hailed the thirteen-year-old Severus Alexander.
events.detail: The Emesene god was sent home and Jupiter restored. Real power passed to Julia Maesa (died c. 224) and then to Alexander's mother Julia Mamaea, governing with a council of senators and jurists including Ulpian.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Date given as 11 or 13 March 222.

events.title: Murder of the jurist Ulpian by the Praetorians
events.summary: Domitius Ulpianus, praetorian prefect and the most prolific Roman jurist, was killed by his own guardsmen in the palace before the emperor and his mother, after three days of street fighting between the Praetorians and the people of Rome.
events.detail: Ulpian had reportedly executed his predecessors Flavianus and Chrestus. His writings supplied about a third of Justinian's Digest, making him perhaps the single most influential legal author in European history. Dio, then governor of Pannonia, was himself threatened by the Guard for disciplining soldiers and spent his second consulship (229) outside Rome for safety.
events.debate: Traditional date 228 has given way to 223 on the basis of P.Oxy. 2565 and Dio's sequence; still disputed.

events.title: Battle of Hormozgan: end of the Arsacids
events.summary: Ardashir, Sasanian king of Persis, defeated and killed the last Parthian great king Artabanus IV on the plain of Hormozgan, ending 470 years of Arsacid rule and founding the Sasanian Empire.
events.detail: Ardashir had built a power base around Istakhr and Ardashir-Khwarrah (Gor/Firuzabad), defeating neighbouring local kings. The Firuzabad rock relief shows the Sasanian dynasts unhorsing their Arsacid opponents in a joust, with Ardashir lancing Artabanus. Arsacid branches survived in Armenia and the Caucasus, giving Armenian kings a long-lasting dynastic grievance against the Sasanians. For Rome the change brought a more centralised, ideologically assertive neighbour that claimed (according to Roman writers) the old Achaemenid lands up to the Aegean.
events.locName: Plain of Hormozgan (exact site unknown, probably in Khuzestan or near Golpayegan)

battle.significance: Replaced the Arsacids with the Sasanians, Rome's principal rival until 628.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Daryaee, Sasanian Persia (2009)
Wiesehöfer, Ancient Persia (1996)
Frye, The History of Ancient Iran (1984)
events.debate: The date 28 April 224 rests on later Arabic-Persian tradition; location disputed.

events.title: Ardashir crowned King of Kings at Ctesiphon
events.summary: Having taken Ctesiphon, Ardashir I was crowned 'King of Kings of Iran' (shahanshah eran), inaugurating a Sasanian era and an ideology tied to Zoroastrian kingship and the land of Eran.
events.detail: Ardashir's coins show the fire altar on the reverse and call him 'Mazda-worshipping divine Ardashir, King of Kings of Iran, whose lineage is from the gods'. Roman authors (Herodian, Dio) report that he claimed all lands once ruled by Darius as far as Ionia and Caria, though this may be a Roman projection.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Date of coronation 226 or 227.

events.title: Cassius Dio's second consulship and the end of his History
events.summary: Lucius Cassius Dio, senator from Nicaea, held his second consulship with Severus Alexander as colleague and retired to Bithynia, where he completed his 80-book Roman History to 229.
events.detail: Dio spent ten years collecting material and twelve writing. Books 36-60 survive largely intact; the books for 193-229, our best source for the Severans, survive only in Byzantine epitomes (Xiphilinus, Zonaras) and excerpts, apart from parts of books 78-79. As a senator and eyewitness of Commodus, Pertinax and the Severans, he is invaluable but hostile to soldiers and to upstarts like Macrinus.

events.title: Ardashir invades Roman Mesopotamia
events.summary: Ardashir attacked Roman Mesopotamia, besieged Nisibis and raided toward Cappadocia and Syria, the first Sasanian war against Rome.
events.detail: An embassy from Alexander urging Ardashir to be content with his own borders was answered (Herodian) with 400 tall Persian horsemen demanding Roman withdrawal from Syria and Asia. Mutinies in the Roman eastern army, including the murder of the governor of Mesopotamia Flavius Heracleo, show the weakness of the Roman position.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Severus Alexander's three-pronged Persian campaign
events.summary: Alexander launched three columns, through Armenia into Media, through Mesopotamia, and under his own command in the centre; the southern column was destroyed, the northern suffered in the winter mountains, and Alexander's own force never pushed hard. Both sides were exhausted and Ardashir did not attack again for several years.
events.detail: Herodian presents the campaign as a humiliating failure caused by Alexander's timidity and Mamaea's influence; Alexander's own coinage and triumph of 233 claimed victory, and the HA invents a great battle. Modern scholarship (e.g. Edwell) sees a costly stalemate that preserved Mesopotamia. The dangerous Germanic incursions on the Rhine and Danube in 233-234 forced the field army to the West.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Edwell, Between Rome and Persia (2008)
events.debate: Outcome disputed: Herodian (defeat) vs HA and coins (victory).

events.title: Murder of Severus Alexander and Julia Mamaea near Mogontiacum
events.summary: Preparing to buy peace from the Germans rather than fight, Alexander and his mother were killed by mutinous soldiers at Vicus Britannicus near Mogontiacum, and the army proclaimed the Thracian officer Maximinus.
events.detail: The end of the Severan dynasty is the conventional start of the 'Crisis of the Third Century' or 'military anarchy': in the next fifty years some 26 recognised emperors and dozens of usurpers reigned, almost all dying violently. Herodian contrasts the soft, mother-dominated Alexander with the giant soldier-emperor, a characterisation modern scholars treat with caution.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Vicus Britannicus is often identified with Bretzenheim near Mainz.

events.title: Battle at the Harzhorn
events.summary: A Roman army returning from a deep penetration into northern Germany fought its way through a Germanic blockade at the Harzhorn ridge in Lower Saxony, some 200 km beyond the limes; the battlefield, found by metal detectorists in 2008, revolutionised views of third-century Roman offensive capacity.
events.detail: Over 2,700 artefacts include catapult bolts, hipposandals, a dolabra stamped for Legio IIII Severiana Alexandriana, and coins down to Severus Alexander, which together date the battle to the campaign of Maximinus in 235/236. Bolt patterns show Roman artillery clearing the ridge and infantry storming it. Herodian had reported Maximinus marching 300-400 stades into Germany and fighting a battle in a swamp, long dismissed as rhetoric; the Harzhorn confirms large-scale operations near the Elbe-Weser region.

sides.strength: legionary vexillations, auxiliaries, Moorish and Osroene archers, artillery

battle.significance: Archaeological proof that Roman armies still campaigned far beyond the Rhine in the 230s.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Pöppelmann, Deppmeyer and Steinmetz (eds.), Roms vergessener Feldzug (2013)
Geschwinde and others, 'Roms vergessener Feldzug', Germania (2009)
events.debate: Identification with Maximinus' campaign is very probable but not explicit in the sources.

events.title: The 'Crisis of the Third Century'
events.summary: Conventional label for the half-century from the murder of Severus Alexander (235) to the accession of Diocletian (284), marked by some 26 legitimate emperors and dozens of usurpers, simultaneous wars on the Rhine, Danube and Euphrates, plague, the temporary secession of Gaul and the East, and the collapse of the silver coinage.
events.detail: The term goes back to nineteenth-century German scholarship (Reichskrise) and was given classic form by Alföldi and Rostovtzeff, who read it as a social revolution of peasant-soldiers against the urban bourgeoisie. Since the 1990s historians have questioned it. Witschel argued that many regions (Africa, much of the East, parts of Spain) show no sign of systemic crisis and that change was regionally varied; Potter treats the period as a test the imperial system ultimately passed; Drinkwater (CAH XII) emphasises the contingency of usurpation driven by the need for emperors on several fronts at once; Liebeschuetz and Ando stress transformation rather than collapse. Harper revived a crisis model driven by plague and climate. What is not disputed: emperors became military men from the Danubian provinces, senators were excluded from army commands, the denarius/antoninianus became nearly pure bronze, and the institutions of the Tetrarchy grew out of improvised responses of the 260s and 270s. The main narrative sources (Historia Augusta, Zosimus, Zonaras, the Latin breviaria) are late and thin, so much reconstruction rests on coins, inscriptions and papyri.
scholarship: Alföldi, Studien zur Geschichte der Weltkrise des 3. Jahrhunderts (1967)
Witschel, Krise, Rezession, Stagnation? (1999)
Potter, The Roman Empire at Bay AD 180-395 (2004, 2nd ed. 2014)
Drinkwater, 'Maximinus to Diocletian and the crisis', CAH XII (2005)
Hekster, Rome and its Empire AD 193-284 (2008)
Liebeschuetz, 'Was there a crisis of the third century?', in Hekster et al. (eds.), Crises and the Roman Empire (2007)
Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)
events.debate: Whether 'crisis' is an apt term at all; whether it was general or regional; whether its causes were external pressure (Persia, Goths), internal politics (the army and usurpation), economics, or epidemic and climate.

events.title: Revolt of the Gordians in Africa
events.summary: Young landowners at Thysdrus killed Maximinus' procurator in a tax revolt and proclaimed the aged proconsul of Africa, Marcus Antonius Gordianus, emperor with his son Gordian II; the Senate recognised them and declared Maximinus a public enemy.
events.detail: The revolt began a year in which six men were called emperor. The Senate formed a committee of twenty consulars (vigintiviri) to defend Italy, a striking revival of senatorial initiative. The Gordians reigned about three weeks.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Chronology of 238 is notoriously difficult; dates for the African revolt range from January to March.

events.title: Battle of Carthage
events.summary: Capelianus, the loyal governor of Numidia, marched Legio III Augusta on Carthage and crushed the Gordians' untrained militia; Gordian II was killed and his father hanged himself.
events.detail: Gordian III later cashiered III Augusta for its role, and its name was erased from inscriptions until the legion was reconstituted in 253.

sides.strength: Legio III Augusta and Numidian auxiliaries

battle.significance: Ended the African revolt but not the senatorial rebellion it had started.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Senate elects Pupienus and Balbinus
events.summary: On news of the Gordians' death the Senate chose two of the vigintiviri, the soldier Pupienus Maximus and the aristocrat Balbinus, as joint Augusti with equal powers, including the pontificate; the Roman crowd forced them to add the thirteen-year-old Gordian III as Caesar.
events.detail: The collegiate emperorship with two equal Augusti, without a senior partner, was unprecedented. Street fighting broke out between the plebs and the Praetorians, and parts of the city burned.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.title: Siege of Aquileia and death of Maximinus
events.summary: Maximinus crossed the Julian Alps but was stopped at Aquileia, defended by the senators Crispinus and Menophilus; his starving army, short of supplies in a stripped countryside, murdered him and his son in their tents.
events.detail: Herodian describes the Aquileians melting down statues for missiles and women giving their hair for bowstrings (a topos also attached to Carthage). The local god Belenus was said to have appeared on the walls. The heads of Maximinus and Maximus were sent to Rome.

sides.losses: emperor murdered by his own troops

battle.significance: Death of the first soldier-emperor; vindicated the senatorial coup.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Date of Maximinus' death (April to June 238) disputed.

events.title: Murder of Pupienus and Balbinus; Gordian III sole emperor
events.summary: After 99 days of quarrelling joint rule, the two senatorial emperors were seized by the Praetorians, stripped, dragged through the city and killed; Gordian III, aged 13, was proclaimed sole Augustus.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

events.debate: Herodian's narrative ends here.

events.title: Goths and Carpi sack Histria
events.summary: Gothic and Carpic raiders sacked Histria near the Danube mouth, the first securely recorded Gothic attack on the empire; Tullius Menophilus, governor of Moesia Inferior, bought them off with subsidies.
events.detail: The Historia Augusta's 'excidium Histriae' is corroborated by a destruction layer at the site. Menophilus' subsidies to the Goths and refusal to pay the Carpi, reported by the fragment of Petrus Patricius (from Dexippus), illustrate the developing system of tribute and divide-and-rule on the lower Danube.
scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)

events.title: Shapur I crowned co-ruler; sole King of Kings from 242
events.summary: Ardashir crowned his son Shapur co-ruler, probably on 12 April 240, and Shapur ruled alone from around 242 to 270, the most dangerous enemy Rome faced in the third century.
events.detail: Shapur's own trilingual (Middle Persian, Parthian, Greek) inscription on the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht at Naqsh-e Rustam (ŠKZ) narrates his three Roman wars, listing defeated emperors and captured cities and recording the deportation of Roman prisoners to build cities such as Gundeshapur (Weh-Andiok-Shabuhr, 'better than Antioch, Shapur built this') and Bishapur.
events.debate: The date 12 April 240 derives from Manichaean sources; sole rule 241 or 242.

events.title: Sasanian capture of Hatra
events.summary: Hatra, which had become a Roman ally with a Roman garrison, fell to Ardashir and his son Shapur after a long siege; the city was destroyed and never reoccupied, which preserved its spectacular temples until ISIS damaged them in 2015.
events.detail: The Cologne Mani Codex dates the fall to the year Mani received his second revelation (240/241). Arabic legend tells of the king's daughter al-Nadira betraying the city for love of Shapur. Persian pressure also took Nisibis and Carrhae around this time, prompting Gordian III's expedition.

sides.strength: city garrison with a Roman cohort

battle.significance: Removed the last buffer between Rome and Persia in the Jazira.

events.debate: King's identity in 240 uncertain (Sanatruq II is the last securely attested king).

events.title: Battle of Rhesaina
events.summary: Gordian III's army, directed by his father-in-law and praetorian prefect Timesitheus, defeated Shapur near Rhesaina and recovered Carrhae and Nisibis.
events.detail: Gordian had opened the temple of Janus before leaving Rome, an antiquarian gesture. The victory was followed by Timesitheus' death from illness, possibly helped along by his successor Philip.

sides.strength: large expeditionary army including Germanic and Gothic contingents

battle.significance: Restored Roman Mesopotamia.

events.title: Battle of Misiche and death of Gordian III
events.summary: Advancing down the Euphrates toward Ctesiphon, Gordian's army was defeated by Shapur at Misiche near modern Fallujah; Gordian died soon after, either of wounds (Persian version) or murdered by his troops at the instigation of Philip the Arab (Roman version).
events.detail: Shapur renamed the place Peroz-Shapur ('victorious is Shapur') and boasts on the ŠKZ that Caesar Gordian was killed and the Roman army destroyed; the Bishapur and Naqsh-e Rustam reliefs show a Roman lying beneath his horse. Roman sources suppress the battle and blame Philip, who raised a cenotaph to Gordian at Zaitha near Circesium. Modern consensus tends to accept a Roman defeat followed by Gordian's death in uncertain circumstances.
events.locName: Misiche (Peroz-Shapur, later al-Anbar), on the Euphrates

sides.strength: Roman field army including Gothic and Germanic contingents (ŠKZ)

battle.significance: First of Shapur's three triumphs over Roman emperors; led to Philip's costly peace.

scholarship: Dodgeon and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars AD 226-363 (1991)
Potter, The Roman Empire at Bay (2004/2014)
events.debate: Roman and Persian narratives are irreconcilable; the cause of Gordian's death is genuinely uncertain.

events.title: Philip the Arab's peace with Shapur
events.summary: The new emperor Philip made peace with Shapur, paying 500,000 denarii (aurei, according to the ŠKZ) and apparently recognising Persian influence in Armenia, while Roman coins proclaimed PAX FUNDATA CUM PERSIS.
events.detail: The ŠKZ calls Philip a tributary. Roman writers say he later reneged on the Armenian clause. Philip also founded Philippopolis (Shahba) in his native Trachonitis and deified his father Marinus.

events.title: Philip celebrates Rome's millennium
events.summary: On 21 April 248 Philip staged the Ludi Saeculares for the thousandth anniversary of Rome's foundation, with games in which, according to later tradition, a thousand pairs of gladiators and exotic animals collected by Gordian III appeared.
events.detail: Coins carry SAECULUM NOVUM. The celebration coincided with Gothic and Carpic invasions and military revolts, an irony later Christian tradition, which also made Philip the first Christian emperor (Eusebius, HE 6.34), exploited. The Christian claim is generally rejected.
events.debate: Philip's Christianity is a later legend; the animal list in the HA is suspect.

events.title: Revolts of Pacatianus and Jotapianus
events.summary: In 248 Tiberius Claudius Marinus Pacatianus was proclaimed by the Danube legions and Jotapianus, claiming kinship with Severus Alexander, rose in Syria or Cappadocia; both were soon killed by their own troops.
events.detail: Philip's offer to resign was answered by the senator Decius, who predicted the usurpers would fall; Philip then sent Decius to the Danube, where the troops proclaimed him instead. Pacatianus' coins, minted at Viminacium, are dated 'year 1001 of Rome'.

events.title: Battle of Verona
events.summary: Decius, proclaimed by the Danubian army, marched into Italy and defeated and killed Philip near Verona; Philip's son Philip II was murdered by the Praetorians in Rome.

battle.significance: Brought the Danubian Decius to power.

events.debate: Location (Verona vs Beroea in Macedonia, a scribal confusion) and date (September or October 249) debated.

events.title: Plague of Cyprian
events.summary: A pandemic, probably originating in Ethiopia and reaching Alexandria by 249, swept the empire for over a decade; Bishop Cyprian of Carthage describes bloody diarrhoea, vomiting, eye haemorrhage, gangrene of the limbs and loss of hearing and sight.
events.detail: Dionysius of Alexandria reports the city's population so reduced that the number of men aged 14 to 80 equalled those aged 40 to 70 in earlier times. The emperors Hostilian (251) and probably Claudius II (270) died of plague. Kyle Harper has argued for a viral haemorrhagic fever (filovirus) and an empire-wide mortality crisis, which others think overstated. The epidemic coincided with the worst military defeats of the century and may have hampered recruitment and tax.
scholarship: Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)
Harper, 'Pandemics and passages to late antiquity', JRA 28 (2015)
Huebner, 'The Plague of Cyprian: A revised view', Klio (2021)
events.debate: Pathogen unknown (smallpox, measles, filovirus proposed); scale contested.

events.title: Decius' edict of universal sacrifice
events.summary: Decius ordered every inhabitant of the empire to sacrifice to the gods, taste the sacrificial meat and obtain a certificate (libellus) from local commissioners; Christians who refused were imprisoned or executed, including Pope Fabian (20 January 250).
events.detail: Over forty libelli survive on papyrus from Egypt, including one for a priestess of Petesouchos, showing the order applied to everyone, not just Christians. The measure was probably a supplicatio for the empire's welfare tied to Decius' Trajanic-traditionalist programme rather than a targeted persecution, but its effect on the Church was severe: mass lapses, purchased certificates (libellatici), and bitter disputes over readmitting the lapsed that produced the Novatianist schism. Origen was tortured at Caesarea and died a few years later.
scholarship: Rives, 'The Decree of Decius and the Religion of Empire', JRS 89 (1999)
Knipfing, 'The Libelli of the Decian Persecution', HTR 16 (1923)
events.debate: Whether Decius intended to target Christians is debated; Rives argues for a universalising religious policy.

events.title: Siege and sack of Philippopolis
events.summary: The Gothic king Cniva besieged Philippopolis in Thrace, whose governor Lucius Priscus, despairing of help from Decius, proclaimed himself emperor and allied with the Goths; the city fell and Ammianus says 100,000 people were killed or captured.
events.detail: A Vienna palimpsest (the 'Scythica Vindobonensia', identified in 2014) preserves fragments of Dexippus describing this campaign in Thrace, including speeches by Decius. Priscus was declared a public enemy and soon disappeared.

battle.significance: First sack of a major Balkan city by the Goths.

scholarship: Martin and Grusková, 'Scythica Vindobonensia', WS 127 (2014)

events.title: Battle of Beroe (Augusta Traiana)
events.summary: Cniva surprised Decius' army in camp near Beroe-Augusta Traiana, routing it and forcing the emperor to retreat to Moesia to regroup, leaving Philippopolis to its fate.

battle.significance: Left Thrace open to the Goths.

events.title: Battle of Abritus
events.summary: Decius and his son Herennius Etruscus were killed when Cniva's Goths lured the Roman army into a marsh near Abritus in Moesia Inferior; Decius was the first emperor to die fighting a foreign enemy, and his body was never found.
events.detail: Herennius was killed by an arrow early in the fighting; Decius reportedly told the troops that the loss of one soldier did not matter. Cniva placed part of his army behind a swamp; the Romans pursuing into it were trapped. Byzantine sources (Zosimus, Zonaras) accuse the governor Trebonianus Gallus of treachery, a claim many moderns doubt. Gallus, proclaimed emperor, allowed the Goths to withdraw with their booty and prisoners and promised an annual subsidy. A large fortified Roman camp excavated near Razgrad and coin hoards in the area have been linked to the battle.

sides.losses: very heavy; emperor and heir killed

battle.significance: First Roman emperor killed by a foreign enemy; symbol of the third-century nadir.

scholarship: Bursche, 'The battle of Abritus, the imperial treasury and aurei in Barbaricum', NC 173 (2013)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
events.debate: Date (June or July 251), Gallus' alleged treachery, and Gothic identity of Cniva's force (perhaps a mixed coalition) debated. Lactantius gloats over the persecutor's unburied corpse.

events.title: Novatianist schism at Rome
events.summary: When Cornelius was elected bishop of Rome in March 251 and favoured readmitting the lapsed after penance, the learned presbyter Novatian had himself consecrated rival bishop, founding a rigorist church that survived for centuries.
events.detail: Cyprian at Carthage backed Cornelius after hesitation and held councils on the lapsed. The Novatianists ('Cathari') spread across the empire; Constantine later tolerated them, and their bishops attended Nicaea. Novatian's De Trinitate is the first major Latin Trinitarian treatise from Rome.

events.title: Battle of Barbalissos
events.summary: Opening his second war, Shapur I destroyed a Roman army of 60,000 (his figure) at Barbalissos on the Euphrates, then overran Syria and Cappadocia; the ŠKZ lists 37 captured cities.
events.detail: Shapur's pretext was Roman interference in Armenia, where the Arsacid king (probably Khosrov II) was murdered and his son Tiridates fled to Rome. Barbalissos opened the road to Antioch.

battle.significance: Left the Roman East defenceless.

events.debate: Date 252 or 253; known only from Shapur's inscription.

events.title: Shapur I sacks Antioch
events.summary: Shapur took and sacked Antioch, the third city of the empire, guided (according to Ammianus and the Thirteenth Sibylline Oracle) by a renegade Antiochene councillor named Mariades; thousands were deported to Persia.
events.detail: Ammianus has the people of Antioch watching a mime in the theatre when an actor's wife cried 'Am I dreaming, or are the Persians here?'. Deportees from Antioch peopled Gundeshapur and Bishapur and helped to spread Christianity in Persia. Shapur later executed Mariades.

battle.significance: The greatest humiliation inflicted on Rome in the East to that date.

events.debate: Date 253 or 256; some argue for two captures (253 and 260).

events.title: Uranius Antoninus defends Emesa
events.summary: Lucius Julius Aurelius Sulpicius Severus Uranius Antoninus, priest of Elagabal at Emesa, led local resistance to Shapur and struck gold and silver coins as emperor in 253-254.
events.detail: Malalas records a priest of Aphrodite (Sampsigeramus) driving off Shapur from Emesa with slingers; the identification with Uranius is widely accepted. His local defence anticipates the larger role of Odaenathus of Palmyra.

events.title: Aemilianus overthrows Gallus; Valerian seizes power
events.summary: Aemilius Aemilianus, governor of Moesia, won a victory over the Goths, was proclaimed emperor and invaded Italy; Trebonianus Gallus and his son Volusian were killed by their own men near Interamna. Three months later Aemilianus met the same fate near Spoletium as Valerian approached with the Rhine army.
events.detail: Valerian, a senior senator in his sixties, made his son Gallienus co-Augustus, dividing responsibility between East (Valerian) and West (Gallienus), a pattern for later joint rule.

events.title: Sasanian siege of Dura-Europos
events.summary: Shapur's army besieged and destroyed the Roman frontier fortress of Dura-Europos on the Euphrates; excavations revealed siege mines and countermines in which some twenty Roman soldiers and one Persian died, perhaps the earliest archaeological evidence of chemical warfare.
events.detail: Simon James has argued that the Persians filled the Roman countermine with toxic smoke from burning bitumen and sulphur crystals, killing the Romans who broke in. To strengthen the wall the defenders had buried the street behind it with an earthen ramp, which preserved the synagogue with its painted biblical cycle, the Christian house-church with the earliest datable baptistery, and the Mithraeum. The city was abandoned after its fall.

battle.significance: Its ramp-buried buildings are among the most important finds of Roman archaeology.

scholarship: James, 'Stratagems, Combat, and Chemical Warfare in the Siege Mines of Dura-Europos', AJA 115 (2011)
James, The Roman Military Base at Dura-Europos (2019)
events.debate: Date of fall 256 or 257 from coin and graffiti evidence.

events.title: Gothic and Boranoi sea raids: Pityus and Trapezus
events.summary: Using ships commandeered from the Bosporan Kingdom, Boranoi and Goths raided the eastern Black Sea, taking Pityus at the second attempt and storming Trapezus, whose large garrison fled by night.
events.detail: Zosimus describes the raiders climbing the walls with tree trunks against the hillside and carrying off immense booty and captives. Gregory Thaumaturgus' Canonical Epistle deals with Christian captives and collaborators after these raids in Pontus. In 258 another fleet raided the Propontis and sacked Chalcedon, Nicomedia and Nicaea.

events.title: Valerian's persecution of the clergy
events.summary: Valerian's first edict (257) ordered clergy to sacrifice and banned Christian meetings and cemeteries; a second (258) ordered execution of bishops, priests and deacons and confiscated property of Christian senators and equestrians.
events.detail: Victims included Pope Sixtus II, beheaded with deacons in the catacomb of Callixtus on 6 August 258, the deacon Lawrence (later legend: the gridiron), and Cyprian of Carthage. Unlike Decius, Valerian targeted the Church's leadership and property, implying awareness of its institutional strength.

events.title: Martyrdom of Cyprian of Carthage
events.summary: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage, was beheaded at the villa Sexti outside Carthage before a large crowd after a trial before the proconsul Galerius Maximus, the first African bishop to be martyred.
events.detail: The Acta Proconsularia record his reply 'Deo gratias' to the sentence. His letters and treatises (De Unitate Ecclesiae, De Lapsis) are the most important sources for third-century church organisation and the plague and persecutions.

events.title: Battle of Mediolanum
events.summary: Gallienus defeated a vast Alamannic army (Zonaras says 300,000) near Milan with a force of 10,000, after the invaders had crossed the Alps and reached the outskirts of Rome, where the Senate armed the plebs.
events.detail: The invasion forced Gallienus to concentrate cavalry in northern Italy, often seen (with caution) as the origin of a mobile cavalry reserve under Aureolus based at Milan.

battle.significance: Saved Italy from the first major barbarian invasion since the Cimbri.

events.debate: Date 259 or 260; numbers absurd.

events.title: Battle at Augusta Vindelicum
events.summary: On 24-25 April 260 the Raetian governor Marcus Simplicinius Genialis, with soldiers and local levies, defeated Semnones or Juthungi returning from Italy laden with booty and freed 'many thousands of Italian captives', as recorded on a victory altar found in Augsburg in 1992.
events.detail: The altar is dated by the consuls of 260 'Postumus Augustus and Honoratianus', showing that Raetia had joined Postumus' Gallic Empire. It is a rare contemporary document of the invasions and of a provincial army acting without the emperor.

battle.significance: Epigraphic snapshot of invasion, captives and the Gallic secession.

scholarship: Bakker, 'Raetien unter Postumus', Germania 71 (1993)
Drinkwater, The Alamanni and Rome (2007)

events.title: Revolts of Ingenuus and Regalianus on the Danube
events.summary: Ingenuus, governor of Pannonia, was proclaimed emperor and defeated by Gallienus' cavalry commander Aureolus at Mursa; his successor as usurper, Regalianus, struck coins at Carnuntum before being killed after Sarmatian (Roxolani) attacks.
events.detail: Regalianus' coins, crude overstrikes on older denarii, include issues for his wife Sulpicia Dryantilla. Both revolts reflect frontier armies' demand for an emperor on the spot.
events.debate: Date 258 or 260 for Ingenuus.

events.title: Battle of Mursa (260)
events.summary: Gallienus and his cavalry commander Aureolus crushed the usurper Ingenuus near Mursa; Ingenuus was killed or drowned himself.

battle.significance: Early display of Gallienus' mobile cavalry.
