events.debate: Procopius's claim that Eudoxia invited Gaiseric to avenge her husband is likely gossip. The Temple spoils' later fate is legendary.

events.title: Avitus proclaimed emperor with Visigothic support
events.summary: Eparchius Avitus, a Gallic aristocrat sent as envoy to the Visigothic king Theodoric II at Toulouse, was proclaimed emperor at Ugernum near Arles on 9 July 455 with Gothic backing and acclaimed by Gallic notables. His son-in-law Sidonius Apollinaris delivered his panegyric in Rome on 1 January 456.

events.title: Battle of the Órbigo: Visigoths crush the Suebi
events.summary: Acting nominally for Avitus, Theodoric II invaded Gallaecia and destroyed the army of the Suebic king Rechiar on the river Órbigo, twelve miles from Asturica (Astorga). Rechiar was captured and executed in December; the Suebic kingdom split into factions for a generation.
events.locName: Campus Paramus on the Órbigo, near Astorga

sides.strength: Visigothic army with Burgundian contingents under Theodoric II

sides.losses: heavy; king captured and later executed

battle.significance: Started the Visigothic shift into Spain that would eventually make it the heart of their kingdom.

events.title: Battle of Placentia: fall of Avitus
events.summary: Ricimer and Majorian turned on Avitus, whose Visigothic allies were away in Spain. He was defeated at Placentia on 17 October 456, his general Messianus killed. Avitus was spared and consecrated bishop of Placentia, but died within months.

battle.significance: Ended the Gallo-Gothic experiment of an emperor from Gaul and established that Italy's army, under Ricimer, made emperors.

events.title: Ricimer defeats the Vandals at Agrigentum and Corsica
events.summary: Ricimer, a general of Suevic and Visigothic royal descent, defeated a Vandal force near Agrigentum in Sicily and then a Vandal fleet of 60 ships off Corsica in 456. The prestige made him the decisive figure in Italy.

battle.significance: Launched Ricimer's sixteen-year dominance as king-maker of the West.

events.title: Accession of Leo I
events.summary: After Marcian's death on 27 January 457, Aspar, who as an Arian Alan could not take the throne himself, chose Leo, a tribune from Dacia. Leo was crowned on 7 February 457, possibly by the patriarch Anatolius, and later began building an Isaurian counterweight to Aspar's Goths.
events.debate: Whether Leo's was the first patriarchal coronation is disputed; De Ceremoniis describes a military raising on the shield with the patriarch present.

events.title: Majorian becomes emperor
events.summary: After months without an emperor in the West, Majorian, Aetius's former officer and Ricimer's comrade, was acclaimed by the army on 1 April 457 at Ad Columellas near Ravenna and became Augustus on 28 December 457. He was the last western emperor to campaign in person with real energy.

events.title: Majorian's legislation
events.summary: Majorian's Novels attacked tax arrears and abuses by collectors, restored the office of defensor civitatis, protected curiales, and in Novel 4 (11 July 458) forbade the stripping of ancient public buildings in Rome for building stone, with fines of 50 lbs of gold for officials who allowed it.

events.title: Majorian defeats Vandal raiders in Campania
events.summary: A Vandal and Moorish raiding force led by Gaiseric's brother-in-law landed at the mouth of the Liris (Garigliano) near Sinuessa and plundered Campania. Majorian's troops caught them laden with booty and drove them back to their ships with heavy losses; the Vandal leader was killed.

battle.significance: A morale boost that encouraged Majorian's plan to strike Carthage directly.

events.title: Vandals burn Majorian's fleet in Spain
events.summary: Majorian, having forced the Visigoths and Burgundians back into alliance, assembled a fleet of about 300 ships in the Spanish harbour of Portus Illicitanus (near Elche) and around Carthago Nova to invade Africa. Traitors guided Vandal raiders who burned or seized much of it in 460. Majorian made peace and returned to Italy.

sides.losses: most of the fleet destroyed or captured

battle.significance: The failure destroyed Majorian's prestige and led directly to his deposition.

events.debate: Procopius's tale that Majorian dyed his hair and visited Carthage in disguise as his own envoy is folklore.

events.title: Ricimer deposes and executes Majorian
events.summary: Returning to Italy after dismissing his army, Majorian was arrested by Ricimer at Dertona on 2 August 461, stripped of his purple, beaten and beheaded on 7 August near the river Iria. Procopius praises him as a ruler surpassing all who had gone before.

events.title: Aegidius defeats the Visigoths at Orléans
events.summary: Aegidius, magister militum per Gallias, refused to recognise Ricimer's puppet Libius Severus and fought the Visigoths, to whom Ricimer had ceded Narbonne. With Frankish help (Childeric?) he defeated a Gothic army near Orléans, killing Frederic, brother of Theodoric II. He died in 464 or 465, perhaps poisoned, leaving a Roman enclave around Soissons to his son Syagrius.

sides.strength: Gallic field army remnant with Frankish allies

battle.significance: Kept northern Gaul out of Visigothic hands, leaving it to be fought over by Romans and Franks.

events.title: Anthemius sent from Constantinople as western emperor
events.summary: After the death of Libius Severus in 465 and nearly two years without an emperor, Leo I sent the eastern aristocrat Anthemius, son-in-law of Marcian, with an army and Marcellinus of Dalmatia. He was proclaimed near Rome on 12 April 467; his daughter Alypia married Ricimer to seal the arrangement.

events.title: Battle of Cape Bon: the great Vandal expedition fails
events.summary: The largest naval expedition of late antiquity, sent by Leo I under his brother-in-law Basiliscus, anchored off Cape Bon (Promunturium Mercurii) some 60 km from Carthage. Gaiseric bought a five-day truce, then sent fireships among the crowded fleet with a favourable wind. Half the fleet was lost; Basiliscus fled.
events.detail: The cost was staggering: John Lydus reports 65,000 lbs of gold and 700,000 lbs of silver; Procopius 130,000 lbs of gold. Later Byzantine sources speak of 1,113 ships and 100,000 men. It nearly bankrupted the eastern treasury for a generation, and its failure ended any realistic hope of restoring the West's African tax base. Simultaneous operations had gone well: Marcellinus cleared Sardinia and Heraclius of Edessa took Tripolitania. Procopius reports the heroism of the general John, who leapt armoured into the sea rather than surrender to Gaiseric's son Genzo. Suspicion that Basiliscus was bribed, or acting for Aspar, who wanted the expedition to fail, appears in the sources.

battle.significance: The decisive failure of the late Roman effort to recover Africa; it sealed the western empire's fiscal fate and crippled eastern finances until Anastasius.

events.debate: Figures for ships and cost differ widely; Heather accepts the scale as broadly real. Blame on Basiliscus and Aspar may be propaganda from Zeno's later regime.

events.title: Battle of Déols: Riothamus defeated
events.summary: Anthemius's ally Riothamus, 'king of the Britons', crossed with an army Jordanes puts at 12,000 to Berry to fight Euric, but was defeated near Bourg-de-Déols before Roman forces could join him and fled to the Burgundians. Euric then took much of central Gaul.

battle.significance: Removed the last field army able to contest Euric's expansion north of the Loire.

events.debate: Whether Riothamus's Britons came from Britain or from Armorica is debated; his identification with a historical Arthur (Ashe) has little support.

events.title: Leo I murders Aspar
events.summary: After fifty years as Constantinople's kingmaker, the Alan general Aspar and his son Ardabur were cut down by palace eunuchs in 471 on Leo's orders; Leo earned the nickname Makelles, 'the Butcher'. The Isaurian Zeno, married to Leo's daughter Ariadne since 466/467, inherited Aspar's role. Aspar's Gothic followers rose under Theodoric Strabo.

events.title: Sieges of Clermont
events.summary: For four summers the Arverni, led by Bishop Sidonius Apollinaris and his brother-in-law Ecdicius (who once broke through the Gothic lines with eighteen horsemen), resisted Euric's Goths. In 475 Julius Nepos ceded Auvergne in exchange for Provence; Sidonius, who felt betrayed, was briefly imprisoned.

sides.strength: citizens and private retainers of Ecdicius

battle.significance: The Auvergne's sacrifice in the 475 treaty marked Ravenna's abandonment of Roman Gaul north of the Durance.

events.title: Ricimer besieges Rome; death of Anthemius
events.summary: Ricimer quarrelled with his father-in-law Anthemius and besieged him in Rome in spring 472, proclaiming Olybrius emperor in April. After famine and street fighting the city fell; Anthemius, hiding disguised as a beggar in St Peter's or Santa Maria in Trastevere, was beheaded by Ricimer's nephew Gundobad on 11 July 472.

sides.strength: Anthemius's guards, citizens and Gothic troops under Bilimer from Gaul

battle.significance: The first time Rome was stormed by a Roman army since 312, and the end of the last East-backed attempt to stabilise the West.

events.title: Death of Ricimer
events.summary: Ricimer died on 18 August 472, vomiting blood, five weeks after killing Anthemius. Olybrius died on 2 November. Gundobad inherited the post of patricius and in March 473 made the comes domesticorum Glycerius emperor before leaving to claim the Burgundian throne.
scholarship: MacGeorge, Late Roman Warlords (2002)
Anders, Flavius Ricimer (2010)

events.title: Zeno becomes emperor
events.summary: Leo I died on 18 January 474, leaving his seven-year-old grandson Leo II, son of Zeno and Ariadne. Leo II crowned his father Zeno co-emperor on 9 February and died in November 474, leaving the Isaurian, born Tarasis son of Kodisa, sole Augustus.

events.title: Julius Nepos deposes Glycerius
events.summary: Leo I refused to recognise Glycerius and sent Julius Nepos, magister militum of Dalmatia and nephew of Marcellinus, who landed at Portus in June 474. Glycerius surrendered without a fight and was consecrated bishop of Salona.

events.title: Zeno's 'endless peace' with Gaiseric
events.summary: Zeno's envoy, the senator Severus, negotiated a perpetual peace: Constantinople recognised Vandal rule in Africa, Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica and the Balearics, and Gaiseric released captives and allowed Nicene worship in Carthage. It held until 533.

events.title: Usurpation of Basiliscus
events.summary: In January 475 Leo's widow Verina and her brother Basiliscus drove Zeno back to Isauria. Basiliscus issued an Encyclical condemning Chalcedon, sparking riots led by Daniel the Stylite, then withdrew it. Illus and Verina's associates switched sides, and Zeno re-entered Constantinople in August 476. Basiliscus and his family were starved to death in a cistern at Limnae in Cappadocia.
events.detail: A great fire in 475 destroyed the Basilica library (said to have held 120,000 books, including a 120-foot dragon-gut copy of Homer) and the Lauseion palace with its famous collection of Greek statues.

events.title: Orestes drives out Nepos; Romulus Augustulus proclaimed
events.summary: Orestes, a Pannonian Roman who had been Attila's secretary and was now Nepos's magister militum, turned the army on his master. Nepos fled from Ravenna to Dalmatia on 28 August 475, and on 31 October Orestes proclaimed his own adolescent son Romulus emperor, mocked as Augustulus.

events.title: Odoacer kills Orestes at Placentia
events.summary: The barbarian federates of the Italian army, Heruli, Sciri, Rugii and Turcilingi, demanded a third of the land of Italy. Orestes refused. They proclaimed the Scirian officer Odoacer king on 23 August 476, besieged Orestes in Ticinum, and captured and executed him at Placentia on 28 August; his brother Paulus was killed in the pine forest outside Ravenna on 4 September.

sides.strength: federate troops of the Italian army

battle.significance: Destroyed the last Roman regime in Italy and transferred power to the federate army that had long been its real base.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.summary: Odoacer entered Ravenna, deposed the boy emperor Romulus but spared him 'because of his beauty', gave him a pension of 6,000 solidi and sent him to live with his relatives at the Castellum Lucullanum near Naples. Odoacer ruled Italy as king, nominally under Constantinople, and did not appoint another western emperor.
events.detail: The Senate sent the imperial regalia to Zeno with a message that one emperor sufficed for both halves and asking that Odoacer be made patricius. Zeno replied that they had a legitimate emperor, Nepos, and should take him back; he addressed Odoacer as patricius anyway. Nepos lived in Dalmatia until 480 and was recognised on Odoacer's coins. Contemporaries barely noticed 476; the idea that the western empire 'fell' then was constructed in the 510s-520s at Constantinople, notably by Marcellinus Comes ('the Hesperian empire of the Roman people perished with this Augustulus'), as Croke showed. Romulus may still have been alive in 507-511, when Cassiodorus's Variae mentions a Romulus receiving a pension.
events.debate: The core of the 'fall vs transformation' debate. Ward-Perkins and Heather insist on a real political collapse with severe material consequences; Goffart, Halsall and the 'Transformation of the Roman World' project stress continuity of Roman administration, law and elites under barbarian kings. Kaldellis argues that from Constantinople's viewpoint the empire continued and merely lost western provinces.
scholarship: Croke, 'AD 476: the manufacture of a turning point', Chiron 13 (1983)
Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization (2005)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007)
Goffart, Barbarian Tides (2006)
Kaldellis, The New Roman Empire (2023)

wars.name: Cantabrian and Asturian Wars
wars.outcome: Roman victory; final conquest of the Iberian peninsula, mass deportation of hill populations to the plains, foundation of Asturica Augusta and Lucus Augusti; gold mines of the north-west opened
wars.summary: The last war of conquest in Spain, fought in the Cantabrian mountains and Asturias by up to seven or eight legions. Augustus campaigned in person in 26 BC but fell ill; the decisive work was done by his legates, ending with Agrippa's brutal pacification in 19 BC.
wars.detail: Statilius Taurus and Calvisius Sabinus had campaigned against the Cantabri and Vaccaei from 29 BC, but the main war began in 26 BC when Augustus took personal command from a base at Segisama, using a three-pronged advance supported by a fleet from Aquitania landing on the Cantabrian coast. After victories at Vellica and the blockade of Aracillum, Augustus retired sick to Tarraco and closed the doors of Janus in 25 BC, prematurely. Publius Carisius and Gaius Antistius continued against the Astures (Lancia) and the Cantabri; revolts followed in 24, 22 and 19 BC. Agrippa ended resistance in 19 BC after his own troops had become demoralised, disgracing legio I (which lost the title Augusta) for cowardice. Survivors of military age were massacred or forced down to the plains. The war secured the gold districts of Las Médulas and the north-west, which by Pliny's day produced 20,000 lb of gold a year. The legions IV Macedonica, VI Victrix and X Gemina remained in the north for decades; Florus and Orosius, both dependent on Livy's lost books, are the main narrative sources, supplemented by archaeology of Roman siege camps at sites such as La Loma and El Cincho.

phases.t: Preliminary campaigns of Statilius Taurus and Calvisius Sabinus
Augustus's personal campaign; Vellica, Aracillum, Lancia
Recurrent risings suppressed by Lucius Aemilius, Gaius Furnius and Publius Carisius

wars.name: Roman-Kushite War
wars.outcome: Negotiated peace at Samos (21/20 BC): Augustus remits the tribute, Rome keeps the Dodekaschoinos with a frontier at Hiera Sykaminos
wars.summary: Kushite forces under the one-eyed 'Candace' (probably queen Amanirenas) and prince Akinidad took Syene, Elephantine and Philae while the Egyptian garrison was weakened by Aelius Gallus's Arabian expedition. The prefect Gaius Petronius drove them back, sacked Napata and garrisoned Primis, but Augustus settled on generous terms.
wars.detail: The Kushites carried off statues of Augustus; the bronze head of Augustus found buried under the steps of a victory temple at Meroë (now in the British Museum) is almost certainly one of them, placed so that visitors trod on it. Petronius counterattacked with fewer than 10,000 infantry and 800 horse, defeated a large army at Pselchis, took Primis (Qasr Ibrim) and razed Napata, then retired, leaving 400 men and two years' supplies at Primis. When the Candace attacked Primis in 22 BC Petronius relieved it. Kushite envoys, sent on to Augustus at Samos, obtained the cancellation of the tribute Petronius had imposed. Strabo, a friend of Aelius Gallus, gives the Roman version; Meroitic inscriptions (the Hamadab stelae of Amanirenas and Akinidad) are still only partly understood. The frontier then remained stable for nearly three centuries.

phases.t: Second Kushite attack on Primis; peace of Samos

wars.name: Augustan Alpine Wars
wars.outcome: Roman conquest of the entire Alpine arc; creation of Raetia, Noricum and the Alpine prefectures; Tropaeum Alpium lists 45 subdued peoples
wars.summary: A series of operations that secured the Alpine passes between Italy and the Rhine-Danube: the destruction of the Salassi in 25 BC, the annexation of Noricum c. 16-15 BC, and the double pincer of Drusus and Tiberius against the Raeti and Vindelici in 15 BC, followed by the reduction of the Maritime Alps in 14 BC.
wars.detail: In 15 BC Drusus advanced from Italy up the Adige and over the Brenner or Reschen pass while Tiberius came from Gaul, fought a naval action on Lake Constance and met his brother near the sources of the Danube; the campaign ended, by tradition, on 1 August, a date Horace celebrated (Odes 4.14). Large parts of the male population were deported. The trophy at La Turbie (7/6 BC) named 45 gentes Alpinae devictae; Pliny copied the text (NH 3.136-137) and fragments survive. The Cottian kingdom of Marcus Julius Cottius was left as a client prefecture (arch at Susa, 9/8 BC).

phases.t: Noricum incorporated; Raeti and Vindelici conquered
Ligurian peoples of the Maritime Alps subdued

wars.name: Bellum Pannonicum (Pannonian War of Tiberius)
wars.outcome: Roman control extended to the Drava and the middle Danube; Illyricum enlarged; Tiberius awarded ovatio (9 BC)
wars.summary: After Agrippa's death in 12 BC Tiberius took over the war in Pannonia, using the Scordisci as allies, and subdued the Breuci and other peoples between the Sava and the Drava, deporting the young men. Velleius and Dio give only outlines.
wars.detail: Agrippa's arrival in winter 13/12 BC had frightened the Pannonians into submission; his death led them to revolt. Tiberius campaigned in 12-9 BC; Augustus's Res Gestae (30) claims that Pannonian peoples never reached by a Roman army before were subdued and the frontier of Illyricum advanced to the Danube. The disarmament and levies imposed in these years were a key grievance behind the great revolt of AD 6. The Senate voted Tiberius a triumph, which Augustus commuted to an ovatio.

wars.name: Augustan Germanic Wars
wars.outcome: Rome abandons the attempt to create a province between Rhine and Elbe after Varus's defeat (AD 9) and Germanicus's recall (16); the Rhine becomes the frontier
wars.summary: Twenty-eight years of campaigning east of the Rhine, from Drusus's offensives of 12-9 BC to Germanicus's last expedition in AD 16. By AD 9 a province was being organised, with towns such as Waldgirmes; the loss of three legions in the Teutoburg region reversed this.
wars.detail: The war began as retaliation for the clades Lolliana (16 BC) but became a war of conquest: Drusus reached the Elbe in 9 BC, Tiberius deported 40,000 Sugambri in 8 BC, Domitius Ahenobarbus crossed the Elbe and built the pontes longi, and Tiberius's immensum bellum of AD 4-5 brought a fleet up the Elbe. The planned pincer against Maroboduus in AD 6 was aborted by the Pannonian revolt. Excavations at Waldgirmes (forum with a gilded equestrian statue of Augustus), Haltern, Anreppen, Hedemünden and Kalkriese show a province in formation, which ancient writers (Dio 56.18) also describe. After AD 9 Germanicus's three campaigns (14-16) avenged Varus and recovered two eagles but at great cost in men and ships; Tiberius recalled him, preferring to leave the Germans to their internal quarrels, and Arminius fought Maroboduus in 17. The eagle of legio XIX was recovered in 15, another in 16 and the third in 41.

phases.t: Tiberius's immensum bellum; fleet on the Elbe
Tiberius and Germanicus secure the Rhine

wars.name: Great Illyrian Revolt (Bellum Batonianum)
wars.outcome: Revolt crushed; Illyricum split into Pannonia and Dalmatia; but Rome's capacity to conquer Germany is fatally weakened
wars.summary: The most dangerous rising Rome faced under Augustus. Triggered by levies for the Marcomannic war, the Daesitiates under Bato and the Breuci under another Bato and Pinnes rose in AD 6. Suetonius calls it the gravest foreign war since the Punic Wars; at its height Tiberius commanded ten legions, 70 auxiliary cohorts and 14 alae.
wars.detail: Velleius, who served in it, claims 800,000 rebels with 200,000 infantry and 9,000 cavalry under arms, and that Augustus warned the Senate the enemy could reach Rome in ten days. Augustus resorted to a levy of freedmen (the first since Cannae). Tiberius's strategy was attritional: wasting the countryside, dividing the rebel zones, and refusing pitched battle; it drew criticism in Rome and Germanicus was sent with a second army. The Breucian Bato betrayed Pinnes and was executed by the Daesitiate Bato, who in turn surrendered at Andetrium in 9 after Germanicus took Raetinium, Splonum and Arduba. Asked why he had rebelled, Bato said 'You Romans are to blame, for you send as guardians of your flocks not dogs or shepherds but wolves' (Dio 56.16). News of the victory reached Rome five days before news of Varus's disaster.

phases.t: Battle of the Volcaean Marshes; Germanicus arrives
Surrender of the Breuci at the Bathinus river
Reduction of the Dalmatian strongholds; Bato surrenders

wars.name: War of Tacfarinas
wars.outcome: Tacfarinas killed at Auzea in 24 by Publius Cornelius Dolabella; Roman control of the Numidian steppe consolidated
wars.summary: A seven-year guerrilla war in Africa led by Tacfarinas, a Numidian deserter from Roman auxiliary service who drilled the Musulamii and their Moorish allies in Roman fashion. Three governors won triumphal ornaments without ending it.
wars.detail: Furius Camillus defeated Tacfarinas in 17; Lucius Apronius in 20 decimated a cohort that had fled (a rare imperial instance) and saw a veteran, Helvius Rufus, win the civic crown at Thala; Junius Blaesus in 22-23 broke his bands into small columns and blockhouses and was the last non-imperial general hailed as imperator. Legio IX Hispana was brought from Pannonia as reinforcement and withdrawn too early. Tacfarinas's demand for land, delivered by envoys to Tiberius, enraged the emperor (Tac. Ann. 3.73). Dolabella finally surprised him at Auzea, where he died fighting; the Senate refused Dolabella triumphal ornaments to avoid embarrassing Blaesus, Sejanus's uncle.

wars.name: Roman conquest of Britain
wars.outcome: Southern and central Britain become a province; Wales subdued by 78; northern Britain overrun by Agricola to Mons Graupius (83/84) but abandoned north of the Forth-Clyde line within a few years
wars.summary: Begun by Claudius in 43 with four legions under Aulus Plautius and continued by a series of governors over four decades, the conquest of Britain was Rome's largest territorial gain of the first century and a test-bed for client kingship (Togidubnus, Prasutagus, Cartimandua).
wars.detail: Claudius needed military glory; the pretext was the flight of Verica of the Atrebates. After the Medway and the fall of Camulodunum, the legions fanned out: II Augusta under Vespasian to the south-west, IX Hispana north towards Lincoln, XIV Gemina and XX into the Midlands. Ostorius Scapula disarmed the allies (provoking an Icenian revolt in 47), founded the veteran colony at Camulodunum (49) and defeated Caratacus (51). The Silures defied Rome for decades. Suetonius Paullinus's attack on the Druid centre of Mona was interrupted by Boudica's revolt (60/61). The Flavians resumed the advance: Petillius Cerialis against the Brigantes (71-74), Julius Frontinus in Wales (74-77), Agricola from 77 to 84 into Caledonia. Tacitus's Agricola, written by the governor's son-in-law, is the main narrative and is panegyric; Vindolanda tablets and the excavated fortress of Inchtuthil, abandoned unfinished c. 86-87, illustrate the withdrawal that followed when troops were needed on the Danube.

phases.t: Didius Gallus, Veranius, Suetonius Paullinus; Mona and Boudica
Cerialis and Frontinus: Brigantes and Silures

wars.name: Boudican Revolt
wars.outcome: Revolt crushed at the battle of 'Watling Street'; Boudica dies; Iceni lands ravaged; Paullinus recalled after a critical report by the freedman Polyclitus
wars.summary: Rising of the Iceni and Trinovantes under Boudica after the annexation of the Icenian kingdom, the flogging of the queen and rape of her daughters, and the exactions of the veterans of Camulodunum and of Seneca's loans. The rebels destroyed Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium before being defeated by Suetonius Paullinus.
wars.detail: Tacitus gives 70,000 citizens and allies killed in the three towns and 80,000 Britons killed in the final battle against 400 Romans; Dio adds lurid detail of atrocities and a speech for Boudica with a hare released for divination. The date is 60 in Tacitus (Annals) but 61 is often preferred from the sequence of governors. Burnt destruction horizons of the period are well attested in Colchester and London. The procurator Decianus Catus fled to Gaul; the camp prefect of legio II Augusta, Poenius Postumus, refused to march and afterwards fell on his sword. Nero reportedly considered abandoning Britain (Suet. Nero 18).

phases.t: Outbreak while Paullinus attacks Mona; Camulodunum, Londinium, Verulamium destroyed
Battle and reprisals; Classicianus and Polyclitus

wars.name: Roman-Parthian War over Armenia (58-63)
wars.outcome: Compromise of Rhandeia: the Arsacid Tiridates keeps Armenia but receives the diadem from Nero in Rome (66)
wars.summary: Nero's war over Armenia, fought by Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, who took Artaxata (58) and Tigranocerta (59) and installed Tigranes VI. After Tigranes provoked Parthia, Caesennius Paetus was humiliated at Rhandeia (62); Corbulo then negotiated the settlement that held for half a century.
wars.detail: Corbulo spent 55-57 restoring the discipline of the Syrian legions (Tacitus describes soldiers who had never seen a camp or done sentry duty) and wintered them in the Armenian highlands under canvas. His campaigns combined manoeuvre with exemplary brutality. The Rhandeia formula, a Parthian prince as king of Armenia crowned by Rome, became the template for Roman-Parthian relations until Trajan. Tacitus's account is pro-Corbulo, probably drawing on the general's own memoirs.

wars.name: First Jewish-Roman War
wars.outcome: Destruction of Jerusalem and the Second Temple (70); end of the high priesthood and Sanhedrin in their old form; legio X Fretensis garrisons Jerusalem; fiscus Judaicus imposed on all Jews
wars.summary: The great revolt of Judaea, which began in 66 with the cessation of sacrifices for the emperor and the defeat of Cestius Gallus at Beth Horon. Vespasian reconquered Galilee and the countryside in 67-68; Titus besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in 70; the last fortresses, Herodium, Machaerus and Masada, fell by 73 or 74.
wars.detail: Causes included procuratorial misrule (Gessius Florus's seizure of 17 talents from the Temple treasury), Greek-Jewish strife at Caesarea, social banditry and apocalyptic expectation. Josephus, a rebel general in Galilee who surrendered at Jotapata and predicted Vespasian's accession, wrote the Jewish War under Flavian patronage, first in Aramaic, then Greek; it is the fullest account of any Roman provincial war but is apologetic both for the Flavians and for the Jewish aristocracy, blaming the 'brigands' and Zealots. Rebel coins (silver shekels 'Jerusalem the holy', bronze 'for the freedom of Zion') give the insurgents' own voice. The war gave the Flavians their legitimating victory, commemorated on the Arch of Titus, the Temple of Peace and IUDAEA CAPTA coinage.

phases.t: Perea, Judaea and Idumaea; operations pause for the civil war

wars.name: Civil War of the Year of the Four Emperors
wars.outcome: Vespasian emerges as emperor, founding the Flavian dynasty; Lex de imperio Vespasiani
wars.summary: The civil wars that followed Nero's fall: Vindex's rising and defeat (68), Galba's brief reign and murder (Jan 69), Otho's defeat at the first battle of Bedriacum (Apr 69), and the Flavian victory over Vitellius at the second battle (Oct 69) and in Rome (Dec 69). Tacitus: 'the secret of empire was out, that an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome'.
wars.detail: Each phase was decided by provincial armies: the Rhine legions for Vitellius, the Danube legions (led by the charismatic Antonius Primus, acting ahead of Vespasian's strategy) and the eastern legions for Vespasian. Mucianus marched the Syrian army west; Vespasian held Egypt and the grain supply. Cremona was sacked for four days; the Capitol burned. Tacitus's Histories 1-3 (our main source, closely parallel with Plutarch's Galba and Otho, implying a common lost source, perhaps Pliny the Elder or Cluvius Rufus) dramatise the moral collapse of the soldiery.

phases.t: Otho vs Vitellius; Flavian rising; Bedriacum II; sack of Rome

wars.name: Batavian Revolt
wars.outcome: Revolt ended by negotiation after defeats by Petillius Cerialis; Batavi keep their privileges; four legions dissolved or reconstituted
wars.summary: Julius Civilis, a Batavian noble and Roman citizen, rose ostensibly for Vespasian against Vitellius in 69 but turned it into a war of independence; Batavian veteran cohorts, Germanic tribes and the 'Empire of the Gauls' joined. The Rhine legions at Vetera surrendered and were massacred, and others swore allegiance to the Gallic empire, the worst humiliation of Roman arms in the first century.
wars.detail: Tacitus portrays Civilis as a one-eyed Sertorius or Hannibal who dyed his hair red and vowed not to cut it until he destroyed the legions. The Bructeran seeress Veleda received the captured legate Munius Lupercus (who died en route) and a captured flagship. Cerialis arrived in spring 70 with legions from Italy, Spain and Britain, won at Rigodulum and at Trier, survived a night attack, and defeated Civilis in a two-day battle near Vetera. Tacitus's narrative breaks off mid-negotiation (Hist. 5.26). Legiones I Germanica, IV Macedonica, XV Primigenia and XVI Gallica were disbanded; IV Flavia and XVI Flavia were raised in their place.

phases.t: Surrender of Vetera; Imperium Galliarum; Cerialis's counteroffensive

wars.name: Domitian's Chattan War
wars.outcome: Roman annexation of the Taunus and Wetterau; road network and watchtowers that grow into the upper German limes; Domitian takes the title Germanicus
wars.summary: Domitian's own campaign against the Chatti, launched from Mogontiacum in 83 under the pretext of a census in Gaul. Tacitus mocked his triumph as a sham with slaves dressed as captives, but archaeology shows real territorial gains and the cutting of 120 Roman miles of frontier roads (limites).
wars.detail: Frontinus, who served on the campaign, describes how Domitian cut limites through forests to expose the Chatti's hiding places (Strategemata 1.3.10) and paid compensation for crops destroyed by forts (2.11.7). Germania Superior and Inferior were formally constituted as provinces around this time (by 90). Coins of 85 proclaim GERMANIA CAPTA. Tacitus (Agr. 39; Germ. 37) and Pliny (Pan. 16) are hostile.

phases.t: Fortification of the Taunus and Wetterau

wars.name: Domitian's Dacian War
wars.outcome: Compromise peace of 89: Decebalus a client king receiving Roman subsidies and engineers
wars.summary: Dacian raids across the Danube killed the governor of Moesia, Oppius Sabinus, in winter 85/86. Domitian came in person; his praetorian prefect Cornelius Fuscus invaded Dacia and was killed with much of his army; Tettius Julianus avenged him at Tapae in 88, but the revolt of Saturninus and trouble with the Marcomanni forced a negotiated peace.
wars.detail: Moesia was split into Superior and Inferior in 86. The peace terms (Dio 67.7) granted Decebalus money and artisans 'skilled in all the arts of peace and war', which Trajan later represented as shameful tribute; Diegis, Decebalus's brother, received a diadem from Domitian. Domitian celebrated a triumph de Dacis in 89. Whether a legion (often supposed V Alaudae) was destroyed with Fuscus is debated. The Tropaeum Traiani's companion altar at Adamclisi may commemorate the fallen of 86 rather than of 102, an unresolved debate.

wars.name: Domitian's Suebic and Sarmatian Wars
wars.outcome: Sarmatians defeated by 93 (Domitian's ovatio, laurel only); fighting with the Suebi continues into 97 when Nerva takes the title Germanicus
wars.summary: The Marcomanni and Quadi refused aid against Dacia and were attacked in 89; in 92 the Iazyges with Suebic allies destroyed legio XXI Rapax. Domitian took the field himself in Pannonia (92-93).
wars.detail: A poorly documented war that set the pattern for the Marcomannic Wars of the 160s. The loss of XXI Rapax is inferred from Suetonius (Dom. 6) mentioning a legion slaughtered with its legate, combined with the legion's disappearance. Pannonia's garrison was raised to four legions in these years, shifting the empire's military centre of gravity to the middle Danube.

phases.t: Punitive campaign against Marcomanni and Quadi
Iazyges invasion; XXI Rapax destroyed; Domitian in Pannonia

wars.name: First Dacian War
wars.outcome: Decebalus submits: surrenders arms, engineers and deserters, demolishes forts, cedes territory (Banat, Oltenia); Roman garrison at Sarmizegetusa
wars.summary: Trajan's first war against Decebalus, launched in March 101 with perhaps nine legions and as many auxiliaries. After a costly victory at Tapae, a Dacian and Roxolanian counterattack into Moesia in winter 101/102, and a converging advance on the Orăștie mountains, Decebalus sued for peace.
wars.detail: Trajan's Column (scenes I-LXXVIII) is the principal visual source, but it is an artistic composition, not a war diary; Trajan's own commentarii (Dacica) survive in a single phrase quoted by Priscian. Dio (via the Byzantine epitome of Xiphilinus) provides the narrative skeleton, including a message written on a giant mushroom by the Buri. Trajan accepted the title Dacicus and triumphed in late 102. Decebalus was allowed to keep his throne as client.

phases.t: Crossing at Lederata; advance on Tapae
Dacian-Roxolanian raid on Moesia; battle near Adamclisi
Assault on the Orăștie mountain fortresses; peace

wars.name: Second Dacian War
wars.outcome: Dacian kingdom destroyed; Decebalus's suicide; province of Dacia created; vast booty
wars.summary: Decebalus rearmed, attacked Roman garrisons, captured the commander Longinus and tried to assassinate Trajan. Trajan crossed by his new stone bridge at Drobeta, besieged Sarmizegetusa Regia in summer 106 and hunted down the king, whose head was displayed on the Gemonian stairs.
wars.detail: John Lydus, citing Trajan's doctor Criton, gives booty of 5 million pounds of gold and 10 million of silver, figures modern scholars (Carcopino's 'gold of the Dacians') have tried to rationalise, perhaps by dividing by ten. Decebalus's treasure had been buried under the diverted river Sargetia and was betrayed by a noble named Bicilis. Longinus took poison to prevent his use as a bargaining chip. The province was colonised with settlers 'from the whole Roman world' (Eutropius 8.6), a claim later fuelling the Daco-Roman continuity debate.

phases.t: Siege of Sarmizegetusa; death of Decebalus; annexation

wars.name: Trajan's Parthian War
wars.outcome: Armenia, Mesopotamia and Assyria briefly annexed, Ctesiphon taken and a client king installed; massive revolts and the Jewish diaspora rising force retreat; Hadrian abandons the conquests in 117
wars.summary: Provoked by Osroes I's deposition of the Armenian king Axidares, Trajan annexed Armenia in 114, conquered northern Mesopotamia in 115 and marched down the Euphrates to Ctesiphon and the Persian Gulf in 116. Revolts across the new provinces and a failed siege of Hatra ended the enterprise.
wars.detail: Trajan refused the submission of Parthamasiris at Elegeia, who was then killed under murky circumstances. Dio has him weeping at Charax that he was too old to follow Alexander to India. Lusius Quietus and Erucius Clarus retook Nisibis, Edessa and Seleucia in 116; Maximus Santra was killed. Trajan crowned Parthamaspates king at Ctesiphon, effectively admitting he could not hold Babylonia. Ancient and modern judgements diverge: Lepper and others see a rational frontier strategy for controlling Mesopotamian trade; others (Bennett) stress glory-seeking. Hadrian's withdrawal was represented by hostile tradition as envy.

wars.name: Diaspora Revolt (Kitos War)
wars.outcome: Jewish communities of Cyrenaica, Egypt and Cyprus destroyed or reduced to insignificance; Jews banned from Cyprus
wars.summary: Simultaneous Jewish uprisings in Cyrenaica, Egypt, Cyprus and Mesopotamia while Trajan was campaigning in Parthia. Dio claims 220,000 killed in Cyrene and 240,000 in Cyprus; papyri and inscriptions confirm widespread devastation in Egypt and Cyrene.
wars.detail: Led in Cyrene by Lukuas/Andreas, the rebels destroyed temples of Apollo, Zeus and Hecate and the Caesareum and baths at Cyrene, as inscriptions recording Hadrianic restoration show. In Egypt the strategos Apollonios of Apollinopolis Heptakomias appears in his family letters fighting the 'impious Jews'; the great synagogue of Alexandria was destroyed. Marcius Turbo was sent with land and sea forces; in Mesopotamia Lusius Quietus crushed the Jewish population, the name surviving in rabbinic 'Polemos shel Qitos'. The causes (messianism, Greek-Jewish hostility, fiscus Judaicus) are debated; the sources (Dio's epitome, Eusebius, Orosius, papyri) are fragmentary.

phases.t: Mesopotamia; suppression by Turbo and Quietus

wars.name: Bar Kokhba Revolt
wars.outcome: Revolt crushed with enormous loss of life; Jerusalem refounded as Aelia Capitolina and closed to Jews; Judaea renamed Syria Palaestina
wars.summary: The second great Jewish revolt, led by Simon bar Kosiba, hailed by Rabbi Akiva as 'Bar Kokhba' (son of the star). Rome had to bring Sextus Julius Severus from Britain and units from across the empire; Hadrian omitted the customary 'I and the army are well' from his letter to the Senate.
wars.detail: Dio (69.12-14) gives 50 fortresses and 985 villages destroyed and 580,000 killed in battle, besides those who died of hunger and disease. Causes cited are the foundation of Aelia Capitolina (Dio) and a ban on circumcision (HA Hadr. 14.2); the relative priority is disputed, as is whether the rebels ever held Jerusalem. The Nahal Hever and Wadi Murabba'at caves have yielded letters from Bar Kosiba himself (in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek), the Babatha archive and land leases dated by the 'redemption of Israel'. Legio XXII Deiotariana may have been destroyed in the revolt, though evidence is circumstantial. Hadrian took a second imperatorial acclamation; the commanders received triumphal ornaments.

phases.t: Outbreak; rebels control Judaean hill country
Julius Severus's war of attrition; fall of Betar
Mopping up in the Judaean desert caves

wars.name: Roman-Parthian War of Lucius Verus
wars.outcome: Roman victory: Armenia restored to a Roman client, Osroene and Dura-Europos under Roman control, Seleucia and Ctesiphon sacked; but returning troops spread the Antonine Plague
wars.summary: Vologases IV invaded Armenia in 161, destroyed a Roman army at Elegeia and defeated the governor of Syria. Lucius Verus was sent east; his generals Statius Priscus, Avidius Cassius and Martius Verus won the war while Verus stayed mostly at Antioch and Daphne.
wars.detail: Priscus took Artaxata in 163 and founded a new Armenian capital, Kaine Polis; Sohaemus, a Roman senator of Arsacid-Emesene descent, was installed as king. Cassius advanced down the Euphrates, won at Dura and Sura, and in 165 sacked Seleucia on the Tigris despite its submission, and burned the palace at Ctesiphon. In 166 he crossed into Media. Lucian's satirical 'How to Write History' mocks the flood of sycophantic histories of this war; Fronto's letters and Principia Historiae offer the court view.

wars.name: Marcomannic Wars
wars.outcome: Rome restores the Danube frontier after near-catastrophe; Marcus's plans for provinces of Marcomannia and Sarmatia abandoned by Commodus in the peace of 180
wars.summary: A generation of war along the middle Danube, beginning with an incursion of Langobardi and Obii in 166/167 and culminating in the first barbarian invasion of Italy for nearly three centuries, when Marcomanni and Quadi besieged Aquileia and destroyed Opitergium. Marcus Aurelius spent most of his last decade at Carnuntum, Sirmium and Vindobona, writing the Meditations.
wars.detail: The war is divided into the first (bellum Germanicum, 166/167-175) and second (expeditio Germanica secunda, 177-180) phases, separated by the revolt of Avidius Cassius. Rome faced a coalition of Marcomanni, Quadi, Iazyges and many smaller peoples, partly pushed by movements further north (the Goths moving towards the Black Sea). The Antonine Plague crippled recruitment; Marcus enrolled slaves, gladiators and bandits and auctioned palace treasures in 169. Captured Germans were settled inside the empire, a precedent for later centuries. The chronology is highly uncertain because Dio survives only in excerpts and the Historia Augusta is muddled; the Column of Marcus, coin legends, and inscriptions such as Laugaricio and the career of Valerius Maximianus provide anchors. Whether Marcus intended to annex Marcomannia and Sarmatia (HA Marc. 24.5, 27.10) is debated.

phases.t: Incursions; Marcus and Verus go north
Failed Roman offensive; invasion of Italy; Costoboci raid Greece
Campaigns against Marcomanni, Quadi, Iazyges; Rain Miracle
Second expedition; Roman garrisons in Quadi lands; death of Marcus

campaigns.name: Augustus in Cantabria
campaigns.strength: Perhaps seven legions in the peninsula, with a fleet from Aquitania; numbers in the main column unknown
campaigns.summary: Augustus's only personal campaign as princeps. From Segisama three columns pushed north into the Cantabrian mountains while a seaborne force landed on the coast; the emperor fell ill and withdrew to Tarraco, leaving his legates to finish the blockade of Aracillum.

path.note: Augustus enters his eighth consulship here; winter headquarters

path.t: Pompaelo region (march through the upper Ebro)
Cantabrian coast (Portus Blendium?), seaborne landing links up

campaigns.note: Order of operations and identification of Vellica and Aracillum are debated; recent archaeology of Roman siege lines at La Espina del Gallego, El Cincho and La Loma supports a campaign in the upper Pisuerga and Besaya valleys.

campaigns.name: Aelius Gallus's expedition to Arabia Felix
campaigns.strength: c. 10,000 Roman and allied troops, including 500 Jews from Herod and 1,000 Nabataeans under Syllaeus; 130 transports
campaigns.summary: Augustus's attempt to seize the incense lands of South Arabia. Misled (so Strabo claims) by the Nabataean minister Syllaeus, the army took six months to reach Marib, failed to take it, and returned in sixty days, having lost most of its men to disease rather than battle.

path.note: Wintered here due to scurvy and disease

path.t: Battle at a river; 10,000 Arabs killed for 2 Romans (Strabo)
Crosses the Red Sea to Myos Hormos
Coptos, then down the Nile to Alexandria

campaigns.note: Strabo (16.4.22-24) was Gallus's friend and companion in Egypt and blames Syllaeus; Res Gestae 26.5 claims the army reached Mariba. Exact inland route and the location of Leuke Kome (Aynunah or al-Wajh) are debated.

campaigns.name: Petronius's campaign in Kush
campaigns.strength: Fewer than 10,000 infantry and 800 cavalry (Strabo)
campaigns.summary: Counteroffensive by the prefect of Egypt after the Kushite sack of Syene: victory at Pselchis, capture of Primis, and the razing of Napata, the old religious capital of Kush.

path.t: Relief of Primis against the Candace

campaigns.note: Strabo 17.1.54; Dio 54.5. Pliny NH 6.181 lists towns taken. Archaeology at Qasr Ibrim confirms a Roman occupation phase.

campaigns.name: Drusus's German campaigns
campaigns.strength: Perhaps 5-6 legions on the Rhine plus auxiliaries and a fleet
campaigns.summary: Four seasons of offensives that took Roman arms from the Rhine to the Elbe: the North Sea expedition and the fossa Drusiana (12 BC), the Lippe-Weser drive and the Arbalo ambush (11 BC), the Chatti (10 BC), and the great march to the Elbe (9 BC), on the return from which Drusus died after a fall from his horse.

path.t: Ems estuary; fleet stranded among the Chauci
Reaches the Weser in Cheruscan territory
Ambush at Arbalo on the return
Through Cheruscan lands to the Harz
The Elbe; apparition of a giant woman warns him back (Dio)
Fall from horse between Saale and Rhine; dies in camp 30 days later

campaigns.note: Routes are reconstructed from Dio 54.32-33 and 55.1, Florus 2.30 and the distribution of Augustan camps (Oberaden, Haltern, Anreppen, Hedemünden); the camp where Drusus died (castra scelerata) is unlocated.

campaigns.name: Varus's last march
campaigns.strength: Legions XVII, XVIII, XIX, three alae and six cohorts with camp followers; c. 15,000-20,000 soldiers
campaigns.summary: Varus left his summer camp near the Weser for winter quarters on the Rhine and was diverted, on Arminius's report of a rising, into difficult country where the army was destroyed over several days.

path.t: Summer camp near the Weser (Porta Westfalica area?)
Diversion west towards the reported rising
First attacks; marching camp with three legions' worth of entrenchment (Tac. Ann. 1.61)
Kalkriese: the trap between Kalkrieser Berg and the Great Moor
Garrison breaks out to the Rhine (Vetera)

campaigns.note: The identification of Kalkriese with the final stage is widely but not universally accepted (coins stop c. AD 9; Varus countermarks VAR). Older theories placed the battle in the Teutoburger Wald near Detmold. The location of the summer camp and of Aliso are uncertain.

campaigns.name: Germanicus's campaigns beyond the Rhine
campaigns.strength: 8 legions of the Rhine armies (c. 40,000) plus 26 auxiliary cohorts and 8 alae; in 16 a fleet of 1,000 ships
campaigns.summary: Three campaigns to avenge Varus: the massacre of the Marsi (14), the raid on the Chatti and visit to the Varian battlefield followed by the near-disaster of Caecina at Pontes Longi (15), and the amphibious invasion via the Ems that won Idistaviso and the Angrivarian Wall but lost much of the fleet to a North Sea storm (16).

path.t: Vetera; after the mutiny the army crosses the Rhine
Marsi massacred at a festival; shrine of Tanfana razed
Mogontiacum; spring raid on the Chatti
Fleet of 1,000 ships assembles at the Insula Batavorum
Return by sea; fleet wrecked by storm, Germanicus's trireme driven to the Chauci

campaigns.note: Tacitus Annals 1.49-71 and 2.5-26 is the only detailed source; topography is vague and site identifications (Idistaviso near Minden or Rinteln, the Angrivarian wall near Leese) are conjectural.

campaigns.name: Aulus Plautius's invasion of Britain
campaigns.strength: Four legions (II Augusta, IX Hispana, XIV Gemina, XX) and auxiliaries, c. 40,000; Claudius brought elephants and the praetorians
campaigns.summary: The Claudian invasion: delayed by a mutiny of troops who refused to campaign 'outside the known world', the army crossed in three divisions, defeated Togodumnus and Caratacus in a two-day battle at a river (the Medway), forced the Thames, and waited for Claudius to lead the final advance on Camulodunum.
campaigns.note: Dio 60.19-22 is the only narrative and names no rivers; the Medway and Richborough are inferences. A landing near Fishbourne in friendly Atrebatic territory has been argued (Hind, Manley).

campaigns.name: Vespasian and legio II Augusta in southern Britain
campaigns.strength: Legio II Augusta with auxiliaries, c. 10,000
campaigns.summary: As legate of II Augusta, the future emperor fought 30 battles, subdued two powerful peoples, took more than 20 oppida and the Isle of Wight (Suet. Vesp. 4), conventionally identified with the Durotriges and Belgae and the Dorset hillforts.

path.t: Hod Hill: ballista bolts concentrated on the chieftain's hut; Roman fort built in the corner
Towards the Exe (later fortress of Isca)

campaigns.note: Suetonius gives no place-names; the route is inferred from archaeology (Hod Hill, Lake Farm, Waddon Hill) and the later base of II Augusta at Exeter (c. 55).

campaigns.name: Suetonius Paullinus: Mona and the Boudican war
campaigns.strength: For the final battle legio XIV Gemina, vexillations of XX and nearby auxiliaries, almost 10,000 men (Tac. Ann. 14.34)
campaigns.summary: Paullinus was storming the Druidic island of Mona when news of Boudica's revolt came. He rode ahead to Londinium, judged it indefensible and abandoned it, then fell back up Watling Street to choose his ground, where he destroyed the British host.

path.t: Flat-bottomed boats and cavalry fording the Menai Strait
Mona: Druids and sacred groves destroyed

campaigns.note: Tacitus does not name the battlefield; Mancetter (Manduessedum) is the favourite of many, but High Cross, Church Stowe and sites near Towcester have been proposed. The year is 60 in Tacitus but often corrected to 61.

campaigns.name: Corbulo's conquest of Armenia
campaigns.strength: Legiones III Gallica and VI Ferrata, plus X Fretensis or IV Scythica in part, auxiliaries and allied kings' contingents
campaigns.summary: After a winter in tents in the Armenian highlands, Corbulo stormed fortresses with exemplary severity, took and razed Artaxata, marched across the Mesopotamian edge to Tigranocerta, which surrendered, and installed Rome's candidate Tigranes VI.

path.t: Upper Euphrates (Satala region), winter under canvas
Erzurum plain; fortress of Volandum stormed
March south through the Mardi country, suffering thirst

campaigns.note: Tacitus Annals 13.35-41 and 14.23-26; the site of Tigranocerta is disputed (Arzan near Silvan is favoured).

campaigns.name: Vespasian and Titus in Judaea
campaigns.strength: Legiones V Macedonica, X Fretensis, XV Apollinaris (from 67) with 23 auxiliary cohorts, 6 alae and allied kings' troops, c. 60,000 (Josephus BJ 3.64-69); XII Fulminata added for Jerusalem
campaigns.summary: Vespasian's methodical reconquest of Galilee in 67, Perea and the Judaean lowlands in 68, followed after his proclamation by Titus's siege of Jerusalem in 70.

path.t: Ptolemais; Titus joins with XV Apollinaris
Japha taken by Trajan (father of the emperor)
Tarichaeae and the battle on the Lake of Gennesaret

path.note: Operations halt on news of Nero's death

campaigns.note: Josephus BJ 3-6, an eyewitness for most of it (first as rebel commander, then as Roman captive and interpreter).

campaigns.name: Caecina's march on Italy
campaigns.strength: c. 30,000 from the upper German army, legio XXI Rapax as core
campaigns.summary: Caecina led the Vitellian southern column from Vindonissa, crushed the Helvetii en route, crossed the Great St Bernard in late winter and reached the Po before Valens.

path.t: Helvetii massacred near Mons Vocetius; Aventicum submits
Crosses the Great St Bernard (Poeninus) in snow
Fails before Placentia, whose amphitheatre burns

campaigns.note: Tacitus Histories 1.61-70; 2.17-45.

campaigns.name: Fabius Valens's march on Italy
campaigns.strength: c. 40,000 from the lower German army, core of legio V Alaudae
campaigns.summary: Valens's larger column marched from Cologne through Gaul, terrorising Divodurum (where 4,000 were massacred) and extorting money from Vienne, crossed the Mont Genèvre and joined Caecina at Cremona days before the battle with Otho.
campaigns.note: Tacitus Histories 1.62-66; 2.27-30.

campaigns.name: Antonius Primus's Flavian offensive
campaigns.strength: Five Danubian legions (VII Galbiana, XIII Gemina, VII Claudia, VIII Augusta, III Gallica) with auxiliaries, c. 30,000-40,000
campaigns.summary: Ignoring orders to wait for Mucianus, the legate of legio VII Galbiana led the Danube legions into Italy in a lightning campaign, won the second battle of Bedriacum, sacked Cremona and forced his way into Rome.

path.t: Fanum Fortunae; over the Apennines in snow

campaigns.note: Tacitus Histories 3.1-35; 3.41-63; 3.78-86.

campaigns.name: Agricola's campaigns in Wales and Caledonia
campaigns.strength: Up to four legions (II Adiutrix, IX Hispana, XX, II Augusta in part); 8,000 auxiliary infantry and 3,000 cavalry in the battle line at Mons Graupius
campaigns.summary: Seven seasons of campaigning that took a Roman army to the Moray Firth: Ordovices and Mona (77/78), the Brigantes and the north (79), the Tay (80), consolidation on the Forth-Clyde isthmus (81), the south-west facing Ireland (82), and the push up the east coast to Mons Graupius (83 or 84), with the fleet circumnavigating Britain.

path.t: Mona taken by auxiliaries swimming beside their horses
South-west Scotland; Ireland in view, 'could be taken with one legion'
Night attack on legio IX in camp beyond the Forth

campaigns.note: Tacitus Agricola 18-38 gives seasons but almost no place-names; reconstruction depends on marching-camp series. Whether Mons Graupius was in 83 or 84 depends on whether Agricola arrived in 77 or 78.

campaigns.name: Trajan's First Dacian campaign
campaigns.strength: Perhaps 9-12 legions in whole or part and as many auxiliaries; c. 100,000-150,000 in the theatre
campaigns.summary: Trajan crossed the Danube on pontoon bridges at Lederata, fought a bloody battle at Tapae, returned to meet a Dacian and Roxolanian counterattack in Lower Moesia over the winter, and in 102 converged on Decebalus's mountain fortresses, forcing a peace.
campaigns.note: Reconstruction depends on Dio 68.8-9, the Column, and archaeology; the Column's scenes cannot be mapped onto a single itinerary with confidence.

campaigns.name: Trajan's Second Dacian campaign
campaigns.strength: Some 14 legions were on the Danube by 105-106; perhaps 100,000+ in the field
campaigns.summary: Trajan left Rome in June 105, crossed the Adriatic, inspected his Drobeta bridge and in 106 besieged Sarmizegetusa Regia; Decebalus fled north and killed himself as Roman cavalry closed in.

path.t: Pursuit of Decebalus to the north

campaigns.note: The place of Decebalus's death (Ranisstorum on the Philippi tombstone of Ti. Claudius Maximus) is unlocated.

campaigns.name: Trajan's Parthian campaign
campaigns.strength: Up to 11 legions in whole or part, with Moorish cavalry of Lusius Quietus
campaigns.summary: From Antioch through Armenia (114), across Mesopotamia (115), down the Euphrates and Tigris to Ctesiphon and the head of the Persian Gulf (116), and back to a failed siege of Hatra (117) before Trajan, stricken by a stroke, died at Selinus.

path.t: Tigris crossed into Adiabene on a boat bridge
Babylon; sacrifices in the room where Alexander died

campaigns.note: Chronology of 115-116 (and whether Mesopotamia was taken in 115 or 116) is debated: Lepper, Trajan's Parthian War (1948), versus Bennett and others.

campaigns.name: Avidius Cassius's Mesopotamian offensive
campaigns.strength: Syrian legions (III Gallica, IV Scythica, XVI Flavia) with reinforcements from the Danube and Rhine (I Minervia, II Adiutrix, V Macedonica)
campaigns.summary: While Statius Priscus retook Armenia, Avidius Cassius, a Syrian disciplinarian, led the main army from the Euphrates crossing at Zeugma down to Dura, Seleucia and Ctesiphon, and in 166 into Media.

path.t: Battle of Europos on the Euphrates
path.note: Lucian mentions Europos; often identified as Carchemish/Jerablus area

path.t: Return to Syria; plague among the troops

campaigns.note: Fragmentary sources (Dio 71.2, HA Verus 7-8, Lucian, Fronto); the order of Dura and Seleucia and the identification of 'Europos' are uncertain.

campaigns.name: Marcus Aurelius on the Danube
campaigns.strength: Up to 16 legions along the Danube, plus the new II and III Italica
campaigns.summary: Marcus's long presence on the northern frontier: from Aquileia (168) through headquarters at Carnuntum (171-173), operations among the Quadi on the Gran (Hron), the war against the Iazyges from Sirmium (173-175), the eastern interruption of 175-176, and the second expedition based at Vindobona (178-180).

path.t: Aquileia; Verus dies at Altinum on the way back (169)
Among the Quadi on the Granua (Meditations Book 1 colophon)

campaigns.note: Chronology of the Marcomannic Wars is notoriously uncertain; this path follows Birley, Marcus Aurelius (rev. 1987).

legions.name: Legio VII (Caesar's Seventh)
legions.endNote: veterans settled at Baeterrae? and Luca; legion reconstituted by Octavian, ancestor of VII Claudia

stations.base: River Sabis (Sambre), battle with the Nervii
stations.note: held the right wing against the Nervii with XII

legions.summary: One of the four veteran legions Caesar inherited in Gallia Cisalpina in 58 BC (VII-X), probably raised by Pompey in Spain in the 60s. It fought at every major engagement of the Gallic War, including both crossings to Britain, then for Caesar at Ilerda, Pharsalus and Thapsus.
legions.detail: In 57 BC on the Sabis the VII and XII were so compressed by the Nervian assault that the standards were bunched and almost every centurion of XII's fourth cohort fell before Caesar himself went to the front line (BG 2.25-26). In Britain in 55 BC the Seventh was ambushed while foraging and rescued by Caesar (BG 4.32). Discharged veterans were settled in colonies (Baeterrae is 'Septimanorum'); the legion was re-formed by Octavian and became VII Macedonica, later VII Claudia.

legions.name: Legio VIII (Caesar's Eighth)
legions.endNote: veterans settled at Forum Iulii (colonia Octavanorum); reconstituted, ancestor of VIII Augusta

stations.note: joined with the IX on the left wing because both were understrength

legions.summary: Veteran legion of Caesar's Gallic army, probably of Pompeian Spanish origin like VII and IX. It was at Gergovia, Alesia, the Dyrrachium lines, Pharsalus and Thapsus, and its veterans were settled in Italy and at Forum Iulii.
legions.detail: At Pharsalus the Eighth was so depleted that Caesar paired it with the Ninth to form a single line unit (BC 3.89). The legion re-formed after 44 BC took the name Augusta, a sign of a re-raising or of a battle honour under Octavian.

legions.name: Legio IX (Caesar's Ninth)
legions.endNote: disbanded after Thapsus, veterans settled in Picenum; re-formed by Octavian (later IX Hispana)

stations.base: River Sabis (Sambre), battle with the Nervii

legions.summary: The Ninth served through the Gallic War and the civil war. Its mutiny at Placentia in 49 BC, when Caesar threatened decimation and executed twelve ringleaders, is one of the classic episodes of late Republican army discipline.
legions.detail: Appian (BC 2.47) and Dio (41.26-35) describe the Placentia mutiny over delayed pay and booty; Caesar's own Bellum Civile passes over it in silence. The legion lost heavily at Dyrrachium in 48 BC (BC 3.45-46). After Thapsus its veterans were settled in Picenum; Octavian raised a new IX that served against Sextus Pompey ('Triumphalis'?) and in the Cantabrian war.
legions.debate: Whether the imperial IX Hispana descends directly from Caesar's Ninth or is a fresh Octavianic creation is disputed.

legions.name: Legio X Equestris
legions.endNote: veterans settled at Narbo (45 BC); re-formed, later merged into X Gemina

stations.note: Caesar mounts its men on Gallic horses to meet Ariovistus

stations.base: River Sabis (Sambre), battle with the Nervii

stations.note: its aquilifer leaps first into the surf
decided the battle on the right

legions.summary: Caesar's favourite legion, raised by him as governor of Hispania Ulterior (61 BC). Its nickname 'Equestris' comes from 58 BC, when Caesar mounted its men on Gallic cavalry horses to escort him to Ariovistus and a soldier quipped that he was making them knights.
legions.detail: The standard-bearer of the X led the jump into the sea off Kent in 55 BC (BG 4.25). In 47 BC the legion mutinied in Campania and marched on Rome; Caesar ended it by addressing the men as 'Quirites' (civilians) rather than 'commilitones' (Suet. Iul. 70; App. BC 2.93). It fought at Thapsus and decided Munda, then its veterans were settled at Narbo. A re-formed X fought for Lepidus and Antony; merged with another legion under Augustus, it became X Gemina.

legions.name: Legio I Germanica
legions.endNote: surrendered to the Gallic empire of Classicus in the Batavian revolt; disbanded by Vespasian, men drafted into VII Gemina

stations.note: probably the legion stripped of the title Augusta by Agrippa in 19 BC

legions.summary: Lower Rhine legion that started the mutiny of AD 14 at Ara Ubiorum and twelve years later the proclamation of Vitellius. It ended in disgrace: after swearing allegiance to the Imperium Galliarum in 70 it was dissolved.
legions.detail: Agrippa took away the honorific Augusta from a legion after its poor performance against the Cantabri in 19 BC (Dio 54.11.5); I Germanica is the usual candidate. Under Germanicus it took part in the campaigns of AD 14-16. On 2 January 69 its legate Fabius Valens hailed Vitellius at Colonia, and a strong detachment marched to Italy and fought at Bedriacum. Besieged at Bonna and later at Novaesium by Civilis, the remnant with XVI Gallica took the oath to the Gallic empire, was paraded to Trier in humiliation (Tac. Hist. 4.62), and was disbanded. Its survivors helped form VII Gemina.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio I Adiutrix
legions.endNote: listed at Brigetio in the Notitia Dignitatum

stations.note: Dacia during and after Trajan's wars

legions.summary: Raised from the marines of the Misenum fleet late in Nero's reign and given legionary standards by Galba (diploma of 22 December 68). After service on the Rhine it became the long-term garrison of Brigetio on the Pannonian Danube from Hadrian's time.
legions.detail: Galba's entry into Rome in October 68 was marked by the slaughter of marines who demanded an eagle at the Milvian Bridge (Tac. Hist. 1.6; Suet. Galba 12); the survivors became I Adiutrix. It fought for Otho at the first battle of Bedriacum and broke XXI Rapax's front line (Tac. Hist. 2.43). Brigetio was its base for three centuries; the legion styled itself pia fidelis bis and later Constans. A Hadrianic-period tile and stamp series documents its building activity throughout Pannonia.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio I Italica
legions.endNote: listed in the Notitia at Novae and Sexaginta Prista

stations.note: stationed at Lugdunum on its way to the East
Vitellian army at both battles of Bedriacum

legions.summary: Raised by Nero in 66 for a planned expedition to the Caspian Gates, its recruits all Italians six Roman feet tall, nicknamed 'the phalanx of Alexander the Great' (Suet. Nero 19.2). From 70 it garrisoned Novae on the Lower Danube for more than three centuries.
legions.detail: Stationed at Lugdunum in 68-69, it sided with Vitellius and fought at both battles of Bedriacum. At Novae Polish-Bulgarian excavations have uncovered its principia, a large valetudinarium and a late-antique episcopal complex built over the fortress. Vexillations served in Mauretania (Antonine period) and in the Crimea at Charax.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio I Minervia
legions.endNote: last attested in the early 4th century at Bonna
legions.summary: Raised by Domitian in 82/83 for his war against the Chatti and named after his patron goddess Minerva. It stayed at Bonna throughout its existence and won the titles pia fidelis for remaining loyal during Saturninus's revolt at Mainz in 89.
legions.detail: Hadrian commanded I Minervia during Trajan's second Dacian war (105-106) (HA Hadr. 3.6). Vexillations fought in Lucius Verus's Parthian war and the Marcomannic wars, and the legion supported Septimius Severus against Clodius Albinus in 197. It struck coins as a Gallic empire unit under Victorinus (269-271).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio I Parthica
legions.endNote: in the Notitia at Constantina (Tella) as Prima Parthica Nisibena

stations.note: Singara captured by Shapur II in 360 and the garrison deported

legions.summary: One of three Parthian legions (I-III) raised by Septimius Severus for his eastern campaigns of 195-198, and the garrison of the new province of Mesopotamia at Singara under the Jebel Sinjar.
legions.detail: Unlike the senatorial legions, the Parthian legions were commanded by equestrian prefects. Singara fell to Shapur II in 360 after a siege in which the two legions inside (I Parthica and I Flavia) were captured (Amm. 20.6.8). The successor unit sat at Constantina after Jovian surrendered Nisibis and Singara in 363.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio I Macriana Liberatrix
legions.endNote: disbanded by Galba after Macer's execution

stations.note: raised in Africa beside III Augusta

legions.summary: Short-lived legion raised in spring 68 by the legate of III Augusta, L. Clodius Macer, who revolted against Nero, struck denarii with the legend LEG I LIB MACRIANA, and threatened Rome's grain supply. Galba had Macer killed and dissolved the legion.

legions.name: Legio II Augusta
legions.endNote: listed at Rutupiae (Richborough) under the comes litoris Saxonici

stations.note: Cantabrian war; veterans settled at Emerita? and Caesaraugusta
built the first legionary fortress at Strasbourg

stations.base: Midlands of Britain (series of campaign bases)
stations.note: Vespasian's campaign in the south-west: 30 battles, 20 oppida, the Isle of Wight (Suet. Vesp. 4)

legions.summary: The Second Augusta invaded Britain in 43 under the future emperor Vespasian and spent more than two centuries at Isca (Caerleon), building large stretches of Hadrian's and the Antonine Walls. Its camp prefect Poenius Postumus refused to join Suetonius Paulinus against Boudica and fell on his sword after the victory (Tac. Ann. 14.37).
legions.detail: Under Vespasian the legion conquered the Durotriges: the war cemetery and ballista bolt in a spine at Maiden Castle are often linked to its assault. Exeter's fortress (c. 55-75) was followed by Caerleon, where the amphitheatre, baths and barracks are the best preserved of any British fortress. Building stones name it on both northern walls. By the late 3rd century part of it held the Saxon Shore fort at Richborough, where the Notitia places it.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Manning, The Fortress Excavations at Caerleon

legions.name: Legio II Adiutrix
legions.endNote: listed at Aquincum in the Notitia
legions.summary: Raised by Vespasian from the marines of the Ravenna fleet (constituted 7 March 70), it served in Britain under Cerialis and Agricola before being pulled out to the Danube after Domitian's Dacian setbacks. From the late 1st century it was the garrison of Aquincum, the capital of Pannonia Inferior.
legions.detail: Its withdrawal from Deva c. 87 forced the abandonment of the newly built fortress at Inchtuthil and of Agricola's Scottish conquests: Tacitus' bitter 'perdomita Britannia et statim omissa' (Hist. 1.2). Hadrian served as one of its tribunes (c. 95). At Aquincum its fortress lies under modern Óbuda, with a large amphitheatre for the garrison.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio II Italica
legions.endNote: listed at Lauriacum and Lentia in the Notitia
legions.summary: Raised with III Italica by Marcus Aurelius in 165-166, from Italian recruits, as the Marcomannic crisis loomed. It became the first legion permanently based in Noricum, whose governor was now its legate.
legions.detail: The new legion's arrival upgraded Noricum to a praetorian province. Lauriacum (Enns) became one of the largest fortresses on the Danube and a late-antique bishopric; the Life of Severinus describes its last Roman garrison and refugees in the 470s-480s.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio II Parthica
legions.endNote: captured at Bezabde by Shapur II (Amm. 20.7.1)

stations.note: first legion permanently stationed in Italy; campaigns in the east under Caracalla, Severus Alexander, Gordian III

legions.summary: Severus's Second Parthian was garrisoned at Castra Albana, 20 km from Rome, a political revolution: a legion in Italy as the emperor's strategic reserve. It took part in nearly every 3rd-century imperial campaign in the East.
legions.detail: Its men were involved in the murder of Caracalla near Carrhae in 217 and then backed Elagabalus against Macrinus at Raphanea/Immae in 218. It acclaimed Maximinus Thrax in 235 and in 238 its men murdered him outside Aquileia. Tombstones at Apamea in Syria record its winter quarters there in 215-218 and 231-233. A detachment served at Bezabde on the Tigris, which Shapur II stormed in 360.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio II Traiana Fortis
legions.endNote: listed at Parembole (Upper Egypt) and Apollonopolis in the Notitia

stations.note: single legion of Egypt after XXII Deiotariana vanished

legions.summary: Raised by Trajan for the Dacian or Parthian wars, II Traiana became the legion of Egypt at Nicopolis outside Alexandria from Hadrian's reign, alone after XXII Deiotariana disappeared.
legions.detail: It sent vexillations to Judaea during the Bar Kokhba war (132-135). From Severus onwards it bore the name Germanica after Caracalla's Alemannic campaign of 213. Egyptian papyri preserve an unusually rich record of its recruits, pay and discharge procedure.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio III Augusta
legions.endNote: disbanded 238 by Gordian III, restored 253; Tertio Augustani among the African comitatenses in the Notitia

stations.note: Hadrian's address to the army of Africa in 128 inscribed on the parade ground column

legions.summary: The single legion of Roman Africa, based successively at Ammaedara, Theveste and Lambaesis, it built roads, aqueducts and towns such as Thamugadi across Numidia. Gordian III dissolved it in 238 because its legate Capelianus had destroyed Gordian I and II at Carthage.
legions.detail: Under Tiberius it fought the seven-year guerrilla war of Tacfarinas (17-24). Its legate was the only commander of a legion in a senatorial province until Caligula transferred control from the proconsul. Hadrian's adlocutio at Lambaesis (CIL VIII 18042, July 128) is the fullest surviving text of an emperor addressing troops, praising manoeuvres and criticising details. Its name was erased from inscriptions in 238 (damnatio) and recut after 253.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Le Bohec, La Troisième Légion Auguste (1989)

legions.name: Legio III Cyrenaica
legions.endNote: listed at Bostra in the Notitia

stations.note: Arabia after the annexation of Nabataea; possibly only from c. 123

legions.summary: Probably raised by Antony or Lepidus with its name from Cyrenaica, III Cyrenaica was part of the Augustan garrison of Egypt. After Trajan annexed Nabataea in 106 it became the legion of Arabia at Bostra, where it stayed into the 5th century.
legions.detail: It took part in Aelius Gallus's expedition into Arabia Felix (26-25 BC) or Petronius's war with Meroe (24-22 BC). A vexillation besieged Jerusalem with Titus in 70. Papyri from Bostra (the letters of Apollinarius, 107) describe the new province: 'while others are breaking stones all day long, I am a principalis and do nothing' (P. Mich. VIII 466).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Bowersock, Roman Arabia (1983)

legions.name: Legio III Gallica
legions.endNote: in the Notitia at Danaba (Phoenice), location not securely identified

stations.note: Syrian garrison, base probably at Raphanea
Moesia; destroyed a Rhoxolani raid in winter 68/69
restored by Severus Alexander; later at Danaba

legions.summary: A Caesarian legion of Gallic recruits that spent most of its life in Syria. At the second battle of Bedriacum (October 69) its soldiers, used to Syrian custom, saluted the rising sun, which the Vitellians took as the arrival of eastern reinforcements (Tac. Hist. 3.24-25).
legions.detail: It fought with Antony in Media Atropatene (36 BC) and with Corbulo in Armenia (58-63). Transferred to Moesia in 68, it was the first Danubian legion to declare for Vespasian. In 218-219 its legate Verus tried to make himself emperor and Elagabalus dissolved the legion (Dio 80.7.1); Severus Alexander re-formed it.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio III Italica
legions.endNote: listed in Raetia (Castra Regina and detachments along the Danube-Iller line) in the Notitia

stations.note: Raetia before the fortress was finished
building inscription of the gate dated 179

legions.summary: Twin of II Italica, raised in 165-166 and sent to Raetia, whose governor became a senatorial legate. Its fortress at Regensburg is dated precisely by the inscription from the Porta Praetoria (CIL III 11965) to 179.
legions.detail: The Regensburg fortress gate (Porta Praetoria) still stands partly in the city. In the late empire the legion was split into detachments along the Danube and the Iller, as the Notitia shows (Not. Occ. 35).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio III Parthica
legions.endNote: in the Notitia at Apatna in Osrhoene (site uncertain)

stations.note: Mesopotamia/Osroene; Rhesaena coins with the legion's emblem

legions.summary: Third of Severus's Parthian legions, garrisoned in Osroene/Mesopotamia, probably at Rhesaena (Ras al-Ayn) where coins of the colonia carry its vexillum.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio IV Macedonica
legions.endNote: disbanded after the Batavian revolt; reconstituted as IV Flavia Felix

stations.note: Hispania Tarraconensis; tile stamps at Herrera de Pisuerga

legions.summary: Raised by Caesar in 48 BC, at Mutina for Octavian in 43, and then for seven decades the garrison of Pisoraca in northern Spain. Moved to Mainz under Claudius, it joined XXII Primigenia in throwing down Galba's images on 1 January 69, the act that launched Vitellius's bid.
legions.detail: In 70 the legion joined Civilis and Classicus' Imperium Galliarum; Vespasian dissolved it and re-raised it as IV Flavia Felix. The rejection of Galba at Mainz is told in Tacitus Hist. 1.55-56.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio IV Flavia Felix
legions.endNote: listed at Singidunum in the Notitia

stations.note: garrison of the new province of Dacia

legions.summary: Re-formed by Vespasian from the dissolved IV Macedonica, it held Burnum in Dalmatia, then Berzobis in Dacia, and from Hadrian's reign Singidunum (Belgrade), its base for three centuries.
legions.detail: Its lion emblem echoes Flavian iconography. The fortress of Singidunum lies under Belgrade's Kalemegdan citadel. Vexillations fought in the Marcomannic wars and in Severus Alexander's Persian war.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio IV Scythica
legions.endNote: in the Notitia at Oresa (Strata Diocletiana)

stations.note: title from M. Licinius Crassus's campaign against Bastarnae and Getae (29-28 BC)
with Corbulo; capitulated with XII Fulminata at Rhandeia (62)
tile stamps confirm the fortress at the Euphrates crossing

legions.summary: Probably an Antonian legion that took its title from victories over 'Scythians' on the Lower Danube. In 62 it was humiliated with XII Fulminata at Rhandeia under Caesennius Paetus, then held the Euphrates crossing at Zeugma for two centuries.
