legions.detail: The Rhandeia capitulation (Tac. Ann. 15.7-17) obliged the Roman army to build a bridge for the Parthians and leave Armenia. At Zeugma, rescue excavations before the Birecik dam flooded the city (2000) recovered a large deposit of clay sealings and military material.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio V Alaudae
legions.endNote: destroyed in Domitian's Dacian wars (86, possibly 92)

stations.note: stood against Juba's elephants, hence its emblem
lost its eagle in the clades Lolliana of 16 BC
with XXI Rapax, later XV Primigenia

legions.summary: Caesar's legion of Transalpine Gauls, raised at his own expense in 52 BC and later given citizenship en bloc: the first legion of non-citizens. The 'Larks' (alaudae, from the crested helmets) took the elephant as emblem after facing Juba's elephants at Thapsus.
legions.detail: It fought at Munda and Philippi, then in Spain and on the Rhine. Its eagle was lost when M. Lollius was defeated by the Sugambri in 16 BC (Vell. 2.97). At Vetera it mutinied in AD 14. Most of it marched with Vitellius in 69 and fought on at Cremona; the rump at Vetera was besieged by Civilis. Sent to Moesia by Vespasian, it vanishes in Domitian's Dacian wars, most likely with Cornelius Fuscus in 86.
legions.debate: Whether the legion lost with Fuscus in 86 was V Alaudae, and whether the legion lost 'with its legate' against the Sarmatians in 92 (Suet. Dom. 6) was XXI Rapax, is argued from absence of later evidence.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Syme, 'Rhine and Danube legions under Domitian', JRS 18 (1928)

legions.name: Legio V Macedonica
legions.endNote: listed at Oescus and Variniana in the Notitia; later a comitatensis unit in Egypt

stations.note: Armenia with Corbulo, then the Jewish war under Vespasian; camp at Emmaus
returned after the evacuation of Dacia

legions.summary: An Augustan legion of the Balkan army that served six centuries in Moesia, Judaea and Dacia. Its tour from Oescus to Troesmis to Potaissa and back to Oescus traces the advance and retreat of the Danubian frontier.
legions.detail: Under Vespasian it besieged Gamala and Jerusalem; tombstones of its soldiers survive at Emmaus. At Potaissa (Turda) it defended Dacia against the Marcomanni and Costoboci, winning the titles pia constans and, under Gallienus, VII pia VII fidelis. After 271 it returned to Oescus, then part of it went to Egypt (Memphis) in the Notitia.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio VI Ferrata
legions.endNote: disappears from the record in the late 3rd century

stations.note: Syrian garrison; with Corbulo in Armenia
possibly the first garrison of Arabia

legions.summary: Caesar's 'Ironclad' Sixth fought at Pharsalus and Zela, served Antony and then garrisoned Syria. From the 120s it held Caparcotna in Galilee; the place-name Legio survives in Arabic Lajjun beside Megiddo.
legions.detail: It defeated the Parthians in Corbulo's campaigns and in 69 its veterans marched with Mucianus to secure Italy for Vespasian. A diploma and building inscriptions place it in Judaea during the Bar Kokhba war. At Lajjun, excavations since 2013 have located its fortress and principia.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Tepper, Adams & David, 'The Roman legionary base at Legio' (2016)

legions.name: Legio VI Victrix
legions.endNote: listed at Eboracum under the dux Britanniarum

stations.note: Tarraconensis garrison; Galba proclaimed with it in 68

stations.base: Vetera II (Xanten, eroded by the Rhine)

stations.note: came to Britain with Hadrian's governor Platorius Nepos

legions.summary: Octavian's Sixth served a century in Spain, where it backed Galba's revolt in 68, then on the Lower Rhine, and from 122 at York, where it helped build Hadrian's Wall and stayed for almost three centuries.
legions.detail: At York, Septimius Severus died in 211 and Constantius I in 306, with Constantine proclaimed emperor by the troops there. The legion is the last legion in Britain recorded in the Notitia, under the dux Britanniarum.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio VII Claudia
legions.endNote: listed at Viminacium in the Notitia
legions.summary: Descendant of Caesar's VII, the legion won the title Claudia pia fidelis by refusing to join the revolt of Camillus Scribonianus in Dalmatia in 42. It held Viminacium, the capital of Moesia Superior, for nearly four centuries.
legions.detail: Claudius awarded the honorific to VII and XI after their loyalty in 42 (Dio 60.15.4). At Viminacium the fortress, cemeteries (over 13,000 graves excavated) and an amphitheatre have been excavated in rescue work near the Kostolac power station.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio VII Gemina
legions.endNote: listed at Legio (León) in the Notitia

stations.note: second battle of Bedriacum for Vespasian
Rhine after the Batavian revolt; merged with survivors of I Germanica

legions.summary: Raised in Spain by Galba in 68 as VII Galbiana, re-formed as VII Gemina in 70 by merger with survivors of I Germanica. From 74 it was the sole legion of Spain, and its fortress gave León its name.
legions.detail: At the second battle of Bedriacum its senior centurions died defending the eagle (Tac. Hist. 3.22). At León it supervised the gold mines of Asturia and Gallaecia (Las Médulas). Trajan, born at Italica, was its legate c. 89 and marched it to the Rhine against Saturninus.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio VIII Augusta
legions.endNote: listed among the comitatenses as Octavani

stations.note: vexillation fortress during the Batavian aftermath

legions.summary: Caesar's Eighth, re-formed after Actium, served in Pannonia and Moesia before the Flavians brought it to Upper Germany. From about 90 it was the garrison of Strasbourg for more than three centuries.
legions.detail: It took part in the Pannonian mutiny of AD 14 at Poetovio. Under Claudius it helped annex Thrace (46). In 69 it marched for Vespasian. At Mirebeau a vexillation fortress with tiles stamped by detachments of several legions has been excavated.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio IX Hispana
legions.endNote: last securely dated at York in 107/108; vanishes before c. 165

stations.note: Pannonia; vexillation against Tacfarinas in Africa 20-24
vexillation fortress; Cerialis's column cut up by Boudica
tile stamps and a pendant at Nijmegen

legions.summary: The famous 'lost legion'. IX Hispana invaded Britain in 43, was mauled by Boudica in 60/61, founded the fortress at York in 71, and then disappears after an inscription of 107/108.
legions.detail: Petillius Cerialis led part of the IX to relieve Camulodunum in 61 and lost most of its infantry (Tac. Ann. 14.32). The legion fought at Mons Graupius country under Agricola, and a night attack on its camp in 82 nearly destroyed it (Agr. 26). The York gate inscription of Trajan's 12th tribunician year is the last dated record in Britain. It is absent from the list of legions on the columna in Rome (CIL VI 3492, c. 165).
legions.debate: Three positions. (1) Destroyed in northern Britain c. 117-120, when Hadrian's biographer says the Britons 'could not be held under Roman control' (HA Hadr. 5.2) and Fronto alludes to heavy losses in Britain; the Victorian thesis behind Rosemary Sutcliff's Eagle of the Ninth. (2) Transferred to Nijmegen (stamped tiles, a silver-plated pendant, careers of officers such as L. Aemilius Karus whose tribunate seems to postdate 120) and destroyed later, either in the Bar Kokhba war (132-135) or at Elegeia in Armenia in 161 when Severianus's legion was annihilated (Dio 71.2.1). (3) Disbanded. The Nijmegen material is often dated to c. 104-120 by vexillations rather than the whole legion, so the debate is open (Birley; Keppie; Campbell, 'The Fate of the Ninth', 2018).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Keppie, 'The fate of the Ninth Legion: a problem for the eastern provinces?' (1989)
Campbell, The Fate of the Ninth (2018)

legions.name: Legio X Fretensis
legions.endNote: listed at Aila in the Notitia

stations.note: Jewish war: winter camp at Jericho, then the Mount of Olives siege camp at Jerusalem
siege of Masada under Flavius Silva

legions.summary: Raised by Octavian in 41/40 BC, its name records the naval war in the Straits of Messina against Sextus Pompey (Fretum Siculum). It destroyed Jerusalem in 70, besieged Masada in 73/74 and then held Jerusalem for more than two centuries before moving to Aila on the Red Sea.
legions.detail: Its siege works at Masada, including the eight camps and the great ramp, are the best preserved Roman siege system anywhere. Coins of Aelia Capitolina and tile stamps (LXF, with boar and ship) mark its presence in Jerusalem; the boar on its standard was later read by Christian and Jewish writers as a deliberate insult. Eusebius notes its transfer to Aila (Onomasticon 6.17-20).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Richmond, 'The Roman siege-works of Masàda', JRS 52 (1962)

legions.name: Legio X Gemina
legions.endNote: listed at Vindobona in the Notitia
legions.summary: Heir of Caesar's Tenth Equestris, re-formed as Gemina by merging two legions after Actium. After a century in Spain and three decades at Nijmegen it settled at Vindobona, the origin of modern Vienna, where Marcus Aurelius may have died in 180.
legions.detail: Veterans of X Gemina and V Alaudae founded Emerita Augusta (Mérida) in 25 BC. At Nijmegen it rebuilt the Hunerberg fortress in stone. At Vindobona its fortress under Vienna's Innere Stadt was its home until the 5th century.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XI Claudia
legions.endNote: listed at Durostorum in the Notitia
legions.summary: Octavianic legion that, with VII, won the title Claudia pia fidelis for loyalty during the revolt of Scribonianus in 42. Burnum, Vindonissa and then Durostorum on the Lower Danube were its bases.
legions.detail: Its Neptune emblem may recall service at Actium. At Durostorum (Silistra) it was the core of Moesia Inferior's eastern defence; the city later produced the general Aetius.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XII Fulminata
legions.endNote: listed at Melitene in the Notitia

stations.note: probably the third Augustan legion of Egypt

legions.summary: The 'Thunderbolt' legion, defeated twice under bad commanders (Rhandeia 62, Beth Horon 66, where it lost its eagle) before settling at Melitene on the upper Euphrates for four centuries.
legions.detail: In the 'Rain Miracle' against the Quadi (c. 172), Dio attributes the storm to an Egyptian magician; the Christian tradition (Apollinaris of Hierapolis, Tertullian, Eusebius HE 5.5) credits the prayers of Christian soldiers of the Melitene legion and claims the name Fulminata dates from then, which is false since it is attested under Augustus. Forty soldiers of the legion are said to have been martyred at Sebaste in 320 (the Forty Martyrs).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XIII Gemina
legions.endNote: listed at Ratiaria/Aegeta (Dacia Ripensis) and at Babylon in Egypt in the Notitia
legions.summary: Heir to the legion with which Caesar crossed the Rubicon in January 49 BC. Re-formed as Gemina by Octavian, it was for 165 years the core of Roman Dacia at Apulum (Alba Iulia).
legions.detail: It fought for Otho at the first battle of Bedriacum and was humiliatingly set to build amphitheatres at Cremona and Bononia by the victors (Tac. Hist. 2.67). At Apulum its fortress became the seat of the consular governor of the Three Dacias. After Aurelian's withdrawal (c. 271-275) it moved to the new Dacia south of the Danube.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XIV Gemina Martia Victrix
legions.endNote: listed at Carnuntum in the Notitia

stations.base: Midlands of Britain (series of campaign bases)
stations.note: invasion and advance into the Midlands
withdrawn by Nero; fought for Otho

legions.summary: The legion that destroyed Boudica's host in 60/61 with part of XX, winning Nero's title Martia Victrix. Later it held Carnuntum, the capital of Pannonia Superior, where Septimius Severus was proclaimed emperor in 193.
legions.detail: Tacitus calls it 'the conquerors of Britain' (Hist. 2.11). It was with Paulinus's raid on Anglesey (60) before the revolt. In 69 it backed Otho and was sent back to Britain by Vitellius. At Carnuntum the imperial conference of 308 (Diocletian, Galerius, Maximian) met to settle the succession.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XV Apollinaris
legions.endNote: listed at Satala in the Notitia

stations.note: Corbulo, then Titus's legion in the Jewish war: Jotapata, Gamala, Jerusalem

legions.summary: Named after Apollo, Octavian's patron, it built the first fortress at Carnuntum, served under Titus at Jerusalem and from Trajan's time guarded the Armenian frontier at Satala.
legions.detail: Arrian's Order of Battle against the Alans (Ektaxis, c. 135) puts XV Apollinaris at the head of the Cappadocian army with XII Fulminata. Titus led it in Judaea while his father commanded the war; it was at the sieges of Jotapata, Gamala and Jerusalem.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XV Primigenia
legions.endNote: destroyed after the surrender of Vetera in March 70
legions.summary: Raised by Caligula in 39 for his German and British expeditions, named for Fortuna Primigenia. It perished in the Batavian revolt: after a winter siege at Vetera the starving garrison surrendered and was massacred on the march.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XVI Gallica
legions.endNote: surrendered to Classicus; disbanded and re-formed as XVI Flavia Firma
legions.summary: Augustan legion of the Rhine army that swore allegiance to the Imperium Galliarum at Novaesium in 70 after its legate Vocula was murdered, and was dissolved by Vespasian.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XVI Flavia Firma
legions.endNote: listed at Sura on the Euphrates in the Notitia
legions.summary: Vespasian re-raised the disgraced XVI Gallica as Flavia Firma ('steadfast') and sent it to the newly organised Cappadocian frontier at Satala. From Hadrian's reign it held Samosata, later Sura on the Euphrates.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XVII
legions.endNote: destroyed with Varus in the Teutoburg Forest, September AD 9; number never reused
legions.summary: One of the three legions annihilated with P. Quinctilius Varus in AD 9. The numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used again, a unique case of numbers left vacant as ill-omened. No base known; perhaps on the Lower Rhine or the Lippe.
legions.detail: The eagles were recovered piecemeal: one by L. Stertinius among the Bructeri in 15 (Tac. Ann. 1.60), one from the Marsi in 16 (Ann. 2.25), the third by P. Gabinius from the Chauci in 41 (Dio 60.8.7). The battlefield at Kalkriese, identified in 1987 by Tony Clunn's coin finds, has yielded a turf rampart, equipment and the iron face mask of a cavalry helmet.
scholarship: Wells, The Battle That Stopped Rome (2003)
Rost & Wilbers-Rost, Kalkriese reports

legions.name: Legio XVIII
legions.endNote: destroyed with Varus in the Teutoburg Forest, September AD 9; number never reused
legions.summary: One of the three legions annihilated with P. Quinctilius Varus in AD 9. The numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used again, a unique case of numbers left vacant as ill-omened. Centurion M. Caelius's cenotaph at Vetera names it.
legions.detail: The eagles were recovered piecemeal: one by L. Stertinius among the Bructeri in 15 (Tac. Ann. 1.60), one from the Marsi in 16 (Ann. 2.25), the third by P. Gabinius from the Chauci in 41 (Dio 60.8.7). The battlefield at Kalkriese, identified in 1987 by Tony Clunn's coin finds, has yielded a turf rampart, equipment and the iron face mask of a cavalry helmet.
scholarship: Wells, The Battle That Stopped Rome (2003)
Rost & Wilbers-Rost, Kalkriese reports

legions.name: Legio XIX
legions.endNote: destroyed with Varus in the Teutoburg Forest, September AD 9; number never reused

stations.base: Dangstetten (Augustan camp on the Upper Rhine)

legions.summary: One of the three legions annihilated with P. Quinctilius Varus in AD 9. The numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used again, a unique case of numbers left vacant as ill-omened. Lead ingots stamped L XIX from Dangstetten and Haltern.
legions.detail: The eagles were recovered piecemeal: one by L. Stertinius among the Bructeri in 15 (Tac. Ann. 1.60), one from the Marsi in 16 (Ann. 2.25), the third by P. Gabinius from the Chauci in 41 (Dio 60.8.7). The battlefield at Kalkriese, identified in 1987 by Tony Clunn's coin finds, has yielded a turf rampart, equipment and the iron face mask of a cavalry helmet.
scholarship: Wells, The Battle That Stopped Rome (2003)
Rost & Wilbers-Rost, Kalkriese reports

legions.name: Legio XX Valeria Victrix
legions.endNote: last attested on coins of Carausius (c. 287-293)

stations.note: Great Illyrian revolt under Valerius Messallinus

legions.summary: Possibly named after M. Valerius Messallinus, under whom it distinguished itself in the Illyrian revolt of AD 6-9, the Twentieth came to Britain in 43 and for two centuries held Chester. Its title Victrix probably dates from the defeat of Boudica.
legions.detail: Agricola commanded it in 70-73. Inchtuthil, on the Tay, was a 21-hectare fortress abandoned before completion c. 86/87; the garrison buried a million iron nails (about 10 tonnes) to keep them from the Caledonians. At Chester the elliptical building inside the fortress has been interpreted as intended for a governor's palace.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Pitts & St Joseph, Inchtuthil (1985)

legions.name: Legio XXI Rapax
legions.endNote: probably the legion destroyed with its legate by the Sarmatians in 92 (Suet. Dom. 6)

stations.note: massacred the Helvetii at Aquae Helveticae in 69

legions.summary: 'The Predator', an Augustan legion of the Rhine, notorious for brutality: in 69 it plundered Aquae Helveticae (Baden) and slaughtered the Helvetii who opposed Vitellius (Tac. Hist. 1.67). After joining Saturninus's revolt at Mainz in 89 it was sent to Pannonia and disappears.
legions.debate: Most scholars identify it with the legion lost with its legate to the Sarmatian Iazyges in 92; V Alaudae is the alternative candidate.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Syme, JRS 18 (1928)

legions.name: Legio XXII Deiotariana
legions.endNote: last attested c. 119; absent from the columna list c. 165

stations.note: Deiotarus's legions drilled in the Roman manner

legions.summary: Born as the Roman-style army of King Deiotarus of Galatia, defeated by Pharnaces at Nicopolis in 48 BC, it was taken into the Roman army when Galatia was annexed in 25 BC and posted to Egypt. It vanishes in Hadrian's reign.
legions.detail: It fought the Alexandrian Jewish riots of 66 and sent a vexillation to Titus in 70. It is last attested around 119.
legions.debate: Its end is unknown: destroyed in the Bar Kokhba war (132-135, based on the inscription of a vexillation at Jerusalem? and a late Talmudic tale of poisoned soldiers, both weak), lost in the Diaspora revolt of 115-117 in Egypt, or disbanded. It is missing from the list of c. 165 (CIL VI 3492).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Keppie, 'The history and disappearance of the legion XXII Deiotariana' (1990)

legions.name: Legio XXII Primigenia
legions.endNote: last attested in the 4th century at Mogontiacum

stations.base: Vetera II (Xanten, eroded by the Rhine)

legions.summary: Caligula's legion, raised in 39 for his German campaign, which threw down Galba's statues at Mainz on 1 January 69 and acclaimed Vitellius. Its loyalty to Domitian during Saturninus's revolt (89) won it pia fidelis and a return to Mainz, its home for three centuries.
legions.detail: The Jupiter Column of Mainz (AD 58/59) and the large number of its tombstones make XXII Primigenia one of the best documented legions. It built much of the Upper German limes in the Antonine period; its stamped tiles are found at forts from the Taunus to the Odenwald.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix
legions.endNote: last attested in the 4th century at Vetera/Colonia Ulpia Traiana

stations.base: Vetera II (Xanten, eroded by the Rhine)

legions.summary: Raised by Trajan c. 105 and numbered thirty because it brought the army to thirty legions. From c. 120 it held Vetera II beside Trajan's new colony at Xanten for three centuries.
legions.detail: It supported Septimius Severus in 193 and fought for him against Albinus in 197. Vexillations served in Mauretania and in the Parthian war of Severus. Under the Gallic emperors (260-274) it struck coin issues with its emblems.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Ioviani (seniores and iuniores)
legions.endNote: Ioviani seniores in the West (Not. Occ. 5), Ioviani iuniores in the East (Not. Or. 5)

stations.note: Illyrian origin; the Martiobarbuli of Vegetius

legions.summary: Senior palatine legion of the late army, named after Diocletian's divine patron Jupiter. Vegetius says two Illyrian legions of 6,000 men, expert with lead-weighted darts (mattiobarbuli), were renamed Ioviani and Herculiani by Diocletian and Maximian (1.17).
legions.detail: The Ioviani acclaimed Jovian emperor in 363 after Julian's death, since Jovian's father had been their commander (Amm. 25.5.8). With the division of 364 the unit split into seniores (West) and iuniores (East). Its shield pattern is drawn in the Notitia.

legions.name: Herculiani (seniores and iuniores)
legions.endNote: Herculiani seniores in the West, iuniores in the East (Notitia)
legions.summary: Twin of the Ioviani, named for Maximian's patron Hercules. The two units headed the precedence of the palatine legions in both halves of the empire.
legions.detail: Ammianus mentions the Ioviani and Herculiani in Julian's Persian campaign (363), where they fought in the rearguard (25.6.3). Maximian's Herculian ideology (Herculius as his signum) is mirrored in the unit's name.

legions.name: Lanciarii seniores
legions.endNote: Notitia, eastern praesental army I

stations.note: tetrarchic comitatus; tombstones at Apamea and in the Balkans

legions.summary: Javelin-armed elite unit of the tetrarchic comitatus, recorded as lanciarii on Diocletianic tombstones and later as a senior palatine legion of the East.
legions.detail: The Lanciarii and Mattiarii formed the strong core of Valens's army at Adrianople (378) and were overwhelmed when the reserve Batavi failed to come up (Amm. 31.13.8).

legions.name: Lanciarii Sabarienses
legions.endNote: Notitia, western palatine legions
legions.summary: Western palatine legion named after Savaria (Szombathely) in Pannonia, one of several late units whose names derive from their original garrison towns.

legions.name: Mattiarii (seniores and iuniores)
legions.endNote: Notitia, eastern praesental armies
legions.summary: Palatine legion armed with lead-weighted darts (mattiobarbuli or plumbatae, from mattea, a mace). It fought in the line at Adrianople, where its commander and many men fell.

legions.name: Divitenses (seniores)
legions.endNote: Notitia, western palatine legions

stations.note: Divitia (Köln-Deutz), bridgehead fort built by Constantine c. 310

legions.summary: Named after the Constantinian bridgehead fort of Divitia opposite Cologne, built c. 310, from which the core of II Italica's or XXII Primigenia's detachments was drawn.

legions.name: Tungrecani (seniores)
legions.endNote: Notitia, western palatine legions
legions.summary: Late palatine legion paired with the Divitenses, named after the Tungri of Germania Secunda. In 365 the two units went over to the usurper Procopius at Constantinople.

legions.name: Cornuti (seniores)
legions.endNote: Notitia, western auxilia palatina

stations.note: Constantine's army at the Milvian Bridge (shown on the Arch of Constantine)

legions.summary: 'The Horned Ones', an auxilium palatinum of Germanic recruits whose horned helmets appear on the frieze of the Arch of Constantine. With the Bracchiati they held the right of the line at Strasbourg (357), raising the barritus war-cry.

legions.name: Petulantes
legions.endNote: Notitia, western auxilia palatina (seniores)
legions.summary: Gallic auxilium palatinum which, with the Celtae, refused Constantius II's order to march east in February 360 and proclaimed Julian Augustus at Lutetia (Paris).
legions.detail: Ammianus (20.4) says the soldiers feared leaving their families exposed to the Alamanni; Julian was raised on a shield and crowned with a neck torque of a standard-bearer.

legions.name: Legio I Iovia Scythica
legions.endNote: listed at Noviodunum in the Notitia
legions.summary: One of the two Diocletianic legions of the new province of Scythia Minor, sharing the name of the emperor's divine patron. Its base at Noviodunum guarded the Danube crossing used by Valens in 369.

legions.name: Legio II Herculia
legions.endNote: listed at Troesmis in the Notitia
legions.summary: Diocletianic legion of Scythia Minor at Troesmis, named after Maximian's patron Hercules, pair to I Iovia at Noviodunum.

legions.name: Legio IV Martia
legions.endNote: listed at Betthorus in the Notitia; fortress abandoned after the earthquake of 551 or earlier
legions.summary: Diocletianic legion of Arabia at Betthorus (el-Lejjun), a 4.6-hectare fortress excavated by S. T. Parker's Limes Arabicus Project; its smaller size reflects late legions of perhaps 1,000-2,000 men.
legions.detail: The fortress shows a reduction of the barracks in the 5th century and a church built inside; the garrison seems to have been demobilised under Justinian, who relied on Ghassanid allies.

legions.name: Legio I Illyricorum
legions.endNote: listed at Palmyra in the Notitia

stations.note: camp of Diocletian built in the western quarter of the city

legions.summary: Legion probably formed from Illyrian troops after Aurelian's destruction of Palmyra in 273 and stationed in the 'Camp of Diocletian' inside the ruined city on the Strata Diocletiana.

legions.name: Legio I Pontica
legions.endNote: listed at Trapezus in the Notitia
legions.summary: Diocletianic legion of the Pontic frontier at Trapezus, guarding the Black Sea end of the road to Satala and Armenia.

legions.name: Legio V Parthica
legions.endNote: destroyed when Shapur II stormed Amida in 359
legions.summary: Garrison legion of Amida on the upper Tigris. In 359 it held Amida for 73 days against Shapur II alongside the Magnentian legions and others; Ammianus Marcellinus, inside the city, escaped and wrote the eyewitness account.

legions.name: Theban Legion (Thebaei)
legions.endNote: Thebaei listed among the western palatine legions; the martyr legion of Agaunum is legendary
legions.summary: Late units called Thebaei appear in the Notitia. The legend of St Maurice and the 6,600 Christian soldiers of the Theban Legion massacred at Agaunum by Maximian is told by Eucherius of Lyon (c. 430-450) and is unhistorical in its numbers and details.

list.name: Augustus
list.note: Sole master of the Roman world from Actium (2 Sep 31 BC) and Alexandria (Aug 30 BC); name Augustus voted 16 Jan 27 BC. Died at Nola 19 Aug AD 14 after 40 years 7 months of sole rule.

list.name: Tiberius
list.note: Died at Misenum 16 Mar 37 aged 77. Tacitus, Suetonius and Dio report rumours that the prefect Macro smothered him or Caligula poisoned him.

list.name: Caligula
list.note: Stabbed in a palace passage 24 Jan 41 by the praetorian tribunes Cassius Chaerea and Cornelius Sabinus; wife Milonia Caesonia and infant daughter killed the same day.

list.name: Claudius
list.note: Died 13 Oct 54. Tacitus, Suetonius and Dio say Agrippina had him poisoned (mushrooms, with the poisoner Locusta and doctor Xenophon); a minority of modern scholars allow natural death.

list.name: Nero
list.note: Declared hostis by the Senate; stabbed himself in the throat with the help of the freedman Epaphroditus at Phaon's villa outside Rome, 9 Jun 68. Last of the Julio-Claudians.

list.name: Galba
list.note: Proclaimed by his troops in Hispania Tarraconensis Apr 68, recognized by the Senate Jun 68; cut down in the Forum near the Lacus Curtius 15 Jan 69 by praetorians who had hailed Otho.

list.name: Otho
list.note: Stabbed himself at Brixellum 16 Apr 69, two days after his army's defeat at the first battle of Bedriacum, reportedly to spare further civil war.

list.name: Vitellius
list.note: Proclaimed by the Lower German legions at Colonia 2 Jan 69; dragged through the Forum and killed at the Gemonian Stairs 20 Dec 69 as Flavian troops stormed Rome.

list.name: Vespasian
list.note: Proclaimed at Alexandria 1 Jul 69 (his dies imperii); died of fever and diarrhoea at Aquae Cutiliae 23 Jun 79, joking 'I think I am becoming a god'.

list.name: Titus
list.note: Died of fever 13 Sep 81 at the Flavian villa near Reate after a reign of 26 months marked by Vesuvius (79) and the fire and plague at Rome (80).

list.name: Domitian
list.note: Stabbed 18 Sep 96 by the steward Stephanus in a plot involving the chamberlain Parthenius and probably Domitia and both praetorian prefects; damnatio memoriae followed.

list.name: Nerva
list.note: Senatorial choice on Domitian's death; humiliated by the praetorian mutiny of Casperius Aelianus (97), he adopted Trajan in Oct 97; died 27 Jan 98 of a fever.

list.name: Trajan
list.note: First emperor born in a province (Italica, Baetica). Died at Selinus in Cilicia c. 8 Aug 117 after a stroke on the way home from Mesopotamia; Hadrian's adoption was announced by Plotina, and Dio doubted it.

list.name: Hadrian
list.note: Died at Baiae 10 Jul 138 after long illness (probably heart failure), having adopted Antoninus on condition he adopt Marcus and Lucius.

list.name: Antoninus Pius
list.note: Died at Lorium 7 Mar 161, giving the watchword 'aequanimitas'. Never left Italy as emperor.

list.name: Marcus Aurelius
list.note: Died 17 Mar 180 at Vindobona or Sirmium on campaign against the Marcomanni and Sarmatians, probably of the Antonine plague.

list.name: Lucius Verus
list.note: First formal joint Augustus with Marcus; nominal commander of the Parthian War (161-166). Died of a stroke at Altinum early 169.

list.name: Commodus
list.note: Augustus 177, sole ruler 17 Mar 180. Strangled in his bath on 31 Dec 192 by the athlete Narcissus in a plot of his mistress Marcia, chamberlain Eclectus and prefect Laetus.

list.name: Pertinax
list.note: Reigned 87 days (1 Jan to 28 Mar 193); speared by mutinous praetorians in the palace after attempting to restore discipline and finances.

list.name: Didius Julianus
list.note: Won the praetorian 'auction' with 25,000 sesterces a man (Dio 74.11); condemned by the Senate and killed in the palace 1 Jun 193 as Severus neared Rome. Reigned 66 days.

list.name: Septimius Severus
list.note: Proclaimed at Carnuntum 9 Apr 193; defeated Niger (194) and Albinus (197). Died at Eboracum 4 Feb 211 during his Caledonian war.

list.name: Caracalla
list.note: Augustus 198, sole ruler from Dec 211. Stabbed while relieving himself on the road from Edessa to Carrhae 8 Apr 217 by the guardsman Julius Martialis, at the instigation of the prefect Macrinus.

list.name: Geta
list.note: Augustus 209; killed in his mother Julia Domna's arms by centurions on Caracalla's orders, 26 Dec 211. His name was chiselled off monuments across the empire.

list.name: Macrinus
list.note: First equestrian emperor and first never to visit Rome as emperor. Defeated near Antioch 8 Jun 218 by Elagabalus' army; caught at Chalcedon/Cappadocia and executed.

list.name: Diadumenian
list.note: Son of Macrinus; Caesar 217, Augustus May 218; seized at Zeugma fleeing to Parthia and killed.

list.name: Elagabalus
list.note: Hereditary priest of the Emesene sun god; proclaimed at Raphanaea 16 May 218. Killed with his mother Julia Soaemias by the praetorians 11 or 12 Mar 222; bodies dragged and thrown in the Tiber.

list.name: Severus Alexander
list.note: Killed with his mother Julia Mamaea by mutinous troops at Vicus Britannicus (Bretzenheim) near Mogontiacum, Mar 235, ending the Severan dynasty.

list.name: Maximinus Thrax
list.note: First emperor risen from the ranks; never visited Rome. Killed with his son Maximus by soldiers of Legio II Parthica during the siege of Aquileia, spring 238.

list.name: Gordian I
list.note: Proconsul of Africa, proclaimed at Thysdrus by rebels against the procurator, aged about 80; hanged himself at Carthage on news of his son's death after about 21 days (date Jan or Mar 238 disputed).

list.name: Gordian II
list.note: Co-Augustus with his father; killed at Carthage fighting Capelianus, governor of Numidia, with Legio III Augusta.

list.name: Pupienus
list.note: Elected by a senatorial commission (vigintiviri) with Balbinus; both tortured and killed in the palace by the praetorians after about 99 days.

list.name: Balbinus
list.note: Co-emperor with Pupienus; murdered with him by the praetorians, who proclaimed the 13-year-old Gordian III.

list.name: Gordian III
list.note: Died Feb 244 on the Persian front. Shapur's ŠKZ claims he was killed in battle at Misiche (renamed Peroz-Shapur); Roman sources blame his prefect Philip; a cenotaph stood at Zaitha.

list.name: Philip the Arab
list.note: From Shahba in Trachonitis; bought peace from Shapur for 500,000 aurei; celebrated the millennium of Rome 21 Apr 248. Killed at or after the battle of Verona against Decius, c. Sep 249.

list.name: Philip II
list.note: Caesar 244, Augustus 247; killed by the praetorians in Rome on news of Verona, aged about 12.

list.name: Decius
list.note: Ordered the universal sacrifice of 250 (libelli survive from Egypt). First emperor killed by a foreign enemy, in the marsh at Abritus against Cniva's Goths, c. Jun 251.

list.name: Herennius Etruscus
list.note: Augustus May 251; killed by an arrow at Abritus shortly before or during the battle.

list.name: Hostilian
list.note: Younger son of Decius, co-Augustus with Gallus; died of the plague of Cyprian (Aurelius Victor) or was killed by Gallus (Zosimus), late 251.

list.name: Trebonianus Gallus
list.note: Governor of Moesia, proclaimed after Abritus; made peace paying the Goths. Killed with his son by their own troops at Interamna, c. Aug 253.

list.name: Volusianus
list.note: Son of Gallus, Augustus late 251; killed with his father at Interamna.

list.name: Aemilianus
list.note: Governor of Moesia proclaimed after a victory over the Goths; reigned about 88 days; killed near Spoletium by his own men as Valerian's army approached.

list.name: Valerian
list.note: Captured by Shapur I in the campaign of Edessa, spring/summer 260, the first emperor taken alive by a foreign enemy; died in captivity. Lactantius' tale that he was used as a mounting block and flayed is Christian polemic.
list.death: died in Persian captivity, date unknown

list.name: Gallienus
list.region: west 253-260; all 260-268 (minus Gallic and Palmyrene territories)
list.note: Co-Augustus 253, sole ruler 260. Killed outside Milan c. Sep 268 while besieging Aureolus, in a plot of his staff (Heraclianus, Marcianus, Cecropius; Claudius and Aurelian implicated).

list.name: Saloninus
list.note: Son of Gallienus, raised to Augustus at Colonia Agrippina while besieged by Postumus; surrendered by the garrison and killed.

list.name: Claudius II Gothicus
list.note: Won the great victory over the Goths at Naissus (269); died of plague at Sirmium Aug/Sep 270. Later claimed as ancestor of Constantine (a fiction of c. 310).

list.name: Quintillus
list.note: Brother of Claudius; reigned between 17 days and a few months at Aquileia; suicide or killed by his troops when the army chose Aurelian.

list.name: Aurelian
list.note: Reunified the empire (Palmyra 272-273, Gallic Empire 274), built the Aurelian Walls, reformed the coinage (274). Killed at Caenophrurium near Perinthus c. Sep/Oct 275 by officers duped by forged lists from his secretary Eros.

list.name: Tacitus (emperor)
list.note: Elderly general proclaimed in late 275; died at Tyana mid-276 after defeating Goths in Asia Minor, of fever (Victor) or murdered (Zosimus). His supposed descent from the historian is HA fiction.

list.name: Florianus
list.note: Tacitus' praetorian prefect and half-brother; killed by his own men near Tarsus after about 88 days when Probus' army avoided battle in the summer heat.

list.name: Probus
list.note: Restored the Rhine frontier; settled barbarians in the provinces. Killed by soldiers at Sirmium Sep/Oct 282, reportedly over forced labour draining marshes, as Carus was proclaimed.

list.name: Carus
list.note: Took Ctesiphon in 283; died near the Tigris Jul/Aug 283, officially struck by lightning; murder by the prefect Aper is suspected.

list.name: Carinus
list.note: Augustus spring 283; won at the river Margus against Diocletian (spring 285) but was killed by his own officers in or after the battle.

list.name: Numerian
list.note: Died Nov 284 near Nicomedia; the stench from his closed litter revealed the corpse. The army chose Diocletian, who killed the prefect Aper with his own hand.

list.name: Diocletian
list.note: Proclaimed at Nicomedia 20 Nov 284; created the Tetrarchy (Maximian Augustus 286; Caesars 293). Abdicated at Nicomedia 1 May 305 and retired to Spalatum; died there c. 311-312.

list.name: Maximian
list.note: Caesar 285, Augustus 1 Apr 286; abdicated with Diocletian 1 May 305, resumed the purple 306-308 with his son Maxentius, and tried again in 310 against Constantine. Forced to hang himself at Massilia 310.
list.death: forced suicide (or executed) at Massilia after his third bid for power

list.name: Constantius I
list.note: Caesar 1 Mar 293, Augustus 1 May 305; recovered Britain from Allectus (296). Died at Eboracum 25 Jul 306.

list.name: Galerius
list.note: Caesar 293 (victor over Narseh 298), Augustus 305; chief driver of the Great Persecution. Died of a gangrenous illness at Serdica c. May 311, days after his edict of toleration (30 Apr 311).

list.name: Severus II
list.note: Caesar 305, Augustus 306. His troops deserted to Maxentius; surrendered at Ravenna and was put to death (or forced to open his veins) at Tres Tabernae, 307.

list.name: Maxentius
list.note: Proclaimed at Rome 28 Oct 306 by praetorians and people; never recognized by the eastern Augusti. Drowned in the Tiber at the Milvian Bridge 28 Oct 312.

list.name: Constantine I
list.note: Proclaimed at Eboracum 25 Jul 306; sole ruler after Chrysopolis (324); founded Constantinople (dedicated 11 May 330). Baptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia and died at Achyron near Nicomedia 22 May 337.

list.name: Licinius
list.note: Made Augustus at the conference of Carnuntum 11 Nov 308. Defeated by Constantine at Adrianople (3 Jul 324) and Chrysopolis (18 Sep 324); abdicated on promise of his life; hanged at Thessalonica 325.
list.death: executed at Thessalonica on a charge of plotting

list.name: Maximinus Daza
list.note: Caesar 305, Augustus 310. Routed by Licinius at Tzirallum 30 Apr 313; died at Tarsus summer 313, by poison he took (Lactantius) or illness.

list.name: Constantine II
list.note: Augustus 9 Sep 337 after the purge of his cousins; killed in an ambush near Aquileia while invading his brother Constans' territory, early 340.

list.name: Constans
list.note: Overthrown by Magnentius at Augustodunum 18 Jan 350; caught and killed by Gaiso at Helena (Elne) at the foot of the Pyrenees.

list.name: Constantius II
list.note: Defeated Magnentius at Mursa (351) and Mons Seleucus (353). Died of fever at Mopsucrenae in Cilicia 3 Nov 361, marching against Julian, whom he named heir on his deathbed.

list.name: Julian
list.note: Proclaimed by his troops at Lutetia Feb 360; sole ruler from Nov 361; attempted pagan restoration. Wounded by a spear in a rearguard action near Maranga/Samarra 26 Jun 363 and died that night.

list.name: Jovian
list.note: Chosen by the army on Persian soil; ceded Nisibis, Singara and five Transtigritane regions to Shapur II for safe passage. Found dead at Dadastana 17 Feb 364, from charcoal fumes or bad food.

list.name: Valentinian I
list.note: Proclaimed at Nicaea 26 Feb 364; made his brother Valens eastern Augustus (28 Mar 364). Died of a stroke at Brigetio 17 Nov 375 while raging at Quadic envoys.

list.name: Valens
list.note: Admitted the Gothic Tervingi across the Danube (376). Killed at Adrianople 9 Aug 378; body never found.

list.name: Gratian
list.note: Augustus 24 Aug 367 aged 8; dropped the title pontifex maximus and removed the Altar of Victory (382). Deserted by his army near Paris to Magnus Maximus; killed at Lugdunum by Andragathius 25 Aug 383.

list.name: Valentinian II
list.note: Proclaimed aged 4 at Aquincum 22 Nov 375. Found hanged at Vienne 15 May 392 after quarrelling with his magister militum Arbogast: suicide or murder.

list.name: Theodosius I
list.note: Made Augustus at Sirmium 19 Jan 379; Nicene Christianity made the state creed (Cunctos populos 380); victor over Maximus (388) and Eugenius at the Frigidus (Sep 394). Died at Milan 17 Jan 395, the last emperor to rule both halves.

list.name: Honorius
list.note: Augustus 393 aged 8; ruled through Stilicho (executed 408). Rome sacked by Alaric 24 Aug 410. Died of oedema at Ravenna 15 Aug 423.

list.name: Constantius III
list.note: Magister militum, husband of Galla Placidia; co-Augustus 8 Feb 421, unrecognized by Constantinople; died 2 Sep 421.

list.name: Valentinian III
list.note: Installed aged 6 by an eastern army after the suppression of Joannes (23 Oct 425). Murdered Aetius with his own hand (Sep 454); killed on the Campus Martius 16 Mar 455 by Optila and Thraustila, Aetius' Hunnic retainers.

list.name: Petronius Maximus
list.note: Twice consul, prefect of Rome; proclaimed 17 Mar 455. Killed by a mob or imperial servants (stoned, by tradition) fleeing Rome 31 May 455 as Gaiseric's fleet approached; the Vandal sack followed (2-16 Jun).

list.name: Avitus
list.note: Gallo-Roman aristocrat proclaimed at Arelate with Visigothic support 9 Jul 455. Defeated near Placentia by Ricimer and Majorian 17 Oct 456 and consecrated bishop of Placentia.
list.death: died 456/457, possibly killed, on his way to Gaul

list.name: Majorian
list.note: Acclaimed 1 Apr 457 (formally 28 Dec 457). His invasion fleet was destroyed at Portus Ilicitanus near Carthago Nova (460); arrested by Ricimer at Dertona and beheaded 7 Aug 461.

list.name: Libius Severus
list.note: Ricimer's puppet, never recognized by Leo I. Died at Rome 14 Nov 465; Cassiodorus and Sidonius hint Ricimer poisoned him.

list.name: Anthemius
list.note: Eastern aristocrat sent by Leo I and proclaimed 12 Apr 467; married his daughter to Ricimer. Besieged in Rome by Ricimer and beheaded by Gundobad 11 Jul 472.

list.name: Olybrius
list.note: Husband of Placidia, daughter of Valentinian III; proclaimed by Ricimer Apr 472; died of dropsy 2 Nov 472.

list.name: Glycerius
list.note: Comes domesticorum proclaimed at Ravenna 3 Mar 473 with Gundobad's backing; deposed by Julius Nepos at Portus Jun 474 and consecrated bishop of Salona.

list.name: Julius Nepos
list.note: Magister militum of Dalmatia, nephew of Marcellinus, installed with Leo I's backing 19 Jun 474. Driven from Ravenna by Orestes 28 Aug 475; kept the title in Dalmatia, recognized by Zeno and named on some of Odoacer's coins, until murdered in his villa near Salona 9 May 480.

list.name: Romulus Augustulus
list.note: Son of the magister militum Orestes, proclaimed 31 Oct 475, never recognized by Constantinople. Deposed by Odoacer at Ravenna 4 Sep 476 and pensioned off to the Castellum Lucullanum near Naples.

list.name: Arcadius
list.note: Augustus 383; ruled through Rufinus, Eutropius and Anthemius. Died 1 May 408.

list.name: Theodosius II
list.note: Augustus 402 aged 9 months. Theodosian Walls (413), University of Constantinople (425), Codex Theodosianus (438). Died 28 Jul 450 after a riding fall near the Lycus.

list.name: Marcian
list.note: Thracian officer who married Pulcheria; stopped tribute to Attila, convened the Council of Chalcedon (451). Died 27 Jan 457, leaving a large surplus.

list.name: Leo I
list.note: Thracian officer raised by Aspar; the 468 armada against the Vandals under Basiliscus cost some 64,000 lb gold and 700,000 lb silver (Lydus). Had Aspar killed (471). Died 18 Jan 474.

list.name: Leo II
list.note: Grandson of Leo I, aged about 7; crowned his father Zeno co-emperor 9 Feb 474; died Nov 474.

list.name: Zeno
list.note: Isaurian chieftain (Tarasis); driven out by Basiliscus Jan 475 to Aug 476. Henotikon (482); sent Theodoric to Italy (488). Died 9 Apr 491.

list.name: Anastasius I
list.note: Palace silentiarius chosen by Zeno's widow Ariadne. Isaurian war (492-497), copper reform (498), abolished the chrysargyron, Anastasian Wall; left 320,000 lb of gold. Died 9 Jul 518.

list.name: Justin I
list.note: Illyrian peasant who rose to command the excubitors; ended the Acacian schism (519). Died 1 Aug 527.

list.name: Justinian I
list.note: Co-emperor 1 Apr 527, sole 1 Aug 527. Corpus Iuris Civilis, Nika riot (532), Hagia Sophia (537), reconquest of Africa (533-534) and Italy (535-554), plague of 541-542. Died 14 Nov 565.

list.name: Justin II
list.note: Nephew of Justinian; refused tribute to the Avars and Persia; lost Dara (573) and went insane; Tiberius ruled as Caesar from 7 Dec 574. Died 5 Oct 578.

list.name: Tiberius II Constantine
list.note: Comes excubitorum, Caesar 574, Augustus 26 Sep 578; famously lavish. Died 14 Aug 582 (by tradition after eating bad mulberries).

list.name: Maurice
list.note: Restored Khosrow II (591) and won the Balkan wars against Avars and Slavs. Overthrown when the Danube army mutinied over wintering north of the river; made to watch five sons beheaded at Eutropius' harbour, Chalcedon, then killed 27 Nov 602.

list.name: Phocas
list.note: Centurion of the Danube army. Khosrow II's war of revenge opened in 603. Beheaded 5 Oct 610 when Heraclius' fleet reached Constantinople.

list.name: Heraclius
list.note: Son of the exarch of Africa; survived the loss of Syria, Palestine, Egypt and the siege of 626, destroyed Persian power at Nineveh (Dec 627), restored the True Cross (630), then lost Syria to the Arabs (Yarmuk 636). Died of oedema 11 Feb 641.

list.name: Constantine III
list.note: Co-emperor since 613; ruled jointly with his half-brother Heraclonas from Feb 641; died of tuberculosis 25 May 641 (rumours blamed Martina).

list.name: Heraclonas
list.note: Son of Heraclius and Martina, co-emperor 638; deposed Sep/Oct 641 after pressure from the army and Constantinopolitan crowd; nose slit and exiled with Martina to Rhodes.

list.name: Constans II
list.note: Son of Constantine III, crowned 641 aged 11. Moved his court to Syracuse (663); killed in his bath there by a chamberlain 15 Jul 668.

list.name: Lucius Arruntius Camillus Scribonianus
list.note: Governor of Dalmatia who called on Claudius to abdicate; his two legions (VII and XI, thereafter Claudia Pia Fidelis) deserted within five days. Killed himself or was killed on Issa.

list.name: Gaius Julius Vindex
list.note: Aquitanian senator who rose against Nero (Mar 68) and offered the throne to Galba; defeated by Verginius Rufus near Vesontio and killed himself. Did not claim the purple.

list.name: Lucius Clodius Macer
list.note: Legate of Legio III Augusta; raised Legio I Macriana liberatrix and cut Rome's grain supply; killed by the procurator Trebonius Garutianus on Galba's orders, Oct 68.

list.name: Gaius Nymphidius Sabinus
list.note: Praetorian prefect who abandoned Nero, then bid for the throne against Galba; killed by the guard in the camp, autumn 68.

list.name: Terentius Maximus (pseudo-Nero)
list.note: One of at least three false Neros (68/69, 79/80, 88); found support in Asia and with the Parthian Artabanus III before being surrendered.

list.name: Lucius Antonius Saturninus
list.note: Seized the savings of two legions at Mogontiacum (1 Jan 89); his Chattan allies were cut off by a thaw on the Rhine and he was defeated by Lappius Maximus. Domitian thereafter forbade double-legion camps.

list.name: Gaius Avidius Cassius
list.note: Victor of the Parthian War, governor of Syria with command over the East; proclaimed himself on a false report of Marcus' death (perhaps with Faustina's encouragement); killed by a centurion after about three months.

list.name: Gaius Pescennius Niger
list.note: Governor of Syria proclaimed Apr 193; beaten at Cyzicus, Nicaea and Issus (194); caught fleeing towards the Euphrates and beheaded.

list.name: Decimus Clodius Albinus
list.note: Governor of Britain; Caesar under Severus 193-195, then Augustus. Defeated at Lugdunum 19 Feb 197 in one of the largest Roman battles; killed himself or was killed, his body trampled by Severus' horse.

list.name: Gaius Petronius Magnus
list.note: Consular accused of plotting to destroy Maximinus' Rhine bridge; possibly a fabricated conspiracy (Herodian 7.1).

list.name: Titus Quartinus
list.note: Proclaimed by Osrhoenian archers loyal to Severus Alexander; murdered by their commander Macedo.

list.name: Sabinianus
list.note: Proclaimed at Carthage; crushed by the governor of Mauretania and handed over by his own followers.

list.name: Tiberius Claudius Marinus Pacatianus
list.note: Proclaimed by Danube troops in 248 (coins with ROMAE AETER AN MILL ET PRIMO); killed by his own men, which led Philip to send Decius to the Danube.

list.name: Marcus Fulvius Rufus Iotapianus
list.note: Claimed kinship with Severus Alexander; revolted against Philip's brother Priscus' exactions; killed by his own troops.

list.name: Julius Valens Licinianus
list.note: Proclaimed in Rome while Decius campaigned against the Goths; killed within days.

list.name: Titus Julius Priscus
list.note: Governor of Thrace who sided with the Goths at the fall of Philippopolis (250); declared hostis; probably died in 251.

list.name: Silbannacus
list.note: Known from two antoniniani (one found 1937); context and date (perhaps 253) uncertain.

list.name: Uranius Antoninus
list.note: Emesene priest-dynast (Sulpicius Antoninus) who repelled Shapur's attack on Emesa (253) and struck gold and silver coins; fate unknown.

list.name: Ingenuus
list.note: Governor of Pannonia proclaimed after news of Valerian's capture (or 258); defeated at Mursa by Gallienus' cavalry commander Aureolus; drowned himself or was killed.

list.name: Regalianus
list.note: Proclaimed by Ingenuus' surviving troops; coins struck at Carnuntum over Severan denarii; killed by his men or the Roxolani.

list.name: Macrianus Minor
list.note: Proclaimed with his brother Quietus after Valerian's capture, backed by their father Macrianus Major and the prefect Ballista; father and son defeated and killed in Illyricum by Aureolus, 261.

list.name: Quietus
list.note: Brother of Macrianus Minor, left in command at Emesa; killed there by the citizens with Odaenathus besieging, 261.

list.name: Postumus
list.note: Founder of the Gallic Empire (consuls, senate and mint at Colonia/Treveri). Killed by his own troops at Mogontiacum after refusing them the sack of the city, which had backed Laelianus.

list.name: Lucius Mussius Aemilianus
list.note: Prefect of Egypt who backed the Macriani then claimed the purple; defeated by Gallienus' general Theodotus, strangled in prison.

list.name: Aureolus
list.note: Gallienus' cavalry commander; declared for Postumus, then himself, at Milan. Surrendered to Claudius II after Gallienus' murder and was killed by the soldiers.

list.name: Laelianus
list.note: Rose against Postumus at Mogontiacum; defeated and killed.

list.name: Marius
list.note: Former smith (by tradition) who briefly succeeded Postumus; killed with a sword of his own making according to the HA; coinage implies a reign of some weeks.

list.name: Victorinus
list.note: Praetorian prefect of Postumus; besieged and sacked Augustodunum (270), which had appealed to Claudius II. Killed at Colonia by an officer (Attitianus) whose wife he seduced.

list.name: Domitianus II
list.note: Known from two coins (the second found at Chalgrove, Oxfordshire, 2003) and a literary mention; brief reign after Victorinus.

list.name: Tetricus I
list.note: Governor of Aquitania raised by Victoria; surrendered to Aurelian at the battle of Catalaunian Fields (Châlons) in 274, possibly by prior arrangement; walked in Aurelian's triumph and was made corrector Lucaniae.

list.name: Septimius
list.note: Proclaimed in Dalmatia during the Juthungian invasion of Italy; killed by his own troops.

list.name: Vaballathus
list.note: Son of Odaenathus; styled 'King of Kings' and corrector totius Orientis, then Augustus in 272 with his mother Zenobia as Augusta; fate after Aurelian's capture of Palmyra unknown.

list.name: Tetricus II
list.note: Son of Tetricus I, Caesar 273, perhaps Augustus 274; spared and later a senator.

list.name: Firmus
list.note: Merchant-supporter of Palmyra who allegedly held Alexandria against Aurelian (HA Firmus); possibly a corrector misrepresented as a usurper.

list.name: Bonosus
list.note: Rhine commander who rebelled after Germans burned the Rhine fleet; defeated by Probus and hanged himself ('an amphora hanging, not a man', HA).

list.name: Proculus
list.note: Rose at Lugdunum with Bonosus; betrayed by the Franks and killed.

list.name: Julius Saturninus
list.note: Moorish-born commander proclaimed in the East; killed at Apamea by Probus' troops.

list.name: Sabinus Julianus
list.note: Corrector Venetiae proclaimed on Numerian's death; defeated and killed by Carinus near Verona.

list.name: Carausius
list.note: Menapian commander of the Channel fleet; seized Britain c. 286, styled himself 'brother' of Diocletian and Maximian on coins (CARAUSIUS ET FRATRES SUI). Killed by his finance officer Allectus after losing Bononia (293).

list.name: Allectus
list.note: Carausius' rationalis and murderer; killed in battle against Constantius' prefect Asclepiodotus, who landed in fog past the British fleet off the Isle of Wight (296).

list.name: Lucius Domitius Domitianus
list.note: Proclaimed in Alexandria amid unrest over Diocletian's tax census; papyri show his regnal years; died during the revolt, succeeded by his corrector Achilleus.

list.name: Aurelius Achilleus
list.note: Led the Alexandrian resistance to Diocletian's eight-month siege; executed after the city fell (spring 298).

list.name: Eugenius
list.note: Tribune of 500 soldiers forced to dig the harbour; proclaimed, marched on Antioch, killed with his men by the citizens.

list.name: Lucius Domitius Alexander
list.note: Vicar of Africa who refused to send his son as hostage to Maxentius; cut off Rome's grain; strangled after Maxentius' prefect Rufius Volusianus took Carthage, which was sacked.

list.name: Valerius Valens
list.note: Dux limitis Daciae raised to Augustus by Licinius during the war of Cibalae; executed at Constantine's demand in the peace of Serdica (1 Mar 317).

list.name: Martinian
list.note: Licinius' magister officiorum raised to Augustus before Chrysopolis; spared at first, then put to death in Cappadocia 325.

list.name: Calocaerus
list.note: Magister pecoris camelorum who rose on Cyprus; suppressed by Constantine's half-brother Dalmatius and burned alive at Tarsus.

list.name: Magnentius
list.note: Germanic-born comes of the Ioviani and Herculiani, proclaimed at Augustodunum 18 Jan 350. Defeated at Mursa (28 Sep 351, among the bloodiest battles of the century) and Mons Seleucus (353); killed himself at Lugdunum 10 Aug 353.

list.name: Vetranio
list.note: Elderly magister peditum proclaimed at Mursa 1 Mar 350, perhaps at Constantina's prompting to block Magnentius; abdicated before the troops at Naissus 25 Dec 350 and retired to Prusa on a pension.

list.name: Julius Nepotianus
list.note: Nephew of Constantine; seized Rome with gladiators 3 Jun 350; killed after 28 days by Magnentius' officer Marcellinus, his head paraded on a lance.

list.name: Decentius
list.note: Brother or cousin of Magnentius, Caesar 351; hanged himself at Senones on news of Magnentius' death, 18 Aug 353.

list.name: Claudius Silvanus
list.note: Frankish magister peditum framed by forged letters; proclaimed at Colonia, killed after 28 days by men suborned by Ursicinus, whose staff included Ammianus (Amm. 15.5).

list.name: Procopius
list.note: Maternal relative of Julian; proclaimed at Constantinople 28 Sep 365 with Constantina's daughter displayed to the troops. Betrayed by his generals at Thyatira and Nacolia (May 366) and beheaded 27 May 366.

list.name: Marcellus
list.note: Procopius' relative and officer who claimed the purple after his execution; captured and killed by Equitius.

list.name: Firmus
list.note: Moorish prince (son of Nubel) who rebelled against the comes Romanus; his supporters may have proclaimed him; hunted down by Count Theodosius and hanged himself.

list.name: Magnus Maximus
list.note: Spanish-born commander in Britain, proclaimed 383; killed Gratian; recognized for a time by Theodosius; invaded Italy 387. Defeated at Siscia and Poetovio, executed at Aquileia 28 Aug 388. Welsh legend remembers him as Macsen Wledig.

list.name: Flavius Victor
list.note: Son of Magnus Maximus, co-Augustus; killed at Treveri by Arbogast after his father's death.

list.name: Eugenius
list.note: Rhetor made emperor by Arbogast 22 Aug 392; patron of the last pagan revival under Nicomachus Flavianus. Defeated at the Frigidus 6 Sep 394 and beheaded; Arbogast killed himself.

list.name: Gildo
list.note: Comes Africae who transferred allegiance to Arcadius and cut Rome's grain; defeated by his brother Mascezel and strangled himself or was killed at Tabraca. Did not claim the purple.

list.name: Marcus
list.note: Proclaimed by the British army in 406; killed by the troops.

list.name: Gratian (usurper)
list.note: British municipal (municeps) proclaimed after Marcus; killed after four months.

list.name: Constantine III
list.note: Soldier proclaimed in Britain for his name; crossed to Gaul after the Rhine crossing of 406 and was recognized by Honorius (409). Besieged at Arelate by Constantius, he surrendered on promise of life, was ordained, and executed before reaching Ravenna (Sep 411).

list.name: Constans (son of Constantine III)
list.note: Former monk made Caesar then Augustus by his father; killed at Vienne by Gerontius' troops 411.

list.name: Maximus of Hispania
list.note: Puppet of the general Gerontius 409-411, fled to the barbarians; re-emerged 420-422; displayed and executed at Ravenna at Honorius' tricennalia (422).

list.name: Priscus Attalus
list.note: Prefect of Rome made emperor by Alaric (Nov 409), deposed by him (Jul 410); raised again by Athaulf at Burdigala (414). Captured 416, paraded in Constantius' triumph, a finger cut off, exiled to Lipari.

list.name: Jovinus
list.note: Gallic noble proclaimed with Burgundian and Alan support (Gundahar, Goar); made his brother Sebastianus co-emperor; captured by Athaulf's Visigoths and beheaded at Narbo by the prefect Dardanus.

list.name: Sebastianus
list.note: Brother and co-Augustus of Jovinus; killed by the Visigoths.

list.name: Heraclianus
list.note: Comes Africae who executed Stilicho; consul 413; invaded Italy, was beaten at Utriculum, fled to Carthage and was beheaded there.

list.name: Joannes
list.note: Primicerius notariorum proclaimed at Rome on Honorius' death, refused recognition by Theodosius II. Betrayed at Ravenna to Aspar's army; hand cut off, paraded on an ass in the Hippodrome of Aquileia, beheaded (mid-425). Aetius arrived with 60,000 Huns three days late.

list.name: Basiliscus
list.note: Brother of Empress Verina; commander of the failed 468 Vandal expedition. Seized Constantinople Jan 475; his Encyclical alienated Chalcedonians. Surrendered to Zeno Aug 476 on promise of no bloodshed and was walled up in a dry cistern at Limnae in Cappadocia to die of starvation and exposure.

list.name: Marcianus
list.note: Son of the western emperor Anthemius and husband of Leo I's daughter Leontia; attacked the palace; ordained priest and exiled to Caesarea.

list.name: Leontius
list.note: Crowned at Tarsus by Verina at the instigation of the Isaurian general Illus; besieged at the fortress of Papyrius; beheaded with Illus 488.

list.name: Vitalian
list.note: Comes foederatorum who led a revolt of Bulgar and Hunnic foederati in the Chalcedonian cause, three times threatening Constantinople; his fleet burned in the Bosporus (515, by tradition with 'sulphur' devised by Proclus). Later consul (520), murdered in the palace in 520, Justinian suspected.

list.name: Hypatius
list.note: Nephew of Anastasius, crowned by the Nika rioters in the Hippodrome (18 Jan 532) against his will; executed the next day after Belisarius and Mundus massacred some 30,000 in the Hippodrome.

list.name: Stotzas
list.note: Leader of the great army mutiny in Byzantine Africa (from Easter 536); defeated by Belisarius and Germanus, fled to the Moors; killed at Thacia 545, mortally wounding the magister militum John.

list.name: Guntharic
list.note: Dux Numidiae who murdered the magister militum Areobindus and seized Carthage; killed at a banquet by the Armenian Artabanes after 36 days.

list.name: Titus Larcius Flavus
list.note: First dictator by Livy's preferred tradition (2.18); others named Manius Valerius. Threat from the Latins and Sabines. Dates of the earliest dictatorships are traditional.

list.name: Aulus Postumius Albus Regillensis
list.note: Victory over the Latins at Lake Regillus, where the Dioscuri reportedly fought for Rome (Livy dates it 499 or 496); vowed the temple of Castor.

list.name: Manius Valerius Volusus Maximus
list.note: Appointed during the debt crisis of the First Secession of the plebs; campaigned against the Sabines and resigned when the Senate rejected debt relief.

list.name: Gaius Aemilius Mamercus
list.note: Doubtful: inferred by Bendel from Lydus' 'dictator in the 48th year of the Republic' and the plague precedent invoked in 363; Broughton thinks Lydus confused an interrex.

list.name: Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus
list.note: Called from his four-iugera farm across the Tiber to rescue the consul Minucius trapped by the Aequi on Mount Algidus; triumphed and resigned after 16 days (Livy 3.26-29).

list.name: Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus
list.note: Second dictatorship, against the alleged regal ambitions of the grain-dealer Spurius Maelius, whom Ahala killed in the Forum. The story is probably an aetiology of the Aequimaelium.

list.name: Mamercus Aemilius Mamercinus
list.note: War with Fidenae and Veii after the murder of Roman envoys by Lars Tolumnius; Aulus Cornelius Cossus won the spolia opima.

list.name: Quintus Servilius Priscus Fidenas
list.note: Capture of Fidenae.

list.name: Mamercus Aemilius Mamercinus
list.note: Second dictatorship; reportedly carried a law limiting the censorship to 18 months.

list.name: Aulus Postumius Tubertus
list.note: Victory over Aequi and Volsci at Mount Algidus; said to have executed his son for leaving his post.

list.name: Mamercus Aemilius Mamercinus
list.note: Third dictatorship; final war with Fidenae, which was destroyed.

list.name: Quintus Servilius Priscus Fidenas
list.note: Second dictatorship; war with the Aequi; capture of Labici.

list.name: Publius Cornelius Rutilus Cossus
list.note: War with the Volsci and Aequi at Antium.

list.name: Marcus Furius Camillus
list.note: Captured Veii after the ten-year siege, reportedly by a tunnel under the temple of Juno; evocatio of Juno Regina to the Aventine.

list.name: Marcus Furius Camillus
list.note: Second dictatorship (Varronian 390 = c. 387/386): named in exile at Ardea after the Gallic sack; the tale of his rescuing the ransom gold ('non auro sed ferro') is later embroidery (Polybius knows the Gauls left with the gold).

list.name: Marcus Furius Camillus
list.note: Third dictatorship; victories over Volsci, Aequi and Etruscans.

list.name: Aulus Cornelius Cossus
list.note: War with the Volsci; imprisonment of Marcus Manlius Capitolinus for agitation over debt.

list.name: Titus Quinctius Cincinnatus Capitolinus
list.note: Victory over the Praenestines at the Allia; captured nine towns.

list.name: Marcus Furius Camillus
list.note: Fourth dictatorship; used against the Licinio-Sextian agitation; abdicated.

list.name: Publius Manlius Capitolinus
list.causa: seditionis sedandae et rei gerundae causa
list.note: Named a plebeian as magister equitum, a concession to the Licinio-Sextian movement.

list.name: Marcus Furius Camillus
list.note: Fifth dictatorship; defeated the Gauls near Alba; reconciled the orders and vowed the temple of Concord as the Licinio-Sextian laws opened the consulship to plebeians.

list.name: Lucius Manlius Capitolinus Imperiosus
list.note: Appointed to drive the nail in the Capitoline temple to end a plague; tried to wage war instead and was forced to resign.

list.name: Appius Claudius Crassus Regillensis
list.note: Victory over the Hernici. The magister's name is preserved in the Fasti only as SCA[.]VLA.

list.name: Titus Quinctius Pennus Capitolinus Crispinus
list.note: Gallic war: the single combat of Titus Manlius, who took the torque of a giant Gaul and the cognomen Torquatus.

list.name: Quintus Servilius Ahala
list.note: Defeated the Gauls at the Colline Gate.

list.name: Gaius Sulpicius Peticus
list.note: Victory over the Gauls.

list.name: Gaius Marcius Rutilus
list.note: First plebeian dictator; defeated the Etruscans and triumphed by vote of the people over the Senate's objection.

list.name: Titus Manlius Imperiosus Torquatus
list.note: War against Caere, which was granted a 100-year truce.

list.name: Gaius Julius Iulus
list.note: Rumoured Etruscan war; tried to secure two patrician consuls.

list.name: Marcus Fabius Ambustus
list.note: Held elections amid the patrician-plebeian struggle over the consulship.

list.name: Titus Manlius Imperiosus Torquatus
list.note: Second dictatorship.

list.name: Gaius Claudius Crassinus Regillensis (?)
list.note: Names missing from the Fasti and not stated by any ancient author.

list.name: Lucius Furius Camillus
list.note: Second dictatorship; war against the Aurunci; vowed the temple of Juno Moneta on the Arx.

list.name: Publius Valerius Poplicola
list.note: Appointed to institute a festival after prodigies (a rain of stones, darkness by day).

list.name: Marcus Valerius Corvus
list.note: Mutiny of the garrison of Campania; Corvus negotiated, and the leges Genuciae followed.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Crassus
list.note: Latin War; operations against Antium.

list.name: Quintus Publilius Philo
list.note: Carried the leges Publiliae: plebiscites binding on all, patrum auctoritas given in advance for centuriate laws, one censor to be plebeian.

list.name: Gaius Claudius Inregillensis
list.note: Abdicated, appointment found vitiated.

list.name: Publius Cornelius Rufinus
list.note: Abdicated on a religious flaw. The Fasti list 333 as the first of four 'dictator years' (333, 324, 309, 301) with a dictator and no consuls; Livy places these dictators under the preceding consuls. The dictator years are a later chronographic insertion.

list.name: Marcus Papirius Crassus
list.note: Gallic scare.

list.name: Gnaeus Quinctilius Varus
list.note: Nail-driving after the 'poisoning' scandal in which 170 matrons were condemned (Livy 8.18). Name possibly Gnaeus Quinctius Capitolinus.

list.name: Marcus Claudius Marcellus
list.note: Abdicated, appointment declared vitiated by the augurs.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Cursor
list.note: Second Samnite War. Papirius tried to execute his magister equitum Fabius for fighting (and winning) against orders; the people and Senate interceded (Livy 8.30-35). 324 is the second dictator year.

list.name: Aulus Cornelius Cossus Arvina
list.causa: rei gerundae or ludorum faciendorum causa
list.note: Sources conflict; most historians think he presided at the Ludi Romani when the praetor fell ill.

list.name: Quintus Fabius Ambustus
list.note: Abdicated on a flaw, in the year of the Caudine Forks.

list.name: Gaius Maenius
list.note: Livy describes an inquiry into conspiracies; causa disputed.

list.name: Titus Manlius Imperiosus Torquatus
list.note: Third dictatorship.

list.name: Lucius Aemilius Mamercinus Privernas
list.note: Second dictatorship; siege of Saticula.

list.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus
list.magisterEquitum: Quintus Aulius Cerretanus; Gaius Fabius Ambustus
list.note: Defeat at Lautulae, where the magister equitum Aulius fell; replaced by Gaius Fabius.

list.name: Gaius Maenius
list.note: Second dictatorship; inquiry into Capuan conspiracy.

list.name: Gaius Poetelius Libo Visolus
list.note: Capture of Nola per Livy and the Fasti; an alternative tradition makes him dictator clavi figendi causa, and Diodorus credits the victories to Quintus Fabius.

list.name: Gaius Sulpicius Longus
list.note: Livy instead names Junius Bubulcus dictator.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Cursor
list.note: Second dictatorship; great victory over the Samnites, whose gilded shields were displayed in the Forum (Livy 9.40). 309 is the third dictator year.

list.name: Gaius Junius Bubulcus Brutus
list.note: War with the Aequi, subdued in eight days (Livy 10.1).

list.name: Marcus Valerius Corvus
list.magisterEquitum: Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus (?) or Marcus Aemilius Paullus (?)
list.note: Second dictatorship; Etruscans and Marsi. 301 is the fourth and last dictator year.

list.name: Quintus Hortensius
list.note: Appointed during the last secession of the plebs (to the Janiculum); carried the lex Hortensia making plebiscites binding on the whole people. Died in office.

list.name: Appius Claudius Caecus (?)
list.note: Possibly dictator suffectus after Hortensius' death (Mommsen); known only from the elogium of Appius, which credits him with a dictatorship.

list.name: Marcus Aemilius Barbula (?)
list.note: Known only from literary sources; Broughton dates him 292-285.

list.name: Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus Maximus
list.note: Also the first plebeian censor to close a lustrum (280).

list.name: Publius Cornelius Rufinus (?)
list.note: Date uncertain (Broughton 292-285; Niebuhr 280, after Heraclea).

list.name: Gnaeus Fulvius Maximus Centumalus
list.note: Nail-driving during the First Punic War.

list.name: Quintus Ogulnius Gallus
list.note: To celebrate the Latin Festival on the Alban Mount in the consuls' absence.

list.name: Marcus Claudius Glicia
list.note: Named in contempt by the consul Publius Claudius Pulcher after his defeat at Drepana; a freedman's son and scribe, he was forced to resign but kept the right to the toga praetexta.

list.name: Aulus Atilius Calatinus
list.note: First dictator to command an army outside Italy (Sicily).

list.name: Tiberius Coruncanius
list.note: First plebeian pontifex maximus.

list.name: Gaius Duilius
list.note: Victor of Mylae (260), the first Roman naval triumph.

list.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus
list.note: Date inferred (Broughton): Livy calls 217 Fabius' second dictatorship, so a first must fall in the gap of 221-219. Plutarch (Marc. 5) tells of a dictator Minucius with Flaminius as magister who abdicated because a shrew squeaked, which may be the same episode.

list.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus
list.note: Elected by the people after Trasimene (Livy calls him prodictator). His delaying strategy earned him the name Cunctator; a plebiscite of the tribune Metilius gave Minucius equal imperium, the only time two dictators served together.

list.name: Lucius Veturius Philo
list.note: Abdicated after 14 days on a flaw.

list.name: Marcus Junius Pera
list.note: After Cannae; enrolled 8,000 slaves (volones), debtors and convicts, and took arms from the temples.

list.name: Marcus Fabius Buteo
list.note: Unique causa: named, without a magister equitum, to fill the Senate's 177 vacancies after Cannae; resigned the same day (Livy 23.22-23). Two dictators held office simultaneously.

list.name: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus
list.note: Nominated by the consul Laevinus amid a quarrel over the right of nomination.

list.name: Titus Manlius Torquatus
list.causa: comitiorum habendorum et ludorum faciendorum causa
list.note: After the death of the consul Marcellus in an ambush near Venusia.

list.name: Marcus Livius Salinator
list.note: Victor of the Metaurus that year.

list.name: Gaius Servilius Geminus
list.note: Last traditional dictatorship; the office then lapsed for 120 years, replaced in emergencies by the senatus consultum ultimum.

list.name: Lucius Cornelius Sulla Felix
list.causa: legibus scribundis et rei publicae constituendae causa
list.note: Appointed under the lex Valeria proposed by the interrex Flaccus, without time limit. Used it for proscriptions and a constitutional overhaul (courts to senators, tribunate gutted, Senate doubled to c. 600, 20 quaestors). Resigned probably early 79 (or 81).

list.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
list.note: First dictatorship, 11 days, named by the praetor Lepidus under a special law to hold the consular elections; also passed debt and amnesty measures.

list.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
list.note: Second dictatorship (Oct 48 to late 47), voted after Pharsalus.

list.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
list.note: Third dictatorship, voted after Thapsus in April 46 for ten years, renewed annually.

list.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
list.magisterEquitum: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus (designated: Gaius Octavius; Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus, non iniit)
list.note: Perpetual dictator from c. Feb 44 (DICT PERPETVO on coins); assassinated 15 Mar 44. The lex Antonia then abolished the dictatorship for ever; Augustus refused it in 22 BC.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Mugillanus and Lucius Sempronius Atratinus
list.note: First censors, created to relieve the consuls (or consular tribunes) of the census (Livy 4.8). Both patrician.

list.name: Gaius Furius Paculus Fusus and Marcus Geganius Macerinus
list.note: Built the Villa Publica on the Campus Martius, where the census was taken.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Crassus (?) and Publius Pinarius Mamercinus (?)
list.note: Uncertain pair.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Mugillanus and unknown
list.note: Mugillanus' second censorship.

list.name: Marcus Furius Camillus and Marcus Postumius Albinus Regillensis
list.note: Imposed a tax on bachelors (aes uxorium) per Valerius Maximus and Plutarch.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Cursor and Gaius Julius Iullus
list.note: Julius died in office and Marcus Cornelius Maluginensis was elected suffect; Rome was taken by the Gauls during that lustrum, after which a censor's death in office required both to resign.

list.name: Marcus Furius Fusus (?) and Lucius Papirius Mugillanus (?)
list.note: Uncertain.

list.name: Spurius Postumius Albinus Regillensis and Gaius Sulpicius Camerinus
list.note: Postumius died; no suffect appointed, the censors resigned and the census lapsed.

list.name: Spurius Servilius Priscus and Quintus Cloelius Siculus
list.note: Census impeded by war and debt agitation.

list.name: Gaius Sulpicius Peticus and Postumius Regillensis Albinus (?)
Marcus Fabius Ambustus and Lucius Furius Medullinus
Gnaeus Manlius Capitolinus Imperiosus and Gaius Marcius Rutilus
list.note: Marcius was the first plebeian censor.

list.name: Lucius Cornelius Scipio and Publius Cornelius Scipio (?)
Spurius Postumius Albinus Caudinus and Quintus Publilius Philo
list.note: Enrolled new citizens in two new tribes (Maecia and Scaptia).

list.name: Lucius Papirius Crassus and Gaius Maenius
list.note: Two new tribes (Oufentina and Falerna).
